title: No Arkansas Rule on How Rent Must Be Paid
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute that requires you to accept, or forbids you to refuse, cash, checks, money orders, cards or electronic payment for rent, and none that bars or caps a fee for a particular payment method. Name the accepted methods in the lease. Rent is due at the time and place the lease sets; if the lease names no place and you have not told the tenant otherwise in writing, rent is payable at the dwelling unit.

If you take payment by check, a dishonored check carries the remedies in Arkansas's check statutes (see the returned-payment row). During an eviction in which the tenant raises defenses, you must give a written receipt for each rent payment the tenant makes, except a payment by check. The same rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Arkansas Algorithmic Rent-Setting Law
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that bans or regulates setting rents with algorithmic pricing or revenue-management software. Federal antitrust law still applies to any agreement among competing landlords to coordinate rents, and Arkansas's general antitrust statutes were not reviewed here, so do not share nonpublic rent or occupancy data with competitors through a pricing service, and set your own rents. Arkansas law also bars cities and counties from controlling the amount of rent (see the rent-control row). This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Application Fees: No State Cap; Local Limits Preempted
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that caps rental application or screening fees, requires a refund of an unused fee, requires a pre-application disclosure of rent, fees or screening criteria, or makes you hold or refund fees in applicant order. Cities, counties and other local governments may not enact, keep or enforce an ordinance that would control the amount charged for rental application fees, so no local cap applies either. Charge a fee that reflects your actual screening cost, state it and your screening criteria in writing before you take it, and apply the same criteria to every applicant, because fair-housing law still governs how you screen. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Statutory Order for Applying Payments
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that sets the order in which you must apply a tenant's payment among rent, late charges and other amounts, so the lease may set the order. Under the Arkansas landlord-tenant act, late charges count as rent but other charges (such as fees or reimbursements) do not, and you may end the lease if rent is not paid within five days after it is due. Applying payments to the oldest regular rent first keeps the record of what rent is unpaid clear if you later rely on nonpayment. The same rules apply to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Collection Costs: Put Them in the Lease
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that sets or bars a fee for collecting past-due rent, so you may recover collection costs only to the extent the lease provides for them or a statute allows them. Two statutes allow specific recoveries. For a dishonored check, the check statute lets you recover the check amount plus a collection fee of no more than $30 and the bank's fees (see the returned-payment row). For attorney fees, the landlord-tenant act allows reasonable fees when the tenant's nonpayment is not in good faith or a non-rent breach is willful, but only if an attorney represents you, and a general statute lets a court award the winning party a reasonable fee in a breach-of-contract case unless the lease or another law provides otherwise. If you hire a collection agency, Arkansas's debt-collection law bars a debt collector from collecting any fee or charge beyond the debt unless the agreement creating the debt expressly authorizes it or law permits it, so list any collection charge expressly in the lease. You are not a debt collector when you collect your own rent in your own name, but you can become one if you use a name suggesting that someone else is collecting. A property manager collecting rent for an owner is not a debt collector for amounts that were not past due when the manager took on the account. The library's default clause lets you recover reasonable costs and expenses, and lets the winning side in a lease lawsuit recover attorney's fees; the library does not offer a separate fixed collection-fee clause for Arkansas, so if you want one, add your own clause and take advice first.

title: Money Due at Signing: The Deposit Cap Counts Every Security Payment
bodyText:
Arkansas does not limit how much rent you collect in advance or list what may be due at signing, but the deposit cap reaches any money you hold as security, whatever you call it: a security deposit, pet deposit, cleaning deposit or last-month deposit held to secure the tenant's performance all count together toward the limit of two months' periodic rent. First month's rent paid at signing is rent, not a deposit.

If you collect last month's rent up front, treat it as rent for that month and keep the total of all security money within the cap; if you instead hold it as security, it counts toward the cap and must be returned or accounted for within 60 days after the tenancy ends. Unless the lease says otherwise, rent is payable at the start of each month (or at the start of a shorter term).

These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. If the cap does not apply, state in the lease what each upfront payment is for.

title: No Arkansas Rental Fee-Disclosure or All-In Pricing Law
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that requires an all-in rent figure, a first-page fee disclosure, a total-price advertisement or a list of mandatory fees in a residential lease. Arkansas's Deceptive Trade Practices Act bars deceptive and unconscionable practices in business and trade, but its definitions of goods and services do not clearly say whether it reaches a residential lease of real property, and case law on the point was not checked, so treat it as possibly applying. List every fee in the lease with its amount and purpose, and advertise rent with any mandatory monthly fee shown alongside it. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Specific Rule on Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that specifically bars charging a tenant for a service you do not provide. Every duty and remedy under the Arkansas landlord-tenant act carries an obligation of good faith, and a fee for a service that is never delivered invites a challenge as a breach of the lease. Charge only for services you actually provide and describe each one in the lease. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Which Charges Count as Rent in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas uses two definitions of rent. Under the landlord-tenant act, rent is what the tenant pays for use of the premises, and it includes late charges but excludes security deposits and other charges. So an unpaid late charge is unpaid rent for the five-day nonpayment termination rule, but other fees (pet fees, utility reimbursements, repair charges) are not, and calling them additional rent in the lease may not change that, because no Arkansas statute lets the lease redefine rent. Treat an unpaid non-rent fee as a lease breach, which needs a written notice giving the tenant 14 days to cure before the lease ends. Under the security-deposit statute, rent means all payments due under the rental agreement, so recurring charges may count when measuring the two-month deposit cap; measure the cap on base monthly rent to be safe. These rules apply to every tenancy type.

title: Passing Local Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that lets or forbids a landlord to pass a local government fee (such as a rental registration, inspection or permit fee) on to the tenant. Such a charge is a lease term like any other: you may recover it only if the lease says so, and during a fixed term you cannot add it unless the lease already provides for it. For a month-to-month (30 days) or week-to-week (7 days) tenancy, you can add it for the future only by ending the tenancy with the required written notice and offering new terms. A city that runs a rental inspection program can require nonresident owners to name an agent for service of process. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Late Fees: No Statutory Cap, and an Unpaid Late Fee Is Rent
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute that caps residential late fees, sets a grace period, or requires notice before you charge one. Charge a late fee only if the lease provides for it, and state the amount and when it applies. Under the Arkansas landlord-tenant act, late charges are part of rent, so an unpaid late fee counts as unpaid rent. The five days the act gives before you may terminate for nonpayment is a termination rule, not a late-fee grace period.

Courts can refuse to enforce a late fee that works as a penalty rather than a reasonable estimate of your loss, so set a modest flat fee charged once per late payment. Accepting rent after you have started an eviction does not waive the eviction; outside that rule, accepting late rent without objection can be argued as a waiver, so keep the lease's non-waiver sentence.

Arkansas law says only that rent is payable at the time and place agreed, so if you want rent falling due on a weekend or holiday to roll forward to the next business day, or not, say so in the lease. The same rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Statutory Late-Fee Limit in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that limits the amount of a residential late fee, whether as a dollar cap, a percentage of rent, a daily fee or a grace period; the only late-fee cap Arkansas sets for renting space applies to self-storage units. A late fee is enforceable as a lease term, but a court can refuse a fee that is a penalty, so keep it modest and charge it once per late payment. See the late-fee row for how late fees count as rent. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Rule Comparing Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Terms
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that bars terms more burdensome for a month-to-month tenant than for a fixed-term tenant, or caps the rent difference between lease types. You may charge different rent or set different terms for different lease lengths. If the lease fixes no definite term, the tenancy is month to month (week to week for a roomer who pays weekly), and either side may end it by written notice given at least 30 days (7 days for week to week) before the termination date. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Arkansas Rule on Rent Concessions
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on rent concessions, such as free months or move-in credits. A concession is a lease term: write it into the lease, saying which periods are free or reduced and whether any part must be repaid if the tenant leaves early, so there is no dispute about the rent actually owed. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Rent Control Is Preempted in Arkansas; Emergency Price Limits Apply
bodyText: Arkansas has no statewide rent control, and cities, counties and other local governments may not enact, keep or enforce any ordinance or resolution that would control the amount charged for rent, rental application fees or rental deposits; the only limit on deposits is the state's two-month cap. The preemption covers landlords, owners, property managers, tenants and prospective tenants. One state limit does reach rent: after the President or Governor proclaims a state of emergency, or a city or county declares a local emergency, for a tornado, flood, fire, storm or other disaster (the statute links the two declarations with "and"; treat either one as enough), it is unlawful for 30 days (extendable in 30-day steps) to rent housing for more than 10% above the price you charged immediately before the proclamation, unless the increase is directly attributable to added costs. Apply that limit to new leases and to any increase on an existing tenancy during the emergency period.

title: No Bar on Collecting Rent for a Defective Unit
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that bars you from demanding or collecting rent while a unit has code violations or is uninhabitable. The opposite rule applies: a tenant may not withhold or offset rent for a breach of Arkansas's implied quality standards, and the tenant's remedy for an unrepaired defect (if rent is current, the defect is not excused, for example tenant-caused or entry refused, and you do not fix it within 30 calendar days after receiving the tenant's written notice) is to end the lease without penalty and get back the deposit refundable under the deposit statute. If you sue for possession and the tenant raises defenses, the tenant must keep paying you the rent as it comes due, and either pay the rent you claim was owed before the order or, if the court allows, submit a receipt or cancelled check showing it was paid, or the court issues a writ of possession. Local housing codes may set stricter standards. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Mid-Term Rent Increases Need a Lease Clause
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on rent escalation clauses and no general anti-retaliation statute with a safe harbor that depends on one. During a fixed term, you may raise rent only if the lease provides for it (for example a scheduled step-up or a clause allowing an increase on notice); without that, the agreed rent holds until the term ends. A month-to-month or week-to-week rent can be changed for the future by ending the tenancy with written notice at least 30 or 7 days before the termination date and offering a new rent. Do not raise rent because a tenant reported a lead hazard or used fair-housing rights, or because a tenant is a domestic-abuse victim; those specific protections apply. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Rent-Increase Notice Period; Use the Termination Notice
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that sets a notice period for a rent increase, for any type of tenancy. During a fixed term, rent can rise only as the lease allows. For a month-to-month tenancy, give written notice at least 30 days before the date the old terms end and the new rent starts; for a week-to-week tenancy, at least 7 days; these are the periods for ending the tenancy, and a tenant who stays on after that date with your consent holds on the new terms. There is no separate duty to give notice that you will not renew a fixed-term lease, though giving it avoids holdover disputes. During a declared emergency, a separate Arkansas price-gouging law bars increasing the price of rental housing by more than 10% (see the rent-control row). This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Rent Installments Are a Lease Choice
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on splitting rent into installments. Unless the lease or your written notice says otherwise, rent is payable at the dwelling unit, at the beginning of any term of one month or less, and otherwise in equal monthly installments at the beginning of each month. The lease may set a different schedule, such as two payments a month; say in the lease that payments on that schedule are not partial payments and when a late fee applies to each one. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: When and Where Rent Is Due in Arkansas
bodyText: Rent is payable without demand or notice at the time and place the lease sets. If the lease does not say and you have not told the tenant otherwise in writing, rent is payable at the dwelling unit, at the start of any term of one month or less, and otherwise in equal monthly installments at the start of each month. State the due date, amount and payment place or method in the lease. If rent is not paid within five days after it is due, you may terminate the lease, and nonpayment for five days also counts as legal notice of your right to start an eviction. The same rules apply to fixed-term, month-to-month and week-to-week tenancies.

title: Rent Receipts: Required Only During an Eviction
bodyText: Arkansas has no general duty to give a receipt for rent, even for cash. One rule applies during an eviction case in which the tenant raises defenses or counterclaims: the tenant must keep paying rent as it comes due, and you must give the tenant a written receipt for each payment, except a payment by check. Give a written or electronic receipt for every cash payment anyway, since it is your best proof of what was paid. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Arkansas Rent-Reporting Law
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that requires you to offer positive rent reporting to credit bureaus, or that restricts reporting rent payment history. If you report, federal consumer-reporting law governs accuracy and disputes. Disclose any reporting program in the lease. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Taxes on Rent: Short-Term Lodging Is Outside the Landlord-Tenant Act
bodyText: Arkansas's state gross receipts tax reaches the furnishing of rooms, rental houses and other accommodations to transient guests, meaning people who rent somewhere other than their regular home on less than a month-to-month basis. County and city lodging taxes, where a county or city has levied them, reach hotel, motel, house, cabin, condominium and similar rentals but exclude rentals of 30 days or more. The Arkansas landlord-tenant act itself does not apply to transient occupancy subject to a lodging tax. An ordinary lease of the tenant's home on a month-to-month or fixed-term basis is not a transient rental under these sections, so do not add a tax charge to it. A week-to-week tenancy of the tenant's regular home is not a rental to transient guests for the state tax, but the local lodging taxes turn on rentals of under 30 days, so check with your city and county before renting by the week. If you rent short stays, check with the Department of Finance and Administration and your city and county about gross receipts and lodging taxes before you charge or collect any tax.

title: No Rule Requiring Fees to Be Listed in the Lease
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that requires a residential lease to list every fee or charge, or that sets a notice period before you add one. In practice you may collect a fee only if the lease provides for it, and you cannot add a new fee during a fixed term unless the lease allows it. For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, a new fee can be added for the future only with the 30-day or 7-day written termination notice and new terms. List each fee, its amount and its purpose in the lease. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Bounced Rent Checks: $30 Collection Fee and Statutory Remedies
bodyText:
If a tenant's rent check is returned for insufficient funds, Arkansas's check statute lets you send a written demand to the address on the check or the tenant's last known address; the tenant then has 15 days to pay the check amount, a collection fee of no more than $30, and any fees your bank charged. If the tenant still has not paid 30 days after a demand sent by certified mail, return receipt requested, the tenant is liable for twice the check amount (at least $50) plus the collection fee and bank fees, and the winner of a later suit may recover court costs and attorney fees.

Writing a check for rent knowing there are insufficient funds, with intent to defraud, is also a crime under the Hot Check Law, which also reaches other forms of presentment that transmit account information.

Set any returned-payment fee in the lease at no more than $30 plus your actual bank charges; the $30 limit is written for checks drawn on a bank, so for a failed electronic payment use the same limit to be safe. You may require future payments by certified funds if the lease says so. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Government-Shutdown Rent Protection in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that delays rent, bars late fees or limits eviction for federal or state workers affected by a government shutdown. Arkansas's military relief act protects service members on state active duty in other ways (see the military rows). Consider a written payment plan for an affected tenant. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Arkansas's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Arkansas sets few money limits on residential leases. Security deposit: no more than two months' periodic rent, whatever you call the money, with a tenant whose deposit is wrongfully withheld able to recover the amount withheld plus twice that amount, costs and attorney's fees (only costs and the amount withheld if you prove a bona fide error despite reasonable procedures or a good-faith dispute over the amount); these deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. Bounced check: a collection fee of no more than $30 plus bank fees, and twice the check (at least $50) after an unanswered certified-mail demand. Willful holdover: up to three months' periodic rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees. Interest under a contract: no more than 17% a year. Emergency price gouging: for 30 days after a declared emergency (longer if extended), no more than a 10% increase in the price of rental housing over the price just before the declaration, unless you can prove the increase is directly attributable to added costs (and even then the price may be no more than 10% above your cost plus your usual markup). There is no cap on late fees, application fees or rent, and local governments may not set any limit on rent, application fees or deposits.

title: No Subsidy Proration Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on reducing or prorating rent for a subsidized tenant when part of the unit becomes uninhabitable, and no general rent-abatement rule: a tenant may not withhold rent for a breach of the implied quality standards, and the tenant's remedy for an unrepaired defect is to end the lease. Federal program rules (such as Housing Choice Voucher abatement) may apply to a subsidized tenancy and are not covered here. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Subsidy Late-Fee Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on late fees for the part of rent a housing subsidy pays, and no residential late-fee cap. Charge any late fee only on the tenant's own share, since the tenant does not control the agency's payment; federal program rules and your housing assistance contract may limit fees and are not covered here. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Passing Property-Tax Increases to Tenants
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that permits, forbids or regulates a lease clause passing real estate tax increases to a residential tenant. It is a contract term: you may pass on an increase during a fixed term only if the lease says so, stating how the tenant's share is figured and when it is billed. For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, you can raise rent for the future with the 30-day or 7-day written termination notice. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Damages
bodyText: Arkansas has no landlord-tenant statute on interest on unpaid rent or damages. If the lease sets an interest rate on past-due amounts, the Arkansas Constitution caps interest on contracts like a lease at 17% a year; any higher rate is unlawful. If the lease names no rate, the default rate on a contract is 6% a year. State any rate in the lease, keep it well under 17%, and do not combine it with a late fee in a way that exceeds the cap on the same amount. The cap and the default rate are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Move-In Condition Form: Optional but Protective
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute that requires a move-in or move-out inspection, a written inventory or a condition checklist for security deposits.

One statute rewards a move-in form: for a lease entered or renewed after November 1, 2021, you are treated as having met Arkansas's implied quality standards at move-in (water, electricity, potable water, code sewer and plumbing, roof and building envelope, and existing heating and air conditioning) if, when possession is available, you give the tenant a written form for listing defects in those items and the tenant signs it without noting a defect and moves in, or does not return it within two business days.

Use one form that covers both those items and the general condition of the unit, and keep the signed copy; it is also your best evidence for any later deposit deduction for damage. The deposit rules themselves do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The rule applies to fixed-term and periodic leases alike; it does not apply to a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right.

title: No Pre-Set Deduction Schedule Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that allows or forbids a lease schedule of preset deposit charges (such as carpet cleaning). Whatever the lease says, you may keep deposit money only for accrued unpaid rent and for damages you suffer because the tenant did not comply with the lease, itemized in a written notice. A preset charge works only as a reasonable estimate of real damage from a lease breach; a flat charge taken regardless of condition risks being treated as wrongful withholding, for which the tenant may recover the amount withheld plus damages of twice that amount, costs and reasonable attorney's fees (you owe only costs and the amount withheld if you prove the error happened despite procedures reasonably designed to avoid it, or that you withheld in a good-faith dispute over the amount). These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: If you mail the deposit refund and itemized notice by first-class mail to the tenant's last known address, you have met the return deadline. If the letter with the payment comes back and you cannot find the tenant after reasonable effort, the payment becomes your property 180 days after the date you mailed it. Keep the returned envelope and a record of your search. Arkansas's Unclaimed Property Act separately treats a security deposit or refund held in the course of business as presumed abandoned three years after it becomes payable; the two statutes have not been reconciled by the legislature, so follow the 180-day steps exactly, and if they do not apply (for example, the tenant never cashed a refund check that was not returned), treat the money as unclaimed property. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. Those exempt owners should treat an unclaimed refund under the Unclaimed Property Act. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Deposit Installment Right
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that gives a tenant the right to pay a security deposit in installments, or that bars you from offering it. If you agree to installments, write the schedule into the lease; the total of all security money still may not exceed two months' periodic rent. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Last Month's Rent and the Deposit
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that restricts how you apply a last-month's-rent deposit, and none that requires you to let a tenant use the security deposit as the final month's rent. You may refuse that use; the tenant owes the last month's rent when due, and you account for the deposit within 60 days after the tenancy ends. Money you hold as security, whatever its label, counts toward the two-month cap. One exception: a service member who ends a lease under Arkansas's military relief act pays the current and next month's rent with the notice, and any prepaid rent, security deposit or other sums you hold may be deducted from those payments. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Advance-Notice Condition on the Deposit Refund
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that lets you make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of move-out or a forwarding address, and none that requires a move-out inspection notice. Your duty is to return the deposit, less itemized deductions for accrued unpaid rent and damages from the tenant's breach, within 60 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant delivers possession; mailing the notice and payment by first-class mail to the tenant's last known address counts as compliance. Ask for a forwarding address in the lease, but do not withhold the refund for lack of one. A notice the lease requires to end the tenancy is separate: a tenant who leaves without it may owe rent, which you may deduct as accrued unpaid rent. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Special Deposit Timing After a Domestic-Abuse Move-Out
bodyText: Arkansas gives a domestic-abuse victim no statutory right to end a lease early and sets no special deposit timing when a tenancy ends because of domestic abuse. If the tenancy ends (by agreement, notice or court order), the ordinary rule applies: return the deposit, less itemized deductions, within 60 days after termination and delivery of possession. Arkansas does bar you from ending, not renewing, refusing or otherwise retaliating in a tenancy because a tenant, applicant or household member is a victim of domestic abuse documented in a court order within the preceding 60 days (or within 60 days after a tenancy ended because of the abuse) (see the domestic-abuse rows). These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Returning the Deposit Early
bodyText: Arkansas has no expedited deposit procedure and no statute allowing an administrative or processing fee for early handling. You may return the deposit sooner than the 60-day limit, but deductions are limited to accrued unpaid rent and damages from the tenant's breach of the lease, itemized in a written notice; do not deduct a processing fee. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Arkansas Rule on Deposit-Alternative Fees
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on fees charged instead of a security deposit (deposit-alternative or surety programs). Offer such a program only as an option, explain in writing that the fee is not refundable and does not limit the tenant's liability for damage, and remember that any money you hold to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit whatever you call it, counting toward the two-month cap and subject to the 60-day return rule. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Furnished-Rental Rules
bodyText:
Arkansas has no special rules for furnished rentals: the deposit cap is the same two months' periodic rent, with no separate furniture deposit, and Arkansas's implied quality standards do not list furniture or appliances. List the furniture you provide in the lease and note its condition on your move-in form; you may deduct from the deposit for damage to it caused by the tenant's breach of the lease, itemized in writing.

These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on holding deposits or other money taken before a lease is signed. The deposit statute governs money held as security from a tenant under a rental agreement, so once the lease is signed, any holding money you keep as security counts toward the two-month cap and the 60-day return rule. Put a holding deposit agreement in writing: say what it holds, whether it becomes part of the security deposit or first month's rent, and when it will be refunded if the applicant is denied or you do not offer the lease. Local governments may not regulate the amount of rental deposits. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Inspection-Notice Penalty
bodyText: Arkansas has no move-in or move-out inspection-notice duty for deposits, so there is no penalty, such as losing the right to deduct, for not offering an inspection. The penalty that applies is tied to the refund: if you wrongfully keep deposit money, the tenant can recover it plus twice the amount wrongfully withheld, costs and attorney fees, unless you show a bona fide error despite reasonable procedures or a good-faith dispute over the amount. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that permits nonrefundable deposits or requires a notice for them. Money you hold to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit whatever you call it, so a "nonrefundable deposit" still counts toward the two-month cap and must be returned within 60 days less only itemized unpaid rent and damages. If you want a charge you keep, make it a fee for a stated service (such as a pet or cleaning fee), name it a fee, not a deposit, and state that it is not refundable. Whether a particular fee is really a disguised deposit is a question for the courts. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Separate Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice
bodyText: Arkansas has no rule requiring a separate written notice, when you collect a deposit, that part of it is nonrefundable, because no Arkansas statute recognizes a nonrefundable deposit. Money you hold to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit whatever you call it, so a "nonrefundable deposit" still counts toward the two-month cap and must be returned within 60 days less only itemized unpaid rent and damages. If you want a charge you keep, make it a fee for a stated service (such as a pet or cleaning fee), name it a fee, not a deposit, and state that it is not refundable. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Deposit Cap: Two Months' Periodic Rent
bodyText:
You may not demand or receive a security deposit of more than two months' periodic rent, however the money is labeled, so a security deposit, pet deposit, key deposit or any other money held as security count together. The cap is the same for fixed-term and month-to-month tenancies; for a week-to-week tenancy the statute still says two months' rent, so keep the total at or under about eight and a half weeks' rent (or lower to be safe). Because the deposit statute treats all payments under the lease as rent, measure the cap on the base monthly rent to be safe. Cities and counties may not set a lower limit; the state cap is the only control.

These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. Even if the cap does not apply, a very large deposit may be hard to justify.

title: No Escrow or Separate-Account Rule for Deposits
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that requires you to keep security deposits in a separate, escrow or trust account, to tell the tenant where the deposit is held, or to post a bond. Keep deposits in a separate account anyway, with a ledger for each tenant, so you can return them on time; if you sell the property, the buyer becomes bound by the deposit rules. A licensed property manager may be subject to trust-account rules under the real estate license law, which are not covered here. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Interest Owed on Deposits
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to pay interest on a tenant's security deposit, whatever the length of the tenancy. If you promise interest in the lease, you must pay it as promised. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Don't Ask Tenants to Waive Deposit Rights
bodyText: Arkansas's deposit statute has no waiver section of its own, but the Arkansas landlord-tenant act forbids a lease in which the landlord or tenant agrees to waive or give up any right, duty or remedy available under the act, and the act makes the deposit statute the source of the parties' deposit rights. Treat the deposit rules (the two-month cap, 60-day itemized return and the double-damages remedy) as rights the tenant cannot give up in the lease, and do not include a clause waiving them. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Selling a Rental: The Buyer Is Bound by the Deposit Rules
bodyText: Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends (a buyer, assignee or other successor) is bound by Arkansas's deposit rules, including the 60-day itemized return and the double-damages remedy. The statute does not say whether the seller is released or how the money must move, so when you sell, transfer each tenant's deposit to the buyer at closing, get the buyer's written assumption of the deposit obligations, and tell the tenant in writing who now holds the deposit. When you buy, insist on receiving the deposits or a credit for them. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Penalty for Mishandling a Deposit: Double the Amount Withheld
bodyText: If you fail to comply with Arkansas's deposit rules (for example, you exceed the two-month cap or do not return the deposit with an itemized notice within 60 days), the tenant may recover the money and property due, damages of twice the amount wrongfully withheld, costs and reasonable attorney fees. Your liability drops to costs and the amount wrongly withheld if you prove the failure came from an error despite procedures reasonably designed to avoid it, or from a good-faith dispute over the amount due. Either side keeps any other remedy the law allows, such as suing the tenant for damages above the deposit. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. The deposit rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Returning the Deposit in Arkansas: 60 Days, Itemized Notice, Double Damages
bodyText:
Arkansas's security deposit statute covers every landlord except an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or run, owns five or fewer dwelling units; that exemption is lost for any unit managed (including rent collection) by a third person for a fee.

If the statute covers you, you must return the deposit within 60 days after the tenancy ends. You may keep only accrued unpaid rent and damages you suffered because the tenant did not comply with the rental agreement, and you must list each deduction in a written, itemized notice delivered with the balance. Mailing the notice and any refund by first-class mail to the tenant's last known address counts as compliance, so keep proof of mailing.

If the refund letter comes back and you cannot find the tenant after a reasonable effort, the money becomes yours 180 days after you mailed it; the state's unclaimed property act separately lists security deposits and refunds as reportable property, so keep a record of your search and the returned envelope.

If you fail to comply, the tenant can recover the deposit owed, damages of twice the amount wrongfully withheld, costs and reasonable attorney's fees; you owe only costs and the amount withheld if you prove the error happened despite procedures reasonably designed to avoid it, or that you withheld in a good-faith dispute over the amount. Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends (for example a buyer) is bound by these rules.

The 60 days run from the end of the tenancy: the end of a fixed term, the date in a 7-day (week-to-week) or 30-day (month-to-month) termination notice, or an earlier termination. If you are exempt, return the deposit as your lease says; following the same 60-day itemized process is the safe course.

title: What an Arkansas Deposit May Be Used For
bodyText:
Arkansas's security deposit statute covers every landlord except an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer dwelling units and does not pay a third person to manage them.

For covered landlords, the deposit may be applied only to accrued unpaid rent and to damages you actually suffered because the tenant did not comply with the rental agreement, each itemized in the written notice you send within 60 days after the tenancy ends.

The statute does not mention ordinary wear and tear, but wear and tear is not a tenant's noncompliance, so do not charge for it. Cleaning can be charged only where the tenant left the unit less clean than the lease or the tenant's statutory duty to keep it reasonably clean requires, and only at what it actually cost. No statute addresses pre-set cleaning or repair charges; because the deposit may cover only damages you suffered, a flat fee that exceeds your actual cost risks being treated as wrongfully withheld (twice that amount in damages, plus costs and fees, unless you prove a bona fide error despite reasonable procedures or a good-faith dispute over the amount). The cautious course is to deduct actual, documented costs.

If a tenant whose rent is current ends the lease because you did not fix a defect in one of the six implied quality standards that was not excused (for example, tenant-caused or entry refused) within 30 calendar days after receiving the tenant's written notice, the tenant is entitled to the deposit refundable under the deposit statute; if you met those standards you may still apply the deposit to damage to the premises. A service member terminating under the state military lease law may have the deposit deducted from the rent payment that law requires. Exempt landlords should follow the same practice and the lease.

title: No Deposit-Standards Disclosure Rule in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring you to post or give tenants the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if you charge different tenants different deposits; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. What applies instead: if the deposit statute covers you (every landlord except an individual who, with a spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units and does not pay a third person to manage them), no deposit, however it is labelled, may exceed two months' periodic rent. Fair housing law reaches nearly every landlord (each Arkansas fair housing statute has its own narrow exemptions, and a landlord exempt from one is usually still covered by another: the Fair Housing Commission law exempts rooms or units in an owner-occupied building of up to four units and a single-family house rented without a broker or discriminatory advertising by an owner of no more than three such houses; the Arkansas Fair Housing Act exempts only an owner-occupied two-family building, a room in a home where the owner or family lives, and the owner's own home rented for up to 12 months while temporarily away; and the Arkansas Civil Rights Act has no small-landlord exemption), so treat it as applying to you: you may not set different deposit terms because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin. Writing your deposit standards down and applying them the same way to every applicant is the safe practice.

title: Utility Deposits You Hold: Treat Them as Part of the Security Deposit
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on a separate utility deposit that a landlord collects from a tenant; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. What applies instead: a deposit you take to secure the tenant's payment of utilities under the lease secures performance of the rental agreement, and the deposit statute caps a security deposit 'however denominated'. So treat a utility deposit as part of the security deposit: if the deposit statute covers you (every landlord except an individual who, with a spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units and does not pay a third person to manage them), the utility deposit and all other deposits together may not exceed two months' periodic rent, and any amount you keep for unpaid utility charges the tenant owed under the lease must be itemized in the written notice sent with the balance within 60 days after the tenancy ends. Deposits a utility company itself requires are set by the utility and its regulators, not by landlord-tenant law.

title: Tenant Alterations in Arkansas: What the Lease Can and Cannot Block
bodyText:
Arkansas law lets your lease require your written consent before a tenant alters the unit, and the tenant must not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises.

A few tenant rights limit that consent rule.
- A tenant may install a battery-powered or plug-in smoke or carbon monoxide detector at the tenant's own expense whatever the lease says; the tenant then must keep it working and pay for any damage its installation or removal causes.
- A tenant may not change the locks without your permission, but a domestic-abuse victim with a qualifying court order may have the locks changed at the tenant's expense with your prior consent, and the new key must be shared.
- Unless a narrow fair housing exemption applies (the Arkansas and federal exemptions differ, so confirm any exemption with your lawyer), fair housing law requires you to allow reasonable modifications, at the expense of the person with the disability, that a tenant or other resident with a disability may need for full enjoyment of the unit; where reasonable you may require the tenant to agree to restore the interior at move-out (reasonable wear and tear excepted), to describe the work in advance, and to assure you it will be done professionally, with permits, and paid for.
- If you have 12 or more rental units, your lease or rules may not prevent a tenant from properly displaying a U.S. flag (except as advertising).

An agreement that the tenant will renovate or remodel the unit must be in writing if you want it to displace the implied quality standards. Anything the tenant leaves in or about the premises when the lease ends is treated as abandoned.

title: No Bed Bug or Pest Statute in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on bed bugs or other pests in rental housing: no disclosure duty, no inspection or treatment schedule, and no specific tenant cooperation duty; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. What applies instead: the tenant must keep the unit reasonably clean and safe, dispose of garbage in a clean and safe manner, and comply with housing-code duties that fall on tenants, and may not unreasonably refuse you entry to inspect or make necessary or agreed repairs, which covers inspection and treatment visits. Pests are not among the six implied quality standards (water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, roof and building envelope, heating and air conditioning), but a local housing code may require pest control, so check yours. If you want specific cooperation duties (reporting, preparing the unit for treatment, paying for treatment the tenant caused), put them in the lease. Promising in the lease to treat or repair can create tort liability you otherwise would not have, so word any promise narrowly.

title: No Professional Carpet Cleaning Rule in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute on professional carpet cleaning at move-out: nothing requires it and nothing forbids a lease term requiring it. Without a lease term, the tenant's duty is to keep the unit reasonably clean and not damage it.

If your lease requires professional carpet cleaning and the tenant does not do it, the reasonable cost you actually pay is a damage caused by the tenant's noncompliance with the rental agreement, which a covered landlord may take from the deposit if itemized in the written notice sent with the balance within 60 days after the tenancy ends. (The deposit statute covers every landlord except an individual who, with a spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units and does not pay a third person to manage them.)

Do not charge a flat fee regardless of condition or cost, and tie the duty to carpets that were professionally cleaned before the tenancy, so the charge restores the move-in condition rather than paying for ordinary wear.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacate Notice in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas law does not require a tenant to warn you before leaving the unit vacant in cold weather, and has no winter rule on evictions or utility shutoffs in the landlord-tenant statutes; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. What applies instead: the tenant must use the plumbing, heating and other facilities in a reasonable manner and may not deliberately or negligently damage the premises, so freeze damage the tenant causes (for example by turning off the heat) is the tenant's responsibility. If you want advance notice before an extended absence or a move-out in freezing weather, or a minimum thermostat setting, put it in the lease.

title: Contractor Liens for Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText:
Arkansas's lien statute gives a contractor, subcontractor or supplier who improves or repairs real estate a lien to secure payment when the work was done under a contract with a person holding an interest in the real estate, or that person's agent. A tenant holds an interest (the leasehold), so a tenant's unpaid contractor can claim a lien on the improvement and the tenant's leasehold term; if the tenant forfeits the lease, the buyer at a lien sale may only remove the improvement within 60 days, and you receive the rent due, through the time of removal, out of the sale proceeds. Whether your own ownership interest can be reached depends on whether the tenant acted as your agent or you contracted for the work. Arkansas has no statute letting a lease clause by itself keep your interest free of liens.

To protect yourself: require written consent before any alteration, say in the lease that consent does not make the tenant your agent or mean you will pay, require the tenant to pay everyone it hires and to remove any lien promptly, and do not order or pay for the tenant's work yourself.

For residential property of four or fewer units, a contractor generally gets no lien unless the owner, the owner's authorized agent or registered agent received the statutory lien notice before work began, so a notice addressed to you is a warning sign to act on.

title: Disturbing Neighbors: The Tenant's Statutory Duty and Your Remedies
bodyText:
Arkansas puts a statutory duty on every tenant covered by the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act: the tenant must behave, and make everyone on the premises with the tenant's permission behave, in a way that does not disturb other tenants' peaceful enjoyment of the premises. The lease's no-disturbance clause repeats and widens that duty (for example to neighboring properties).

If a tenant breaches it, you may give a written notice describing the conduct and stating that the rental agreement will end on a date at least 14 days after the tenant receives the notice unless the conduct is remedied within 14 days; if the breach is not cured, the agreement ends on that date. If the conduct materially affects health and safety, the 14-day notice applies unless an emergency requires faster action. You may recover actual damages, and attorney's fees if the breach was willful and an attorney represents you.

Separately, using the premises as a common nuisance (premises used to facilitate a continuing series of three or more criminal violations, or used to sell, store, make or use illegal drugs) or for illegal gambling, prostitution or illegal alcohol sales supports an eviction under the state nuisance-eviction procedure. A periodic tenancy can also simply be ended with the 7-day (week-to-week) or 30-day (month-to-month) written notice; a fixed-term lease needs the 14-day breach notice or must run out.

title: No Extended-Absence Statute in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you about an extended absence, and none giving you a special right to enter while the tenant is away or to treat a long absence as abandonment. An absence-notice duty therefore exists only if the lease creates it, and the damages for breaking it are ordinary contract damages you can prove.

What applies instead: unless otherwise agreed the tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling unit; the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect, repair or supply services, and there is no statutory notice period for entry, so a lease entry clause (with an emergency provision) governs access during an absence. A long absence does not by itself end the tenancy; property left after the lease actually ends is treated as abandoned.

title: No Tenant Right to Run a Home Child Care in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring a landlord to allow a tenant to run a family child care home or day care in a rental unit, and none limiting the conditions you may set; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. What applies instead: unless the lease says otherwise, the tenant must occupy the unit only as a dwelling unit and may not conduct illegal activities there, so the lease decides whether home child care is allowed. If you allow it, require the tenant to hold any state child care license or registration the operation needs, to carry liability insurance naming you, and to follow occupancy and safety rules. The state home-based work law limits what cities and towns may regulate; it does not limit what a landlord's lease may restrict. Fair housing law still applies to how you treat families with children as residents.

title: Home-Based Work: Cities Are Limited, Leases Are Not
bodyText: Since 2021 Arkansas has limited how cities and incorporated towns may regulate home-based work, meaning an occupation or business a resident runs inside a residence that is clearly incidental and secondary to living there. A city or town may license or regulate it and may restrict it only on listed grounds, such as signs and other exterior evidence of business use, nuisances (noise, odor and similar disturbances), health, fire and safety codes, traffic and parking codes, limits on the number of employees, customers and tenants at the residence, and prohibitions or limitations related to public health, safety and welfare. The law limits local governments only; it does not mention landlords or leases, and it expressly leaves homeowners' association agreements and deed restrictions in force. Your lease may therefore restrict or prohibit business use: the residential-use rule (the tenant occupies the unit only as a dwelling unit unless otherwise agreed) applies, and a residential-use-only clause controls. If you allow home-based work, set limits in the lease on customer visits, signs, employees, deliveries and insurance.

title: No Co-Tenant Liability Statute in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute setting how co-tenants share liability under a residential lease, so the lease's joint-and-several liability term governs: you may collect the full rent, or full damages, from any tenant who signed.

Two statutes bear on co-tenants in specific cases. If a court order requires a domestic-abuse offender to stay away from a co-tenant, you may refuse the offender access to the victim's residence unless a court order permits it, and you may seek to terminate the offender's tenancy, evict the offender, and recover from the offender unpaid rent the offender owes and damages from the abuse; you may not end, refuse or fail to renew the victim's tenancy because of the abuse.

A service member or spouse who ends the lease for the primary residence under the state military lease law (orders for more than 180 days, a move of more than 50 miles, or qualifying discharge) does so by written notice with the current and next month's rent; the statute does not say what happens to co-tenants who stay, so if other adults will remain, sign a new lease with them.

title: Occupancy Limits in Arkansas: Two per Bedroom Presumed Reasonable
bodyText:
Arkansas sets no statewide maximum number of occupants for a rental unit and no floor-area-per-person standard; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found only the fair housing rule.

Under the state fair housing law (the Fair Housing Commission law), an occupancy limit of two persons per bedroom residing in a dwelling unit is presumed reasonable statewide, and you may refuse to rent because of reasonable occupancy standards you set if they apply to persons of all ages and were adopted and published before the application or event in question. Reasonable local or state occupancy restrictions also apply, so check your city's code.

Keep your standard in writing, apply it the same way to every applicant, and list every permitted occupant in the lease; a limit that counts children differently from adults, or is stricter than two per bedroom without a sound reason, risks a familial-status claim.

title: What Arkansas Law Forbids Tenants to Do
Illegal Use of the Premises: No Automatic Voiding, but a Nuisance Eviction
bodyText: No Arkansas statute makes a lease void or automatically ended when the tenant uses the premises for an illegal purpose; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. What Arkansas provides instead: a tenant who uses or lets others use the leased premises as a common nuisance (a place used to facilitate a continuing series of three or more criminal violations, or used to sell, store, make or use illegal drugs) or for illegal gambling, prostitution or illegal alcohol sales may be evicted under a special nuisance-eviction procedure brought by the prosecuting attorney, the city attorney, or you (the tenant has 5 days, excluding Sundays and legal holidays, after service to object in writing). You may still sue for rent, repairs and other damages up to the eviction date, and you are immune from claims for breach of quiet enjoyment for acting under that procedure. Separately, a court abating a nuisance can order the building closed and its costs made a lien on the property, so act promptly when you learn of criminal use. Your ordinary remedies also remain: the 14-day breach notice and eviction, and ending a periodic tenancy with the 7-day or 30-day notice.

title: Residential Use: The Statutory Default and Your Remedy
bodyText:
Arkansas law says that unless otherwise agreed, a tenant must occupy the dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit and must not conduct or permit illegal activities there. A residential-use-only clause therefore restates the default and may lawfully go further (for example by banning all commercial use or short-term subletting); a clause allowing limited home business use is the "otherwise agreed" exception. The state home-based work law limits cities and towns, not landlords.

If a tenant uses the unit for another purpose, Arkansas sets no special penalty: your remedy is the 14-day written notice to remedy or end the rental agreement, actual damages, and attorney's fees if the breach is willful and you are represented by an attorney, or ending a periodic tenancy with the 7-day (week-to-week) or 30-day (month-to-month) notice. Criminal use can also support a nuisance eviction.

title: Smoking Bans and Arkansas's Medical Marijuana Amendment
bodyText:
Arkansas lets you ban smoking (tobacco or marijuana) and vaping of tobacco or nicotine anywhere on your rental property; no statute limits a landlord's smoking rules or requires a particular disclosure.

The medical marijuana amendment to the Arkansas Constitution adds three limits.

First, you need not allow a qualifying patient to smoke marijuana on leased property, but you may not prohibit a qualifying patient's medical use of marijuana through means other than smoking (for example edibles, oils, tinctures or patches). The amendment does not define smoking and treats vaporizing as a different method from smoking or combusting, so the cautious course is not to ban a qualifying patient's vaporized medical marijuana; the library's Arkansas smoking clause is written that way.

Second, you may not refuse to lease to, or otherwise penalize, someone solely because the person is a qualifying patient or designated caregiver, unless doing so would put you in violation of federal law or regulations (this matters for federally assisted housing).

Third, the amendment itself does not let anyone smoke marijuana in the presence of a person under 14, knowingly in the presence of a pregnant woman, where tobacco smoking is prohibited by law, or where the smoke is likely to put someone else under the influence, and it does not let a patient under 21 smoke marijuana for medical use at all.

Arkansas has no recreational marijuana law, so non-patients' marijuana use remains illegal and may be banned outright.

The state Clean Indoor Air Act bans smoking in enclosed public places and enclosed areas of workplaces, but says a private residence is neither (unless used as a licensed childcare, adult day care or healthcare facility); it does not mention apartment common areas, so whether it reaches an enclosed lobby, hallway or leasing office open to the public or used by your staff is not settled by its text, and a lease ban is the reliable way to keep those areas smoke-free.

title: Subletting and Assignment: No Arkansas Statute
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute on residential subletting or assignment: none gives a tenant a right to sublet, requires you to be reasonable in consenting, or treats silence as consent. The lease controls, so a clause requiring your prior written consent is enforceable as written.

Two consequences follow from the definitions. A tenant who sublets becomes a 'landlord' to the subtenant under the landlord-tenant act and the deposit statute, which define landlord to include a sublessor, so the original tenant owes the subtenant the landlord's duties (including deposit return, if the deposit statute covers that tenant). And fair housing law treats subleasing as renting, so a sublet cannot be refused or conditioned on a discriminatory ground. If you consent, put the consent in writing and say whether the original tenant stays liable.

title: No Statute on Tenant Insurance Claims in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on whether you may require a tenant to make a claim on the tenant's renter's insurance, or on filing a claim against a tenant's policy; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. A lease may require renter's insurance, and the lease decides how losses are handled. What applies instead: you are not liable to a tenant or the tenant's guests for injury or property damage caused by a defect or disrepair unless you agreed (for consideration) or took on by conduct a duty to maintain or repair and then failed to perform it reasonably, so the tenant's own insurance is usually the tenant's source of recovery for the tenant's belongings. Do not use a tenant's policy to pay for repairs the implied quality standards make yours (water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning), since the lease cannot shift those standards to the tenant except by a written renovation agreement. Contact the tenant before any claim on the tenant's policy; filing one without the policyholder's cooperation is generally not possible.

title: The Arkansas Tenant's Statutory Duties
bodyText: Under the Arkansas Residential Landlord-Tenant Act every tenant must: comply with the duties building and housing codes put mainly on tenants that materially affect health and safety; keep the unit and the parts of the premises the tenant uses reasonably safe and reasonably clean; dispose of ashes, garbage, rubbish and other waste in a reasonably clean and safe manner; keep plumbing fixtures reasonably clean; use electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances (including elevators) reasonably; not deliberately or negligently damage or remove any part of the premises or knowingly let others do so; behave, and make guests behave, so as not to disturb other tenants; and comply with the lease and enforceable rules. The tenant must also not unreasonably refuse you entry for the listed purposes, not change locks without permission, use the unit only as a dwelling unless otherwise agreed, and not conduct illegal activity there. A tenant who installs a battery or plug-in smoke or carbon monoxide detector is solely responsible for keeping it working. These duties apply whether or not the lease repeats them. If a breach materially affecting health and safety can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning and the tenant does not fix it within 14 days after your written notice (or as promptly as an emergency requires), you may enter, have the work done in a workmanlike manner and charge the tenant the cost; you may also give the 14-day notice to remedy or end the rental agreement.

title: Tenant Upkeep in Arkansas, Including Wells and Septic Systems
bodyText:
An Arkansas tenant's upkeep duty comes from the statute and the lease: keep the unit reasonably clean and safe, use its systems reasonably, and not deliberately or negligently damage it. The statute does not make a tenant repair ordinary wear or defects the tenant did not cause, and, for leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021, the six implied quality standards (water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning) stay your responsibility unless the tenant agrees in writing to renovate or remodel the unit.

Arkansas has no statute on who maintains a private well or septic system serving a rental. A well is the property's source of drinking water and a septic system is part of its sewer system, so treat both as yours under the implied standards; a lease may still make the tenant responsible for using them properly (for example not flushing grease or wipes) and for damage the tenant causes.

Be careful what you promise: a lease promise by you to maintain or repair can create tort liability you would not otherwise have.

title: Yard Work and Other Tenant Chores: No Separate-Writing Rule in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas does not require tenant chores such as mowing, raking, watering or other yard work to be in a separate signed writing or supported by separate consideration; a lease clause assigning them is enforceable as a lease term, for single-family homes and apartments alike. A search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found no statute on tenant yard or irrigation duties and no separate-writing rule.

Two cautions. City weed and lot-cleanup orders are generally aimed at the property owner (those statutes were seen only in search results, not read in full), so if the tenant neglects the yard you may still be the one cited; keep the right to do the work yourself and charge the tenant.

And a separate written agreement matters for one thing in Arkansas: the six implied quality standards (water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, roof and building envelope, heating and air conditioning) can be shifted to the tenant only by the tenant's written agreement to renovate or remodel.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas fair housing law closely tracks the federal Fair Housing Act on disability, though the exemptions differ. You may not refuse to rent to, or set different terms for, a tenant because of a disability of the tenant, a household member or someone associated with them. You must allow reasonable modifications of the unit, at the expense of the person with the disability (the tenant or a household member), when they may be necessary for that person's full enjoyment of the premises, and you may reasonably condition permission on (1) the tenant's agreement to restore the premises to their prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted, where that is reasonable, and (2) a reasonable description of the work and assurance that it will be done professionally, with permits obtained and the work paid for. You must also make reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices and services, including for common areas. Arkansas has no rule requiring a separate restoration deposit or an interest-bearing account for one, and no rule requiring the lease itself to contain the restoration condition, so put any restoration agreement in a signed writing when you grant the modification. You need not rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property. A tenant with a disability may be accompanied by a trained service animal in housing with no extra fee or charge, though the tenant is liable for damage the animal causes. Some small owner-occupied buildings and certain single-family houses rented by an owner without a broker are exempt from the Arkansas section, but federal law has its own, narrower exemptions; treat every request as covered unless your lawyer confirms an exemption. The library does not offer a standing restoration clause, because the agreement should describe the specific modification.

title: Can the Lease Change Arkansas's Implied Quality Standards?
bodyText: Mostly no. For leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right), Arkansas implies six standards into every residential lease: an available source of hot and cold running water, an available source of electricity, a source of drinking water, a code-conforming sanitary sewer system and plumbing, a functioning roof and building envelope, and a functioning heating and air conditioning system to the extent one served the premises when the lease was signed. These standards override any contrary oral or written lease term, and neither side may agree in the lease to waive the rights, duties or remedies of the landlord-tenant act. There is one way to shift them: the tenant agrees in writing to take responsibility to renovate, remodel or complete the renovation, remodeling or construction of the unit. Use that only for a genuine renovation arrangement, in a separate signed writing that describes the work. Two built-in limits are not waivers: the standards do not apply while compliance is temporarily prevented by an act of God, a public utility failure or other force majeure (including an epidemic causing labor or material shortages), and the heating and air conditioning standard reaches only a system that served the premises at signing, so you are not required to add one. Because the water and electricity standards require only an available source, a lease may still make the tenant arrange and pay for those utilities. The same rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies; for an older month-to-month tenancy, assume each renewal after November 1, 2021 brings it under the standards.

title: Which Defects Count Under Arkansas's Quality Standards
bodyText: Arkansas does not use a general materiality test. Its statutory standards are a closed list of six items: an available source of hot and cold running water, an available source of electricity, a source of drinking water, a sanitary sewer system and plumbing that met the building and housing codes in effect when installed, a functioning roof and building envelope, and a functioning heating and air conditioning system to the extent one served the premises when the lease was signed. A defect outside that list (a cosmetic problem, a broken appliance, a worn carpet) is not a breach of the statutory standards, though it may breach your lease or a local housing code. Within the list the tests are availability and function, so an outage or failure counts even if short, unless it is temporarily caused by an act of God, a utility failure or other force majeure. You are also treated as complying when the defect was caused by the deliberate or negligent act of the tenant, the tenant's family, an occupant or visitor, or anyone other than you or your agent, or when the tenant refused you entry to fix it. Answer every written complaint promptly and in writing, whether or not you think it is covered: if the tenant's rent is current, the defect is not excused, and you do not remedy it within 30 calendar days after receiving the tenant's written notice, the tenant may end the lease without penalty and recover the deposit (the tenant's sole remedy; rent may not be withheld).
