The standards apply to leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021, other than a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right. This applies equally to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Your Repair and Maintenance Duties in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas's landlord-tenant act imposes only one statewide condition duty on you: the six implied quality standards (hot and cold running water and electricity available, drinking water, code-conforming sewer and plumbing, a functioning roof and building envelope, and a functioning heating and air conditioning system if one served the premises at signing), at move-in and throughout the term, for leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021. There is no general statutory duty to keep the unit fit and in repair, no repair deadline other than the tenant's 30-day termination right, and no rent withholding.

Local governments may impose stricter housing standards, and the state law expressly preserves them, so check the city or county housing, property maintenance and rental inspection ordinances where the property sits.

Tort liability works differently in Arkansas: you are not liable to a tenant or the tenant's guests for injury or property damage caused by a defect or disrepair unless you agreed, for consideration, or undertook by conduct to maintain or repair the premises and then failed to do it reasonably. A lease clause promising that you will maintain and repair the property can therefore create liability you would not otherwise have, which is why the library's Arkansas default maintenance clause only asks the tenant to report conditions in writing. If you do make repairs, do them in a reasonable, workmanlike way. These rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: What an Arkansas Tenant Can Do When You Breach
bodyText: Arkansas gives tenants few statutory remedies against a landlord. For the six implied quality standards (leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021, other than a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right), the tenant must give you written notice (by certified mail or any other method your lease provides) describing the problem; if rent is current, the problem is not excused (for example, tenant-caused or entry refused) and you do not fix it within 30 calendar days of receiving the notice, the tenant's sole remedy is to end the lease without penalty and get back the deposit refundable under the deposit statute. The tenant may not withhold or offset rent for those defects. When you sue for possession and the tenant raises defenses or counterclaims under the act or the lease, the tenant must keep paying rent as it comes due after the court's order to vacate or show cause, and pay or prove payment of rent claimed before it; if the court later finds less or no rent due, judgment follows that finding. Other statutes add specific remedies: the deposit money due plus damages of twice the amount wrongfully withheld, costs and reasonable attorney's fees (only costs and the sum withheld if you prove a bona fide error despite reasonable procedures or a good-faith dispute over the amount), where the deposit statute applies (it does not cover the units of an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their entities, owns five or fewer units, unless a third person manages them for a fee), and protections for domestic-abuse victims and military members. For any other breach of the lease, the tenant's remedy is an ordinary contract claim, and the prevailing party in a contract action may be awarded attorney's fees unless the lease or a statute provides otherwise. Injury claims for defects are limited unless you agreed or undertook to repair. These rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike, though a periodic tenant may also simply end the tenancy with 7 or 30 days' written notice.

title: Who Pays Utilities in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas lets the lease decide which utilities the tenant pays; no statute requires you to furnish or pay for any utility. The implied quality standards require only that the unit have an available source of hot and cold running water and of electricity, a source of drinking water, and working sewer, plumbing and heating and air conditioning (if any served the premises at signing), so you must make those services available to the unit, but the lease may make the tenant open the accounts and pay the bills. The standards are excused while a public utility's own failure temporarily prevents service.

Arkansas water law follows the customer, not the property, in two ways: a person who owes an undisputed water, wastewater or sewer bill and moves to another system's area can be refused service by the new system until the debt is cured, and a court may make a delinquent customer pay the system's collection fees. A water system not regulated by a city may cut off service once a bill is more than 25 days past due and after mailing a notice giving at least 15 days.

Arkansas has no statute making a tenant's unpaid utility bill an eviction ground in itself; if your lease requires the tenant to keep utilities in the tenant's name and paid, nonpayment is a lease breach you can act on with the act's 14-day written notice to remedy. Put the allocation in the lease for every tenancy type; the same rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Keeping Utilities On in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute that specifically forbids a landlord to shut off a tenant's utilities or makes a shutoff an illegal eviction, and none that requires a tenant to keep utilities on.

Do not treat that as permission. Water and electricity must be available to the unit throughout the term under the implied quality standards, so for leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021, cutting them off breaches the implied standards and, if the tenant's rent is current and you do not restore service within 30 calendar days after receiving the tenant's written notice, lets the tenant end the lease without penalty and recover the deposit, and a self-help shutoff to force a tenant out exposes you to damages claims; use the court eviction process instead.

On the tenant's side, the lease controls: the library's clause requires the tenant not to let water, gas, electricity, sewer or trash service be interrupted, and a breach is a noncompliance you can address with the act's 14-day written notice, or with your own entry and repair, at the tenant's cost, if it materially affects health and safety.

When the water account is in your name and service is about to be cut off, Arkansas's public-records law lets a water system or municipally owned utility disclose your account information to your tenant so the tenant may receive notice of the pending termination. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Submetered Utilities: No Arkansas Interruption Rules
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute governing a landlord who submeters, master-meters or allocates electricity, gas or water and bills tenants for it, and none giving a landlord a right to interrupt submetered service for nonpayment; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Do not cut off service you control for nonpayment. Water and electricity must remain available to the unit throughout the term under the implied quality standards, so a shutoff breaches the lease and exposes you to the tenant's termination right and damages claims. Treat unpaid utility charges you bill under the lease as a lease breach and use the act's notice and eviction procedures. Public Service Commission rules and utility tariffs may limit reselling electricity or gas; check them, and your utility's tariff, before you submeter. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Checking a Tenant's Utility Payments in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas gives you no statutory right to see a tenant's utility account. Personal information of public water system and city-owned utility customers, including addresses and usage data, is closed to public-records requests and may be disclosed only to the customer and a few others; a landlord is not among them unless the account is in the landlord's name. The one exception that helps you runs the other way: when the account is yours, the water system may tell your tenant of a pending termination. So if the lease makes the tenant responsible for a utility, rely on the lease: the library's clause lets you ask the tenant for reasonable evidence of payment, and a tenant's written authorization lets you confirm the account with the utility. Arkansas has no statute on this beyond the lease, for any tenancy type.

title: Can a Tenant's Unpaid Utility Bill Land on Your Property?
bodyText: For water, Arkansas's collection statutes follow the customer, not the property: a person who owes an undisputed water, wastewater or sewer bill and moves can be refused service by the next water system until the debt is cured, a court may make the delinquent customer pay collection fees, and a water system not regulated by a city may cut off service after a bill is more than 25 days past due and a mailed notice giving at least 15 days. No Arkansas statute found makes you, as owner, personally liable for a tenant's water bill, and none sets an affidavit or lease procedure to protect you. Sewer and garbage service can be different. A city's sewer rates are paid by each user of the system, and an unpaid rate can be sued for with a 10% penalty and attorney's fees; where one city's sewer system serves another city by contract, the served city sets rates against the owners of the premises served, and the statute calls those charges a lien. Counties may charge rural garbage fees to each property owner or renter who benefits, with collection methods the quorum court sets. Before you let a tenant open a city sewer, water or garbage account, ask the city or county whether unpaid charges can become a lien on the property or be collected from you, keep the account in the tenant's name only if they cannot, and require the tenant in the lease to pay and show proof of payment. This applies to every tenancy type.

title: Heating and Air Conditioning in Arkansas
bodyText: For leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right), Arkansas requires a functioning heating and air conditioning system only to the extent one served the premises when you and the tenant signed the lease; if it did, it must work at move-in and throughout the term. You are not required to install heat or air conditioning where none served the unit, and Arkansas sets no minimum indoor temperature, heating season or cooling standard; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. The duty to keep the system functioning cannot be shifted to the tenant by an ordinary lease clause; the only exception is a tenant's written agreement to take responsibility for renovating or remodeling the unit. The lease may still make the tenant pay for the gas or electricity that runs the system and change filters, and the tenant must use the system reasonably. If the system fails, the tenant's rent is current, the failure is not excused (for example, tenant-caused or entry refused), and you do not fix it within 30 calendar days after receiving the tenant's written notice, the tenant may end the lease without penalty and recover the deposit, but may not withhold rent. Local housing codes may set temperature standards; check them. The duty is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors in Arkansas Rentals
bodyText: The Arkansas landlord-tenant act has no section requiring you to install or maintain smoke or carbon monoxide detectors in a dwelling unit. It does guarantee the tenant's right to install a battery-powered or plug-in smoke or carbon monoxide detector correctly at the tenant's own expense, and neither the act nor the lease may forbid it. If the tenant installs one, the tenant alone is responsible for checking that it works, keeping it in working order, and any damage or repairs caused by installing or removing it. Separately, Arkansas fire-safety law requires hotels, motels and apartment buildings with more than three floors above ground to have a fire alarm system meeting the Arkansas Fire Prevention Code, an emergency lighting system and fire escape stairways or ladders, and the Fire Prevention Code and local codes may require smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in other dwellings. Install working smoke alarms (and carbon monoxide alarms wherever there is fuel-burning equipment or an attached garage) as a matter of course, test them at move-in, and say in the lease who replaces batteries. The rules are the same for every tenancy type. The library does not offer an Arkansas alarm-duties clause, because the right allocation depends on the alarms installed; if you add your own, do not bar the tenant from installing a battery-operated or plug-in detector.

title: Common-Area Lighting: No Arkansas Landlord-Tenant Rule
bodyText: Arkansas's landlord-tenant statutes do not require you to light hallways, stairways or other common areas, and do not address whether a tenant may be made to pay for common-area lights wired to the tenant's meter; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found no such rule. Two other sources apply. Fire-safety law requires hotels, motels and apartment buildings with more than three floors above ground to have an emergency lighting system, including exit, corridor and exit-stairway lights with an emergency power source, and the Arkansas Fire Prevention Code and local codes may require more. And because an Arkansas landlord can become liable for injuries from conditions it agrees or undertakes to maintain, keep common-area lighting working once you provide it. Put common-area lights on a house meter; if any are wired to a tenant's service, say so in the lease and adjust the rent.

title: Appliances Left at the Property: No Arkansas Presumption
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute presuming that appliances present at the property are supplied by you, and none barring a lease from excluding appliances; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. The lease decides: list the appliances you supply and say that anything else at the property (for example a refrigerator left by a former occupant or the tenant's own washer) is not supplied or maintained by you. One limit: you cannot exclude the systems behind the implied quality standards, namely hot and cold running water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, and a heating and air conditioning system that served the premises when the lease was signed, so a water heater or furnace serving the unit stays your responsibility. The tenant must use all appliances reasonably whoever supplies them. This applies to every tenancy type. The library does not offer a separate appliances-excluded clause for Arkansas; list the appliances you supply in the lease's appliance clause, and anything not listed is not supplied by you.

title: Appliances You Supply in Arkansas
bodyText:
Appliances you supply are governed by the lease, not by Arkansas's implied quality standards, which cover only water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, the roof and building envelope, and a heating and air conditioning system that served the premises at signing. So a broken refrigerator, range or dishwasher you supplied is a lease issue, not a ground for the tenant's statutory termination right, and nothing in the act lets the tenant withhold rent over it.

List the appliances you supply in the lease and say how repairs work. Be aware that promising to maintain and repair appliances is an agreement to repair that can create injury liability if you then repair unreasonably, so handle appliance repairs promptly and competently. The tenant must use appliances reasonably and is responsible for damage the tenant causes. This applies to every tenancy type.

title: Agreements for the Tenant to Do Repairs in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas lets the lease assign repairs and upkeep to the tenant, with one firm limit. Ordinary repair and maintenance tasks (filters, light bulbs, yard work, minor fixes) may be put on the tenant by an ordinary lease clause; Arkansas has no rule requiring a separate signed writing or separate consideration, for single-family homes or apartments. The six implied quality standards (hot and cold running water, electricity, drinking water, code-conforming sewer and plumbing, a functioning roof and building envelope, and a heating and air conditioning system that served the premises at signing) are different: a lease term shifting them to the tenant is overridden, and the act bars agreeing to waive its rights and duties, unless the tenant agrees in writing to take responsibility to renovate, remodel or complete the renovation, remodeling or construction of the unit. Reserve that written renovation agreement for a genuine fixer-upper arrangement, describe the work, and keep it separate from routine chores. The agreement is lawful, but the library does not offer a clause for it, because the work, the parts of the unit it covers and how it is credited against rent differ for every deal; a landlord who wants one should have it written for the specific project, with advice. Remember that your own agreement to repair can create injury liability if you then perform unreasonably, and that a tenant's repair duty does not cover ordinary wear or defects the tenant did not cause unless the lease clearly says so. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Arkansas Duty to Provide Alternate Housing
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to relocate a tenant, pay for a hotel or provide a substitute unit while repairs are made or after a fire, flood or other casualty; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found no such rule. If the unit fails an implied quality standard, the tenant's rent is current, the failure is not excused, and you do not fix it within 30 calendar days after receiving the tenant's written notice, the tenant's sole statutory remedy is to end the lease without penalty and receive the refundable deposit; the standards do not apply while compliance is temporarily prevented by an act of God, a utility failure or other force majeure. The lease decides what happens to rent while a unit is uninhabitable; consider a clause that abates rent for any period the unit cannot be lived in. This applies to every tenancy type. The library's optional Arkansas casualty clause abates rent while a unit cannot reasonably be lived in after a fire or other casualty.

title: Condemned or Closed Premises: No Arkansas Rent Bar
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute barring you from collecting rent once a unit is condemned, placarded or ordered vacated, and none barring you from renting a condemned unit; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Do not collect rent for a unit the tenant cannot lawfully occupy. A unit that lacks water, electricity, sewer service or a functioning roof fails the implied quality standards, so, for leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021, a tenant whose rent is current may end the lease without penalty and recover the deposit if you do not remedy the defect within 30 calendar days after receiving the tenant's written notice (unless the defect is excused, for example because the tenant caused it), and local housing codes may impose stricter rules. Where a city's criminal nuisance abatement board declares a property a public nuisance, it may order the premises closed, the responsible tenants evicted, background checks of new tenants, and code compliance before the property is reoccupied. Arkansas also has no relocation duty when a unit is closed.

title: Designated Repairers: No Arkansas Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on lease clauses naming who must make repairs, because Arkansas gives tenants no general right to repair and charge you: there is no repair-and-deduct remedy, and a tenant may not withhold or offset rent for defects in the implied quality standards. A search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found no designated-repairer rule. The one narrow repair-and-deduct statute concerns sidewalks: in first- and second-class cities, when the owner fails after notice to build or repair a sidewalk the city has ordered, a tenant who builds it may deduct the cost from rent or hold possession until the rental value covers it. Your lease may require the tenant to use only you or your named contractors for any work the tenant arranges, and to get your written consent first. Separate licensing rules apply to some trades (for example electrical and plumbing work), so require licensed contractors where the law does.

title: Double-Letting: No Arkansas Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute addressing double-letting, that is, renting the same room or unit to more than one tenant for the same period, and no statutory rent penalty for it; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. A dispute would be decided under ordinary contract and possession law, and the tenant kept out could claim damages for your breach. Do not sign a second lease for a unit until the first tenancy has ended and possession has been returned. This applies to every tenancy type.

title: Employee Background Checks: No Arkansas Mandate
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring landlords or property managers to run background checks on employees, including maintenance staff with keys to units; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Screening you choose to do is governed by employment and consumer-reporting law (including the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act), not landlord-tenant law. The closest rule concerns tenants: a city criminal nuisance abatement board that declares a property a public nuisance may order the owner or the owner's agents to run criminal background checks on tenants before renting. Screen staff who enter units as a matter of prudence, and limit and log key access.

title: Arkansas's Move-In Defect Form: When You Are Deemed to Comply
bodyText:
Arkansas has no presumption that you breached the implied quality standards or took too long to repair. Instead, the statute tells you when you are deemed to comply.

At move-in, if you give the tenant a written form for listing defects in the six standards when possession becomes available, you are deemed in compliance if the tenant signs it without noting a defect and takes possession, or does not return it within two business days.

During the tenancy, you are deemed in compliance with a defect the tenant reports in writing if you could not fix it because the tenant refused you entry, or if it was caused by the deliberate or negligent act of the tenant, the tenant's family, an occupant or visitor, or anyone other than you or your agent.

Use the defect form at every move-in and keep the signed copy, and document any refused entry.

The move-in form does not cover a defect that arises later: unless that defect is excused as above, a tenant whose rent is current may end the lease without penalty if you do not fix it within 30 calendar days after receiving the tenant's written notice. These rules apply to leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021, other than a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right, whatever the tenancy type.

title: No Required Fitness Statement in Arkansas Leases
bodyText: Arkansas does not require your lease to state that the unit will be delivered fit for habitation; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found no such requirement. The duty exists anyway: for leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or with a purchase right), the six implied quality standards are read into every residential lease whether or not the lease mentions them, at move-in and throughout the term, except while an act of God, a utility failure or another force majeure event temporarily prevents compliance. Do not add a lease statement promising more than you will deliver, such as that the unit meets all codes, and do not try to disclaim the six standards, because a contrary term is overridden unless the tenant agrees in writing to take on renovating, remodeling or completing construction of the unit. This applies to every tenancy type.

title: Habitability Rules Other States Have That Arkansas Lacks
bodyText: Many tenant protections common in other states have no Arkansas statute; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none of the following. (1) No rent withholding, rent escrow or general repair-and-deduct remedy: the tenant may not offset or withhold rent for defects in the implied quality standards; the only repair-and-deduct statute covers a city-ordered sidewalk the owner fails to build or repair. (2) No repair deadline other than the 30 calendar days after you receive the tenant's written notice that can trigger the tenant's right to end the lease. (3) No minimum indoor temperature or cooling duty, and no duty to add heating or air conditioning that did not serve the unit at signing. (4) No landlord-tenant statute requiring you to install smoke or carbon monoxide detectors (the tenant may install battery or plug-in ones). (5) No duty to provide alternate housing during repairs or after a casualty. (6) No bar on collecting rent for a condemned unit. (7) No presumption that you breached or delayed repairs; instead a move-in defect form can make you deemed in compliance. (8) No general warranty that the unit is fit for habitation beyond the six listed standards. (9) No small-landlord exemption from the quality standards. What Arkansas does have: six implied standards for leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, roof and envelope, heating and air conditioning that served the unit at signing) that override contrary lease terms; the tenant's sole remedy of ending the lease without penalty and recovering the deposit, available only if rent is current, the defect is not excused (for example, tenant-caused or entry refused) and you have not remedied it within 30 calendar days after receiving the tenant's written notice; and preserved stricter local housing standards. Local codes and case law may add duties.

title: Health Department Rental Rules: None Statewide in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute letting health districts or boards of health adopt rental-housing regulations, no duty to give tenants a copy of health rules, and no statute sending tenants to a health agency over repair complaints; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Three related rules apply. Lead: after a Department of Health lead inspection or investigation, the Department notifies both the owner and the tenant of its findings, and an owner who has not properly abated a lead hazard within 30 days after the notice is in violation; after notice of lead hazards you may not retaliate against the occupant, especially by eviction or threat of eviction, though you may agree with the occupant on other suitable housing during abatement. Local codes: cities and counties may set stricter housing standards, which the implied-quality-standards statute preserves, and some cities run residential rental inspection programs that require out-of-state owners to designate an agent for service of process. Check the city or county where the property sits. These rules apply to every tenancy type.

title: Tenant Duty to Forward Legal Papers: No Arkansas Statute
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you about, or forward, a summons or other notice of a lawsuit or proceeding to recover the property, and no statute on attornment (a tenant's acknowledgment of a new owner or lender). The duty exists only if the lease creates it, which the library's clause does: a tenant who receives notice of a proceeding to recover the property or its possession must tell you immediately and give you any written notice.

Because there is no statutory penalty, your remedy for a breach is the act's ordinary 14-day notice to remedy and your damages.

When you sell, tell the tenant in writing who the new landlord is and where to pay rent; the buyer takes the deposit obligations with the property where the deposit statute applies (it does not cover the units of an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their entities, owns five or fewer units, unless a third person manages them for a fee). This applies to every tenancy type.

title: Shifting Repair Duties to the Tenant in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no rule, as some states do, that lets you hand particular repair duties to the tenant only through a separate signed writing. Instead, Arkansas imposes six implied quality standards on you (an available source of hot and cold running water and of electricity, drinking water, code-conforming sewer and plumbing, a functioning roof and building envelope, and a functioning heating and air conditioning system if one served the unit when the lease was signed), and those standards override any contrary lease term. Neither side may waive rights under the landlord-tenant act in the lease. The statute allows one exception: the standards do not override the lease where the tenant agrees in writing to take on renovating, remodeling or completing the construction of the unit, and a property leased only so the tenant can renovate it is not a dwelling unit under the act at all. Use that route only for a genuine renovation deal, in a signed writing that describes the work. Ordinary chores that are not among the six standards (yard work, snow removal, filters, light bulbs) may be assigned to the tenant in the lease itself; no separate writing is needed, and the tenant must already keep the unit reasonably safe and clean. The standards apply to leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (not to a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right), and the rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Arkansas List of Other Facilities You Must Supply
bodyText: Apart from fire-safety equipment in tall buildings (below), Arkansas has no statute that requires you to supply facilities beyond the six implied quality standards, such as door locks, window screens, garbage receptacles, extermination, smoke detectors or appliances. An apartment building or similar multiple-occupancy facility with more than three floors above ground must have an emergency lighting system, fire escape stairways or ladders, and a fire alarm system meeting the Arkansas Fire Prevention Code. What applies instead: the six standards (an available source of hot and cold running water and of electricity, drinking water, code-conforming sewer and plumbing, a functioning roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning that served the unit when the lease was signed), any stricter local housing or property maintenance code, which the state law expressly preserves, and anything you promise in the lease. A tenant may install a battery-powered or plug-in smoke or carbon monoxide detector at the tenant's own expense, and a tenant may not change the locks without your permission. Check the city or county code where the property sits, since local codes often require locks, screens, smoke alarms or trash service. The rule is the same for every type of tenancy.

title: Repair Promises Can Create Injury Liability in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that requires a promise to clean, repair or improve the unit to be in writing, to carry a completion date or to be made before the lease is signed. What a promise does matter for is injury liability. Arkansas shields you from liability to a tenant, or the tenant's guests, for death, injury or property damage caused by a defect or disrepair, unless you agreed for consideration to maintain or repair the premises, or took on that duty by your conduct, and then failed to carry it out reasonably. A repair promise in the lease, in an addendum, in a message to the tenant, or simply starting a repair can therefore create liability you would not otherwise have. Make only the promises you intend to keep, put them in writing with a clear scope and target date, and do the work in a reasonable, workmanlike way. Avoid broad promises to maintain the whole property; the library's Arkansas maintenance clause asks the tenant to report problems in writing instead. A written promise is also an ordinary contract term the tenant can enforce, and in a contract suit the winner may be awarded attorney's fees unless the lease or a statute says otherwise. For leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021, your duties under the six implied quality standards apply whether or not you promise anything. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Statutory Covenant of Quiet Possession in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that writes a covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment into residential leases. The Code does assume such covenants exist: when you act to evict a tenant under the state's nuisance-eviction law (drug, gambling, prostitution or illegal-alcohol use of the premises), you are immune from claims that you breached an express or implied covenant of possession or quiet enjoyment. Whether, and how far, an implied covenant binds you otherwise is case law; assume a court will find one. Two statutes protect the tenant's possession directly: no one may enter and hold property except when the law allows it, and then only peaceably, and putting the occupant out of doors or carrying away the occupant's goods is a forcible entry and detainer. So never lock a tenant out, remove belongings or otherwise force a tenant out; end the tenancy by notice and use a court eviction. Enter only on the consent rules in the lease and the statute. These rules apply to every type of tenancy.

title: No Arkansas Rule on Splitting Rent Collection from Repair Duties
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that deals with separating the right to collect rent from the duty to keep the unit habitable, for example by assigning the rents, a deed, a deed of trust or a management contract. What applies instead: the six implied quality standards are written by law into every residential lease entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right, and except while an act of God, a utility failure or another force majeure event temporarily prevents compliance), they override contrary lease terms unless the tenant agrees in writing to take on renovating, remodeling or completing construction of the unit, and neither you nor the tenant may waive rights under the landlord-tenant act in the lease. Under the act, the landlord is the owner, lessor or sublessor, and also a manager who fails to disclose as the act requires, although the act contains no section setting out what must be disclosed. Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by the deposit statute. If you sell, assign the rents or hire a manager, make the transfer documents say who will carry out the habitability and deposit duties, and tell the tenant in writing where to pay rent and send notices. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. The deposit statute does not apply to the units of an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their entities, owns five or fewer units, unless a third person manages them for a fee.

title: Rental Inspections and Inspector Entry in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statewide rental registration or inspection program. State law does recognize city programs: in a city with a systematic residential rental property inspection program, owners who live outside Arkansas must designate an agent for service of process, and a real estate licensee who serves as that agent is protected from liability if the licensee forwards papers to the owner's last known address within three business days (or the time a pre-August 12, 2005 ordinance sets). Check your city's ordinances for registration, inspection and fee rules. Government inspectors enter on their own authority, not under your lease: the Department of Health may get a court warrant to enter a dwelling to look for lead hazards (or enter without one in an exigent health threat), and a judicial officer may issue an inspection warrant for premises suspected of being a criminal nuisance. No statute lets a lease clause make the tenant admit a housing inspector without the tenant's own consent. You may enter yourself to inspect the premises, and bring workers or contractors, and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent; if a city inspection is required, schedule it with the tenant, accompany the inspector and get the tenant's agreement. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Rent Escrow, So No Escrow Exemption Notice, in Arkansas
bodyText: This does not arise in Arkansas: there is no rent-escrow procedure for repairs, so there is no exemption notice to give. A tenant may not withhold or offset rent for a defect in the implied quality standards; the tenant's sole remedy, if rent is current, the defect is not excused (for example, tenant-caused or entry refused) and you do not fix it within 30 calendar days after receiving the tenant's written notice, is to end the lease without penalty and recover the deposit.

title: How Tenants Give Repair Notice in Arkansas
bodyText:
For the six implied quality standards (an available source of hot and cold running water and of electricity, drinking water, code-conforming sewer and plumbing, a functioning roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning that served the unit at signing), the tenant's notice must be written, must describe what is wrong, and must be delivered by certified mail or by any other method your lease provides. Your 30 calendar days to fix the problem run from when you receive it, and the tenant's remedy (ending the lease without penalty) applies only if rent is current and the problem is not excused, for example because the tenant refused you entry to make the repair or the tenant, the tenant's household or guests caused it.

Your lease may add a method (an e-mail address or an online portal) but should not take away certified mail, which the statute itself allows; the library's optional Arkansas clause does this. A verbal report does not meet the statute, but act on any report you get: once you start a repair, you must finish it reasonably.

No statute sets a notice method for other repairs; the lease controls, and the library's default maintenance clause asks for written reports. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Arkansas Lock, Deadbolt or Rekeying Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring you to install deadbolts, door viewers or other security devices, or to rekey locks between tenants. The statutes that do touch locks: a tenant may not change the locks without your permission, and a domestic-abuse victim's locks may be changed at the tenant's expense with your prior consent. Local building and property maintenance codes may require locks or other devices, and the state law preserves stricter local housing standards. Whether you can be liable for a crime on the property because of inadequate security is case law; Arkansas does shield you from injury claims for defects or disrepair unless you agreed or undertook to maintain or repair. Rekeying between tenants and keeping a key log is the cautious course. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Staff Work-Card Rule for 55+ Housing in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring work cards or background checks for employees of senior (55 and older) housing. Arkansas's fair housing law does recognize housing for older persons (62 and older, or 55 and older with at least 80% of occupied units having a resident 55 or older, plus published age policies and occupancy verification), but that exemption concerns familial status, not staff. Screen employees who hold keys under your own policy and the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act.

title: What Services and Utilities Arkansas Requires You to Provide
bodyText:
Arkansas requires the unit to have, at move-in and throughout the term, an available source of hot and cold running water and of electricity, a source of drinking water, code-conforming sewer and plumbing, and a functioning heating and air conditioning system if one served the unit when the lease was signed (for leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021). The statute requires these to be available, not that you pay for them: the lease decides who holds and pays each utility account, so list what you provide and what the tenant pays.

A failure caused by the public utility, an act of God or another force majeure event (including an epidemic that causes labor or material shortages) is excused while it lasts. Arkansas has no statute voiding a lease term that limits your liability for interruptions beyond your control, so the library's services clause works here.

The tenant must use the electrical, plumbing, heating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances in a reasonable manner. Stricter local codes still apply. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to supply a stove, oven or refrigerator; they are not among the six implied quality standards. Appliances matter in one way: an occupant whose unit lacks a landlord-provided toilet, bathtub or shower, refrigerator, stove or kitchen sink, where one or more of those facilities are shared with other occupants of the building, is a roomer, and a roomer who pays rent weekly with no fixed term has a week-to-week tenancy that either side may end on 7 days' written notice (otherwise a tenancy without a fixed term is month to month, 30 days' notice). If you do provide appliances, list them in the lease; the tenant must use them reasonably, and the habitability remedy does not reach them, so your repair duty for them is what the lease says. Local codes may require cooking or refrigeration facilities.

title: No Code-Enforcement Receivership for Rentals in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute letting a court appoint a receiver to take over and repair substandard rental housing, or setting code-enforcement repair orders for multi-unit rentals. Receivers in the Code serve other purposes, mainly bond defaults on public projects. What applies instead: local housing, building and property maintenance codes, which the state's implied quality standards expressly leave in force; city nuisance abatement; and, where a city has a criminal nuisance abatement board that declares a property a public nuisance, orders that can require the owner to evict responsible tenants, run criminal background checks on tenants, or bring the property up to state and local safety codes before anyone moves back in, with fines of up to $250 a day for violations. Answer city code notices promptly, because local procedures can lead to fines, liens or condemnation.

title: No Arkansas Cable, Satellite or Broadband Access Statute for Rentals
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute giving tenants a right to cable, satellite or broadband service, giving providers access to apartment buildings, or barring a rent difference for subscribers. Your lease may set reasonable rules for installations and alterations. A federal rule of the Federal Communications Commission limits restrictions on small satellite dishes and antennas placed in areas a tenant exclusively uses, such as a balcony or patio; it was not reviewed here, so check it before banning dishes outright. Federal rules on exclusive service contracts in multifamily buildings were not reviewed either.

title: Tenant Remedies When Repairs Are Not Made in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas gives a tenant one statutory remedy for repairs, and it covers only the six implied quality standards (an available source of hot and cold running water and of electricity, drinking water, code-conforming sewer and plumbing, a functioning roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning that served the unit at signing), and only in leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021, other than a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right. The tenant must send you written notice describing the problem by certified mail or a method your lease provides. If rent is current, the problem is not excused (for example, the tenant refused you entry or the tenant's household or guests caused it) and you do not fix it within 30 calendar days of receiving the notice, the tenant's sole remedy is to end the lease without penalty and get back the deposit refundable under the deposit statute. There is no repair-and-deduct, no rent escrow and no rent withholding: the tenant may not offset or withhold rent for these defects. If you sue for possession and the tenant raises defenses or counterclaims under the act or the lease, the tenant must keep paying you rent as it comes due after the court's order to vacate or show cause, and pay or prove payment of the rent claimed before it. Injury claims are limited unless you agreed or undertook to repair. Stricter local housing codes may be enforced by the city. The rules apply to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies alike, though a periodic tenant may also simply end the tenancy on 7 or 30 days' written notice. The deposit statute does not apply to the units of an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their entities, owns five or fewer units, unless a third person manages them for a fee.

title: Utilities You Pay: What Arkansas Adds
bodyText:
No Arkansas statute regulates which utilities you include in the rent, so the lease controls; list each utility you pay. Two Arkansas rules matter if you hold the account.

First, the implied quality standards require an available source of hot and cold running water and of electricity, and drinking water, throughout the term; a shutoff for your own unpaid bill is not the kind of utility failure the statute excuses, so, for leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021, it can let a tenant whose rent is current end the lease without penalty and recover the deposit if service is not restored within 30 calendar days after you receive the tenant's written notice.

Second, Arkansas has no statute letting tenants pay your utility bill and deduct it, so the tenant's statutory remedy stays termination; utility-side rules may give tenants notice of a building shutoff and were not reviewed. Pay landlord-held accounts on time. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Arkansas Limit on Utility Allowances or Master-Meter Pass-Through
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute that limits a utility allowance in a lease or bars passing master-metered utility costs to tenants except through a fixed rent; the Arkansas Code and Constitution were searched, but Public Service Commission rules were not. So the allowance and any overage charge are contract terms; the library's allowance clause works here.

An overage charge is not rent under Arkansas's landlord-tenant act, which counts late charges as rent but excludes other charges, so an unpaid overage is handled as a lease breach (written notice and at least 14 days to cure), not by the 5-day nonpayment-of-rent route.

Charge tenants only your actual cost: Arkansas's public-utility definition leaves out an owner who furnishes gas, electricity, water or sewer service only to its own tenants when the service is not resold to or used by others, and the Commission's resale rules were not reviewed, so marking up utility service could raise regulatory questions. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: Charging Tenants for Shared Utilities: No Arkansas Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that bars or regulates charging tenants for utilities that are not separately metered to their unit (ratio or allocation billing), sets a formula, or requires a disclosure. So a shared-utility charge is a contract term: state in the lease which utilities are shared, the formula (square footage, occupants, or another method), how often you bill, when payment is due and any fee you add, and give the tenant copies of the underlying bills on request. The charge is not rent under the landlord-tenant act (rent excludes other charges), so nonpayment is a lease breach handled by written notice and at least 14 days to cure. Bill only your actual cost: Arkansas's public-utility definition leaves out an owner who furnishes gas, electricity, water or sewer service only to its own tenants when the service is not resold to or used by others, and Public Service Commission rules on resale were not reviewed. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Arkansas Statute on Landlord Notice of a Tenant Utility Shutoff
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that lets you authorize a utility to tell you when a tenant's service is about to be disconnected, or lets a tenant designate you to receive copies of shutoff notices. Whether a utility will do this is a matter of its own policies and Public Service Commission rules. Ask the utility, and get the tenant's written consent in the lease or an addendum, since the account is the tenant's. If a tenant-held utility is shut off, treat it as a lease breach (written notice and at least 14 days to cure) where the lease requires the tenant to keep service on, and remember that a lack of water or electricity caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant (or the tenant's family, occupants or visitors) does not count against you under the implied quality standards. A tenant's written consent for a utility to copy you on disconnection notices for the tenant's account is lawful, but the library does not offer a clause for it, because each utility uses its own consent form; ask the tenant to sign the utility's form at move-in.

title: Landlord-Held Utility Accounts: No Arkansas Tenant Pay-and-Deduct Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that protects tenants when a utility account in your name goes unpaid: no right to pay the bill and deduct it from rent, no rent receiver, and no statutory damages. What applies instead is the implied quality standards: the unit must have an available source of water and electricity throughout the term, and a shutoff for your own nonpayment is not an excused utility failure, so the tenant may give written notice and, if service is not restored within 30 calendar days after you receive the notice and rent is current, end the lease without penalty and recover the deposit. The tenant may not withhold rent. Keep landlord-held accounts current. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: Utility Shutoffs in Arkansas: No Code Rule, and No Landlord Cutoffs
bodyText: The Arkansas Code has no statute setting disconnection notices, winter or extreme-weather protections, or medical protections for residential electric, gas or water customers. As a landlord, never shut off or interrupt a tenant's utilities to force payment or move-out. Arkansas has no statute that expressly names a landlord utility cutoff, but the implied quality standards require an available source of water and electricity throughout the term, and taking possession other than peaceably and by law is a forcible entry and detainer. To end a tenancy, give the required notice and use a court eviction. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Arkansas Submetering or Utility-Billing Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that sets disclosures, billing limits or late-fee caps for submetered or landlord-billed utilities; the Arkansas Code and Constitution were searched, but Public Service Commission rules were not. Disclose it in the lease anyway: which utilities you bill, whether by submeter or formula, the rate (your actual cost), the billing cycle, the due date, any administrative or late fee, and that the tenant may see the meter readings and the utility's bills. A utility charge is not rent under the landlord-tenant act, so nonpayment is a lease breach (written notice and at least 14 days to cure), and do not cut off service to collect it. Arkansas's public-utility definition leaves out an owner who furnishes gas, electricity, water or sewer service only to its own tenants when the service is not resold to or used by others, and Public Service Commission rules on resale were not reviewed, so bill only your actual cost. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Arkansas Rule on Transferring Utilities to the Tenant
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute about putting utilities in the tenant's name at move-in or about cutting off utilities left in your name that the tenant did not transfer. The lease controls: say which utilities the tenant must place in the tenant's own name and by what date (the library's utilities clause does). If the tenant does not transfer them, do not cut off service to a tenant in possession: the implied quality standards require an available source of water and electricity, and pressure by shutoff risks a forcible entry and detainer claim. Instead, bill the tenant for the usage as the lease provides and treat the failure as a lease breach (written notice and at least 14 days to cure). The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: Lock Changes for Domestic-Abuse Victims in Arkansas
bodyText: If a tenant, an applicant or a member of the household is a victim of domestic abuse shown by a court order (a documented incident within the last 60 days, or within 60 days after a tenancy ended because of the abuse), you or a tenant other than the abuser may change the locks to the tenant's home, at the tenant's expense and with your prior consent. Whoever changes the locks must give the other a copy of the new key right away, or as soon as possible if the other is unavailable. You are immune from civil liability for a good-faith lock change under this rule. If the abuser is under a court order to stay away from a co-tenant, the abuser may enter only as a court order allows, and you may refuse the abuser access unless a court order permits it. The statute does not set a deadline for your consent; respond quickly and do not refuse without a sound reason, because you also may not retaliate against a victim because of the abuse. Apart from this rule, a tenant may not change the locks without your permission. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Arkansas Key-Control or Staff Background-Check Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring a key-control policy, limits on master keys, or background checks for employees with key access, for any size of complex. One related power exists: where a city criminal nuisance abatement board declares a property a public nuisance, it may order the owner to run criminal background checks on tenants before renting. As good practice, keep a key log, limit and secure master keys, rekey after lost keys or staff turnover, and screen employees who hold keys under the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act. The domestic-abuse lock-change rule and the bar on tenant lock changes without your permission still apply.

title: Entering the Unit in Arkansas: Consent, Not a Notice Period
bodyText:
Arkansas sets no notice period or hours for your entry. Instead, the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect; make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements; supply necessary or agreed services; investigate possible rule or lease violations or criminal activity; or show the unit to prospective or actual buyers, lenders, tenants, workers or contractors.

The 24 hours' notice in the library's entry clause is your lease promise, not a statutory figure, and you should keep it. Because the statute is framed as consent, the cautious course is to ask, give the lease's notice, and reschedule if the tenant has a reasonable objection to the time; enter without notice only in a real emergency.

If the tenant refuses lawful access, you may get a court order compelling access, without posting bond, or end the lease, and in either case recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. A tenant's refusal of entry also excuses you from the 30-day repair deadline under the implied quality standards, and after 14 days' written notice of a health-and-safety breach you may enter and do the repair at the tenant's cost. No Arkansas statute gives the tenant a specific remedy for an improper entry; a tenant could still sue for trespass or breach of the lease. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: Scheduled-Service Entry: No Special Arkansas Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on entry for regularly scheduled services (pest treatment, filter changes, grounds work) and none requires that right to be written conspicuously into the lease. Because Arkansas sets no entry notice at all and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry to supply necessary or agreed services, a schedule written into the lease works as the tenant's advance agreement. Use the library's optional scheduled-services clause, and set its notice at no less than the 24 hours in the entry clause so the two agree.

title: Shorter Notice for Showings: Nothing to Waive in Arkansas
bodyText: This does not arise in Arkansas: the state sets no entry-notice period, so there is no statutory notice for a tenant to waive or shorten for showings. The notice is whatever the lease says, and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry to show the unit to prospective buyers, lenders or tenants; the library's optional shorter-notice clause for showings works here as a lease term.

title: No Arkansas Smart-Lock Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute regulating smart locks, keypad or app-based entry systems in rentals. The ordinary rules apply: your entries are governed by the lease and the tenant's duty not to unreasonably withhold consent, the tenant may not change or add locks without your permission, and a domestic-abuse victim's locks may be changed (or codes reset) with your consent. Good practice: tell tenants what entry data the system records and who can see it, reset codes between tenants, offer a way in that does not require a smartphone app, and do not use entry logs to monitor tenants beyond security needs.

title: A Tenant's Belongings Left Behind in Arkansas
bodyText:
When a lease ends, voluntarily or not, Arkansas treats property the tenant leaves in and about the premises as abandoned: you may dispose of it as you see fit, and the tenant has no claim against you for it. You also have a lien on property the tenant placed on the premises for all sums the tenant agreed to pay.

Make sure the lease has actually ended first (expiry, a termination notice, a court judgment or the tenant's written surrender). Removing belongings while the tenant may still be in possession is a forcible entry and detainer, so never empty a unit the tenant has not clearly given up.

After a court eviction, the sheriff executing the writ removes belongings still there 24 hours after service to a warehouse or other reasonably safe storage under your control until the court decides the case; if you win a money judgment, the court orders the goods sold in a commercially reasonable way, with the proceeds paying storage, then your judgment, and any excess going to the tenant. In a criminal-nuisance eviction the tenant may reclaim stored goods within 7 business days by paying the storage cost.

For a manufactured or mobile home on a lot you lease, a separate notice to the lienholder applies once the home is unoccupied and the lot rent is 60 days past due.

The Arkansas Constitution exempts some personal property from court sale for contract debts, and how that interacts with these rules is case law; keep records and photos, and hold valuables and documents for a reasonable time before disposing of them. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: Tenant Abandonment and Re-Renting: No Arkansas Statute
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute that defines when a tenant has abandoned the unit, and none that requires you to re-rent (mitigate) or says the lease ends if you do not. When a lease is terminated, you are entitled to possession, to rent, and to a separate claim for actual damages for the breach plus reasonable attorney's fees. Whether you must try to re-rent before collecting rent for the rest of a fixed term is case law; the cautious course is to make and document reasonable efforts to re-rent and credit any rent you receive.

Before treating a unit as abandoned, end the lease (for unpaid rent, you may terminate once rent is 5 days late; give the tenant written notice) or get a written surrender, and only then deal with belongings left behind. A month-to-month tenant who leaves without notice generally owes rent through the 30-day notice period (7 days for week-to-week); a fixed-term tenant's exposure is the remaining rent, subject to the mitigation question.

title: Attorney's Fees in Arkansas Landlord-Tenant Cases
bodyText: Arkansas statutes let you recover reasonable attorney's fees for: a tenant's willful breach other than nonpayment, and nonpayment of rent that is not in good faith (in both cases only if you are represented by an attorney); your claims after the lease is terminated; a tenant's refusal of lawful access; a holdover that is not in good faith, and a willful holdover (which also allows up to three months' periodic rent or twice actual damages, whichever is greater); and a criminal-nuisance eviction. A tenant may recover fees if you wrongfully keep a deposit covered by the deposit statute. The deposit statute does not apply to the units of an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their entities, owns five or fewer units, unless a third person manages them for a fee. Beyond those, in any suit for breach of contract the court may allow the winning side a reasonable fee unless a statute or the contract provides otherwise. No Arkansas statute requires a lease fee clause to be mutual or limits which fees a lease may shift, but the general rule already lets either winning party ask for fees, so a mutual prevailing-party clause (as in the library's default clause) matches it. Fee awards are discretionary, and a landlord who represents itself cannot recover attorney's fees. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: The Federal 30-Day Notice Compared with Arkansas Notices
bodyText: Arkansas's own nonpayment notices are short: under the landlord-tenant act, rent unpaid 5 days after it is due is itself legal notice that you may begin an eviction; an unlawful detainer requires a 3-day written notice to quit and demand for possession; and the old criminal failure-to-vacate statute uses a 10-day written notice. For other lease breaches the landlord-tenant act's notice must give the tenant at least 14 days after receiving it to remedy the breach, and it ends the lease on the date stated unless the tenant remedies a breach that can be remedied before then. If the property has a federally backed mortgage or is in a covered federal housing program, the federal CARES Act's 30-day notice to vacate (see the federal row) is longer than any of these, so give at least 30 days' written notice to vacate before filing. For ending a month-to-month tenancy, Arkansas's 30-day notice already matches it; a week-to-week tenancy needs only 7 days under Arkansas law, so give 30 for a covered property.

title: Fire and Casualty Damage: No Arkansas Statute
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute that lets either side end the lease, or reduces rent, when fire, storm or another casualty damages the unit.

What applies instead: the implied quality standards (including a functioning roof and building envelope and available water and electricity) are excused only while you are temporarily prevented by an act of God, a utility failure or another force majeure event; otherwise, for leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right), the tenant may give written notice and, if rent is current, the problem is not excused (for example, tenant-caused or entry refused) and you do not fix it within 30 calendar days after receiving the notice, end the lease without penalty. The tenant may not withhold rent for a breach of those standards, and in an eviction in which the tenant raises defenses, rent is not reduced for a condition the tenant or the tenant's household or guests caused. Whether rent stops when the unit is destroyed is otherwise case law.

Put a casualty clause in the lease that says when either side may end the lease, how rent is reduced while the unit is unusable, and that the tenant must let you retrieve or protect property. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Arkansas Condominium Conversion Notice Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring notice to tenants, a right of first refusal, or any lease statement when rental property is converted to condominiums or cooperatives. Tenants keep their lease: a fixed-term lease runs to its end, and a periodic tenancy ends only on 7 days' (week-to-week) or 30 days' (month-to-month) written notice.

title: Criminal Activity by Tenants: Arkansas Rules and Eviction Routes
bodyText:
Unless the lease says otherwise, an Arkansas tenant must use the unit only as a dwelling and may not conduct or permit any illegal activity there, and the tenant may not unreasonably refuse your entry to investigate possible criminal activity.

**Ordinary route:** criminal activity breaches the lease, so give written notice ending the lease on a date at least 14 days after the tenant receives it (the lease continues only if the breach can be remedied and the tenant remedies it before that date); where it materially affects health and safety, the statute lets you act as promptly as an emergency requires.

**Fast route:** a tenant who uses, or lets someone use, the premises as a common nuisance (drug activity, or a continuing series of three or more crimes) or for illegal gambling, prostitution or illegal alcohol sales may be evicted under a separate nuisance-eviction law by you, the owner, your agent, the prosecutor or the city attorney: the tenant has 5 days (not counting Sundays and holidays) after service to object, the court may award attorney's fees, and you are immune from claims that the eviction breached the covenant of quiet enjoyment. File it in circuit court; district courts may hear it only if a Supreme Court rule permits.

Your exposure as owner is real: abatement costs and damages for a drug nuisance may be recovered from the owner, and a city criminal nuisance abatement board may order you to evict responsible tenants and to run criminal background checks.

Limits: you may not end or refuse a tenancy because a tenant or household member is a domestic-abuse victim, a tenant cannot waive the right to call the police or for emergency help, and fair-housing law still applies, though it allows refusing a person convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance. The library's criminal-activity clause fits these rules. The rules apply to every type of tenancy.

title: Grounds for Eviction and Cure Periods in Arkansas
bodyText:
You may start an eviction in Arkansas when the tenant fails to pay rent when due or demanded, when the term has ended, or when the tenant has violated the lease.

**Unpaid rent:** if rent is not paid within 5 days after it is due you may terminate the lease, and that nonpayment is itself legal notice that you may begin an eviction under the landlord-tenant act; there is no further cure period in that act. If you use the separate unlawful detainer procedure instead, you must first give a 3-day written notice to quit and demand for possession. Late charges count as rent; other charges do not.

**Other breaches:** give written notice describing what the tenant did or failed to do and stating that the lease will end on a date at least 14 days after the tenant receives the notice; if the breach can be fixed by repairs or otherwise and the tenant fixes it in time, the lease continues. For a breach of the tenant's upkeep duties that affects health and safety and can be repaired, you may after the same 14 days (or sooner in an emergency) enter and do the work at the tenant's cost; for other health-and-safety breaches you may terminate on those terms.

There is no limit on how many times a tenant may cure, and no just-cause requirement: a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy may be ended without a reason on 7 or 30 days' written notice, and a fixed term ends on its date. Time periods are counted under the Arkansas Rules of Civil Procedure, so count conservatively. Domestic-abuse and military protections still apply.

title: Tenant Default in Arkansas: How the Library Clause Fits
bodyText:
The library's default clause works in Arkansas. The statutory periods it refers to are: 5 days after rent is due before you may terminate for nonpayment (3 days' written notice to quit if you use unlawful detainer), and a written notice with at least 14 days to cure for other breaches.

Arkansas counts late charges as rent, so the clause's promise not to terminate over an unpaid late fee alone gives up a route the statute would allow; that is a choice in the tenant's favor, not a legal requirement. The clause also makes a rent default depend on written notice from you; Arkansas's 5-day route needs no notice, so send a written notice once rent is 5 days late to stay within the clause. Attorney's fees and mitigation are explained in the attorney-fee and abandonment rows. See the eviction-grounds row for the full notice rules.

title: After a Declared Disaster in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that ends a tenancy, suspends rent or sets landlord duties after a declared natural disaster. Two rules do apply. First, your implied quality-standard duties (water, electricity, roof and envelope, sewer, heating and air conditioning) are excused only while you are temporarily prevented by an act of God, utility failure or similar event; once repair is possible the duty returns, and the tenant's remedy remains written notice and termination after 30 days. Second, Arkansas's price-gouging law covers rental housing: after the President or Governor proclaims a state of emergency, or a city or county declares a local emergency, for a tornado, flood, fire, storm or other disaster, you may not charge more than 10% above your price immediately before the proclamation for 30 days (extendable in 30-day steps), unless the increase is directly attributable to added costs; treat either kind of declaration as enough (see the rent-control row). Whether rent is owed while a damaged unit is unusable is otherwise case law, so put a casualty clause in the lease. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: Drug-Free and Crime-Free Lease Addenda: No Arkansas Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that requires, authorizes in special terms, or limits a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum. Such a term is an ordinary lease provision, and the library's criminal-activity clause covers it. It is worth having: an owner can be charged abatement costs and damages when rental property becomes a drug nuisance, and a tenant's drug activity also supports the fast nuisance-eviction route. Keep the clause's carve-outs for domestic-abuse victims and calls for police or emergency help, which Arkansas protects.

title: Domestic-Abuse Eviction Protections in Arkansas
bodyText: If a tenant, an applicant or a household member is a victim of domestic abuse shown by a court order (identified within the last 60 days, or within 60 days after a tenancy ended because of the abuse), you may not end or refuse to renew the tenancy, refuse to rent, or otherwise retaliate in leasing because of the abuse. Domestic abuse means causing physical injury, or a reasonable fear of injury or harm, to a household member by a current or former household member, or a sex crime or stalking against a household member. You may still evict for reasons unrelated to the abuse, such as unpaid rent. If the abuser is under a court order to stay away from a co-tenant, you may refuse the abuser access to the victim's residence unless a court order permits it, terminate the abuser's tenancy, evict the abuser whether or not the abuser is on the lease, and sue for unpaid rent and for damages from the abuse; a court must order termination or eviction on proof that the person is a domestic abuse offender. A tenant cannot waive the right to call the police or for other emergency help, so never treat such calls as a lease violation. These rules apply to every type of tenancy.

title: No Early-Termination Right for Domestic-Abuse Victims in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas gives a domestic-abuse, sexual-assault, stalking or trafficking victim no statutory right to end a lease early or be released from it. What Arkansas does provide: you may not end, refuse to renew or refuse a tenancy, or retaliate, because of documented abuse; the victim's locks may be changed at the tenant's expense with your consent; and, if the abuser is under a court order to stay away from a co-tenant, you may refuse the abuser access to the victim's residence and go to court to end the abuser's tenancy or evict the abuser. Consider agreeing to a written early release when a victim asks; it avoids a vacant unit with a tenant who cannot safely stay. The lease's own early-termination option, the military termination right and the habitability termination right still apply.

title: What Proves Domestic Abuse Under Arkansas Housing Law
bodyText: Arkansas's housing protections for domestic-abuse victims turn on one kind of document: a court order containing evidence of the abuse, such as an order of protection. The person must be identified in that order within the preceding 60 days, or within 60 days after a tenancy was ended by the person, a household member or you because of the abuse. A police report, an advocate's letter or the tenant's own statement does not trigger the statute, though you may accept them voluntarily. The abuser is the person the order identifies as committing the abuse. An order of protection may itself exclude the abuser from the shared home or the victim's residence. Keep these documents confidential, and ask only for what you need.

title: When an Arkansas Tenant May End a Lease Early
bodyText:
Arkansas gives tenants few statutory early-termination rights.

**Military:** a soldier or airman (or spouse) may terminate the lease of the primary residence when ordered to state active military service for more than 180 continuous days, assigned a permanent change of station more than 50 miles away, or discharged under honorable conditions after at least 180 continuous days of active duty. The tenant must deliver written notice (by mail, courier or personal delivery with a written receipt) stating the service dates, the commanding officer's unit, address and phone, and that the tenant claims the benefit, together with the current month's rent and the next month's rent and regular monthly charges; you may deduct prepaid amounts and the deposit from those payments. The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act adds federal rights.

**Habitability:** a tenant whose rent is current may end the lease without penalty if the defect in the implied quality standards is not excused (for example, tenant-caused or entry refused) and you do not fix it within 30 calendar days after receiving written notice.

There is no domestic-abuse termination right and no general right to leave early. Early-termination fees are not regulated by statute; whether a fee is an unenforceable penalty is case law, so keep it reasonable. These rights matter mainly for fixed terms; a periodic tenant can end the tenancy on 7 or 30 days' written notice.

title: Condemnation of Rental Property: No Arkansas Lease Rule
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute saying what happens to a lease, or to the tenant's rent, when the property is taken by eminent domain. The Constitution requires just compensation when private property is taken or damaged for public use, and whether a tenant's leasehold shares in the award is case law.

When a public body's project, financed at least partly with federal funds, displaces people from their homes, Arkansas law authorizes it to give relocation assistance and payments to the displaced persons under the federal Uniform Relocation Act, and those payments are not compensation for the property taken.

Put a condemnation clause in the lease: that the lease ends on the taking (or on a partial taking that makes the unit unusable), that rent is prorated to that date, and that the award belongs to you except any separate payment the tenant receives for moving costs.

title: Who Can File for an LLC or Corporate Landlord in Arkansas
bodyText: The Arkansas eviction statute lets a landlord or the landlord's agent file the eviction complaint, with a supporting affidavit signed by someone with personal knowledge of the grounds. That does not settle who may represent a company in court: Arkansas statutes let only persons admitted by the Supreme Court practice law, and make it unlawful for a corporation or voluntary association to practice or appear as an attorney for any person in court, though a company may employ attorneys for its own litigation. Court rules add a limit for small claims (cases up to the small-claims cap): attorneys may not take part, collection agencies and assignees may not sue, and a corporation may sue only if closely held and represented by an officer; limited liability companies are not mentioned. Whether a non-lawyer agent may file or appear for a company is a case-law question, so the cautious course for an LLC or corporate landlord is to file evictions through an Arkansas-licensed attorney. You also need an attorney to recover attorney's fees for a willful breach or bad-faith nonpayment. An individual owner may represent himself or herself.

title: No Arkansas Environmental-Event Termination Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute letting either side end a lease after an environmental event such as wildfire smoke, a chemical release or an air-quality emergency. A lease may give you an opt-in right to end the tenancy in such an event, as a contract term, but write it narrowly, refund prepaid rent and the deposit as the deposit rules require, and remember that a periodic tenancy can be ended anyway on 7 or 30 days' notice. The implied quality standards are excused only while you are temporarily prevented by an act of God or similar event. The library's optional Arkansas casualty clause covers damage from fire or other casualty; a broader right to end the lease after an environmental or government-ordered closure is lawful as a contract term, but the library does not offer one, so a landlord who wants it should add their own clause and take advice first.

title: Stays of Eviction in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no general hardship stay of eviction.
