The stays that exist: Military: during a service member's state active military service, if the rent is under $1,200 a month you may not evict the service member or dependents for nonpayment, or hold their property, except by court order, and in any possession case the court may on its own stay the case for up to three months unless the service member's ability to pay is not materially affected; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act adds federal protections. Appeals: an appeal does not stop the eviction unless the tenant posts an appeal bond within the time the statute sets (the eviction chapter has two bond provisions, one requiring a bond for costs and damages within 5 days of the notice of appeal, the other allowing a stay on a bond to pay rent as it comes due; expect the court to require the bond and rent payments). If the tenant misses a bond payment by 5 days, a writ issues on your application. Unlawful detainer: a tenant may keep possession only by posting, within 5 days after the writ issues, security of at least the unpaid rent plus rent accruing while the tenant stays. Bankruptcy filings have their own federal automatic stay.

title: How Evictions Work in Arkansas
bodyText: Never remove a tenant yourself: entering and holding property other than peaceably and by law, or putting the occupant or the occupant's goods out, is a forcible entry and detainer. Arkansas has three court routes. 1. Landlord-tenant act eviction (district court): file a complaint and an affidavit signed by someone with personal knowledge. The court orders the tenant to vacate or show cause within 10 calendar days after service; the order is served like a summons, or posted on the premises if service fails and no one is in possession. If the tenant does not appear, the court enters judgment and the sheriff evicts; if the tenant contests, the case is tried like any civil case, and after judgment for you the writ issues within 3 days. A tenant who raises defenses must keep paying you the rent as it comes due, and either pay the rent you claim was owed before the order or, if the court allows, submit a receipt or cancelled check showing it was paid, or the court issues the writ. Accepting rent after the order does not waive the eviction. 2. Unlawful detainer (circuit court): for nonpayment, first give a 3-day written notice to quit and demand for possession. After a complaint and affidavit, the tenant has 5 days (excluding Sundays and holidays) to file an objection, or a writ issues; after a hearing the court may issue the writ, and the tenant can stay only by posting security for unpaid and accruing rent. Judgment includes rent and, for residential property, liquidated damages equal to the rental value for each month or part of a month of unlawful detention. District courts may hear unlawful detainer only if a Supreme Court rule permits, and none currently does. 3. Nuisance eviction for drug, gambling, prostitution or illegal-alcohol use (see the criminal-activity row). An old statute also makes it a misdemeanor to refuse to vacate after 10 days' written notice following nonpayment; whether it is still enforceable is a case-law question, so do not rely on it. At a writ, the sheriff may remove locks and, after 24 hours, the tenant's belongings to storage. Time periods are counted under the Arkansas Rules of Civil Procedure, which skip weekends and holidays inside short periods; use the longer count. Federal CARES Act notices and military protections may also apply.

title: No Arkansas Eviction-Record Sealing Law
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that seals, expunges or removes eviction case records, automatically or on request, and none that gives a landlord a right to object. Under the Supreme Court's public-access order, court records are open unless a statute, court rule or protective order closes them, so eviction filings and judgments generally stay public. You may consider eviction records in screening, but apply your criteria consistently.

title: Eviction Papers: The Lease Cannot Name Who Accepts Service in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas law has no provision letting the lease name a person to accept eviction court papers for the tenant. The order to vacate in a landlord-tenant act eviction is served the way a district court summons is served, and if service fails and no one is found in possession, it may be posted on the most conspicuous part of the premises; in unlawful detainer, the sheriff or a process server serves the summons, complaint and statutory notice. For ordinary written notices (not court papers), the tenant receives notice when it comes to the tenant's attention, or when it is handed to the tenant or mailed by registered or certified mail to the place the tenant has designated for notices, or otherwise the tenant's last known residence, and proof of mailing is enough; so it helps to have the tenant name a notice address in the lease. Separately, a city rental inspection program may require out-of-state owners to name an agent for service of process. The only Arkansas address-confidentiality provision the search found is for driver's licenses (a domestic-violence victim's license may show a post office box), and it sets no rule for serving court papers.

title: Fast Eviction for Drug, Gambling, Prostitution and Nuisance Activity
bodyText: Arkansas has a separate, faster eviction procedure for a tenant who uses or lets others use the home as a common nuisance (a place used for illegal drug activity, or to commit a continuing series of three or more crimes) or for illegal gambling, prostitution or the unlawful sale of alcohol. You, the owner's agent, the county prosecutor or the city attorney may file it. The court serves a summons and a notice; if the tenant files no written objection within five days (not counting Sundays and legal holidays), the clerk issues a writ of possession at once. If the tenant objects, you must present enough evidence at a hearing to make a prima facie case of the criminal activity. The sheriff or police may remove the tenant 24 hours after serving the writ and store the belongings; the tenant has seven business days to reclaim them after paying storage, after which the court orders them sold. The court may award you attorney's fees and costs, you keep your separate claim for rent and repairs, and you are immune from claims for breach of quiet enjoyment for acting under this procedure. File in circuit court: the statute lets district courts hear these cases only if a Supreme Court rule or order allows, and none was found. Two related tools: a housing authority evicting after a controlled-substances conviction gets a hearing within ten days of the tenant's objection in an unlawful detainer case, and you may still use the ordinary 14-day notice for criminal activity that breaks the lease. Do not evict a tenant because the tenant or a household member was the victim of domestic abuse. The procedure is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no just-cause or good-cause eviction law; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none, and no subset of tenancies (such as mobile home lots) needs a reason to end. A fixed-term lease ends when its term expires, and you may then sue for possession if the tenant stays without your consent. A week-to-week tenancy ends on written notice given at least 7 days before the termination date, and a month-to-month tenancy on written notice given at least 30 days before it. Some limits apply whatever the lease says: you may not end, refuse to renew or otherwise retaliate against a tenant because the tenant or a household member was the victim of documented domestic abuse; you may not take retaliatory action, especially eviction, against an occupant because of lead hazards after you have been notified of them; you may not retaliate against anyone for exercising fair-housing rights or end a tenancy for a discriminatory reason; and a landlord may not evict an Arkansas National Guard member called to state active duty (for more than 180 continuous days, or for any period under an emergency management compact or a governor's proclamation), or the member's dependents, for nonpayment of rent under $1,200 a month without a court order.

title: Foreclosure of a Rental: No Arkansas Tenant-Protection Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute of its own protecting tenants when a rental property is foreclosed, and none requiring you to tell tenants or applicants that the property is in foreclosure; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Federal law generally lets a bona fide tenant stay to the end of the lease, or for at least 90 days after notice, when the buyer at a foreclosure sale takes over; check it before a buyer tries to remove a tenant. One Arkansas rule does follow the property: whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends, including a buyer at foreclosure, is bound by the deposit statute and must return the deposit as it requires. The deposit statute does not cover an individual who, with a spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units and does not pay a third person to manage them; the same course is still the safe one for them. If you are behind on your mortgage, telling tenants early is good practice even though Arkansas does not require it.

title: No Right to Pay and Stay After Nonpayment
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that lets a tenant who is behind on rent undo the end of the tenancy, or stop your eviction case, simply by paying what is owed; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. A tenant who does not pay rent when due forfeits the right to keep occupying, and if rent is still unpaid five days after the due date you may end the rental agreement and start an eviction. Two court rules give the tenant some room. In an unlawful detainer case the court may, on motion and good cause, let the tenant keep possession if within five days after the writ issues the tenant posts security of at least the delinquent rent plus the rent that will accrue. In an eviction under the 2007 Act, a tenant who raises defenses must pay the rent owed and the rent as it comes due, or the court issues the writ. Once the court has issued its order to vacate or show cause, taking rent does not waive your right to the eviction. Before that point no statute says what accepting full payment does, so decide whether you will take the money before you take it, and put any agreement to let the tenant stay in writing. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Lease Guarantors: No Arkansas Guaranty Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on lease guaranties: nothing limits a guarantor to the original term, requires a guaranty to state a maximum or an end date, or sets its form; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Whether a guarantor stays liable after a renewal, a month-to-month holdover or a rent increase depends on the guaranty's wording and on case law. Arkansas's statute of frauds does reach a guaranty: a promise to answer for another person's debt cannot be enforced unless it, or a note of it, is in writing and signed by the guarantor. Have the guarantor sign a written guaranty, and say in it whether it covers renewals, extensions, holdover periods and rent changes. If you take money from a guarantor as security, count it toward the deposit cap: a landlord covered by the deposit statute may not demand or receive a security deposit, however labelled, of more than two months' periodic rent. The deposit statute does not cover an individual who, with a spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units and does not pay a third person to manage them; the guaranty rules above still apply to them.

title: Tenant Holds Over: What You Can Recover in Arkansas
bodyText:
If a tenant stays after the lease ends or after you have ended it, and you have not agreed to the stay, you may sue for possession. If the holdover is not in good faith you may also recover reasonable attorney's fees, and if it is a willful violation of the lease or the 2007 Act you may recover up to three months' periodic rent or twice your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus reasonable attorney's fees. If you use an unlawful detainer action instead, the court awards the rent due (or the fair rental value) and, in every case, liquidated damages equal to the rental value for each month or part of a month the tenant wrongfully stayed.

If you consent to the tenant staying, for example by taking rent for a new period, the tenancy becomes week-to-week (for a roomer paying weekly) or month-to-month, and you must then give 7 or 30 days' written notice to end it. Arkansas has no older double-rent holdover statute alongside these rules. The lease's holdover clause should not promise less than these measures, and you cannot collect the same loss twice.

title: No Cap on a Lease Holdover Rate
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute capping the holdover rent or holdover damages a lease may set.

The statutes give you their own measures whatever the lease says: for a willful holdover, up to three months' periodic rent or twice your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees; and in an unlawful detainer case, the rent due plus liquidated damages equal to the monthly rental value for each month or part of a month. A lease rate far above the regular rent may be treated by a court as an unenforceable penalty. The safe course is a holdover rate tied to the rent or the rental value, without asking for both the lease rate and the statutory damages for the same days.

title: Tenants' Property Exemptions: Don't Ask for a Waiver
bodyText: Arkansas's Constitution protects some of a debtor's property from being seized or sold to pay a contract debt, which includes unpaid rent. An unmarried resident who is not the head of a family may keep personal property he or she selects worth up to $200, plus wearing apparel; a married resident or head of a family may keep up to $500, plus the family's wearing apparel. The homestead exemption protects a home the debtor owns, so it rarely matters to a renter. To use an exemption the tenant files a sworn schedule of property after an execution or attachment issues, and the court may hold a hearing. No Arkansas statute lets a lease waive these exemptions, and a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none; whether a lease waiver would be enforced is case law, so leave waivers out of the lease. An agreement waiving a right the Arkansas Constitution protects must at least be in a writing signed by the person giving it up. Arkansas also gives you a lien on property the tenant places on the premises for sums the lease requires; enforce it through the court, where the tenant can claim the exemptions, and never seize belongings yourself during the tenancy (see the landlord-lien row). The rules are the same for every kind of tenancy.

title: No Early Termination for Illness or Moves to Care
bodyText: Arkansas gives tenants no statutory right to end a lease early because of illness, disability, old age or a move to a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. A month-to-month tenant can always leave on 30 days' written notice (7 days for week-to-week), so the question matters mainly for fixed-term leases, where the tenant stays liable under the lease unless you agree otherwise. The statutory early-exit rights Arkansas does have are for service members and for a defect in the implied quality standards that you do not fix within 30 days (see the statutory early-termination row). You may agree in the lease or later to let a tenant leave early for a move to care, and fair-housing law may require you to consider a disabled tenant's request for a reasonable accommodation. Tenant death is covered separately.

title: Arkansas Landlord's Lien on a Tenant's Property
bodyText: Arkansas gives you a lien on all property the tenant places on the premises, for the payment of all sums the tenant agreed to pay. The statute gives no procedure for enforcing it, and the Uniform Commercial Code's secured-transaction rules do not cover a landlord's lien, so you cannot perfect or foreclose it like a security interest. Do not take or hold a tenant's belongings yourself during the tenancy: carrying away or putting out the goods of the person in possession is a forcible entry and detainer, the tenant's personal-property exemptions (up to $200 or $500, plus clothing) apply against process to collect a contract debt, and taking and holding the property of a deployed Arkansas National Guard member or family for unpaid rent under $1,200 a month needs a court order. Ask the court to enforce the lien when you sue for rent. After the lease ends, property the tenant leaves is treated as abandoned and you may dispose of it. Separate liens exist for crops on farm land and for unpaid lot rent on an unoccupied manufactured home; neither reaches an ordinary home rental. Whether and how the lien can be enforced against exempt property is case law.

title: Your Remedies When the Lease Ends for the Tenant's Breach
bodyText: When the rental agreement has been terminated, Arkansas gives you a right to possession, a right to the rent, and a separate claim for actual damages for the tenant's breach, plus reasonable attorney's fees; you may pursue them together. Before termination you may recover actual damages and get injunctive relief, judgments or eviction in circuit or district court without posting a bond for any lease violation. Attorney's fees for a willful non-rent violation, or for nonpayment of rent that was not in good faith, are available only if a lawyer represents you. In an unlawful detainer case the court adds liquidated damages equal to the monthly rental value for each month the tenant wrongfully stayed. Rent keeps accruing at the old rate while an eviction under the 2007 Act is pending and the tenant remains, and taking that rent does not waive the eviction. Whether you must try to re-rent to reduce your damages is case law; making reasonable efforts is the safe course. The remedies are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies, but rent for the rest of a fixed term is in practice the largest item, so keep records of your re-renting efforts.

title: Fixing a Tenant's Health-and-Safety Breach Yourself
bodyText: If a tenant's failure to keep up the unit materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by a repair, by replacing a damaged item or by cleaning, you may give written notice describing the problem and asking the tenant to fix it within 14 days (or as promptly as an emergency requires). If the tenant does not, you may enter, have the work done in a workmanlike manner, and require the tenant to reimburse you; your other remedies, including termination, remain. Arkansas defines rent as the payment for use of the premises including late charges but excluding other charges, so a repair bill is not rent even if the lease calls it additional rent: do not use the five-day nonpayment route to evict over it. Collect it as a lease charge, from the deposit at move-out where the deposit statute allows, or by suit, and treat an unpaid bill as a lease violation with the 14-day notice. For problems that are not health-and-safety items, Arkansas gives no statutory self-cure right; rely on the lease and the 14-day notice. The rule is the same for every kind of tenancy. Because the statute already gives you this right, the library does not offer a separate self-cure clause for Arkansas.

title: Liquidated Damages: The Statute's Measure and Lease-Set Amounts
bodyText: Arkansas law itself awards liquidated damages when you win an unlawful detainer case: in every case, on top of the rent due, the court assesses the rental value for each month or part of a month the tenant wrongfully stayed in a home (three times the rental value for commercial or mixed-use property). No Arkansas statute governs liquidated-damages amounts that a residential lease sets for a tenant's breach, such as a fixed early-termination charge. Whether such an amount is enforceable or an unenforceable penalty is case law. The safe course is an amount that is a reasonable estimate of your likely loss when the lease is signed, stated plainly, and not added to actual damages for the same loss.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that lets a residential landlord change the locks or lock a tenant out for unpaid rent, even with notice and even if the lease allows it; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none (a self-storage operator's right to deny access to a storage unit does not apply to homes). Arkansas law points the other way: entering by breaking doors or windows, putting the occupant's goods out of doors, or turning the occupant out by force, threats or frightening circumstances is a forcible entry and detainer, the court can award a dispossessed tenant damages, and taking or keeping possession of real estate by force or violence without legal authority is a misdemeanor. Use the court process: an eviction under the 2007 Act or an unlawful detainer action, after which the sheriff executes the writ and may remove locks. A lease clause allowing a lockout does not protect you. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Minors in Arkansas Eviction Cases
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute barring you from naming a minor in an eviction or setting special rules for minor tenants; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. In an eviction under the 2007 Act the landlord is the plaintiff and the tenant is the defendant, and a tenant is a person entitled under the rental agreement to occupy the unit. Name the adults who signed the lease or who are otherwise entitled to occupy under it; do not name the tenants' children. Whether a lease signed by a minor binds the minor is case law: if you rent to someone under 18, get an adult co-signer. In an unlawful detainer case the sheriff ejects the named defendants and anyone who entered after the writ issued; whether a writ reaches other occupants already living there is not settled by statute, so name every adult occupant. Children ordinarily leave with the parent who is named, so you do not need to name them.

title: Notice Before a Nonpayment Eviction in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has three routes after a tenant fails to pay rent, each with its own notice. (1) Eviction under the 2007 Act: if rent is unpaid five days after it is due, you may end the rental agreement, and the statute itself says that nonpayment within five days of the due date is legal notice to the tenant that you may begin eviction, so no separate written notice is required before you file the complaint and affidavit; many landlords still send a written demand, which does no harm. (2) Unlawful detainer: you must first give a written three-day notice to quit and demand for possession; count the three days the long way (excluding the day of service, weekends and holidays) because whether court-rule counting applies to this notice is unsettled. (3) A criminal statute makes a tenant who willfully refuses to vacate after ten days' written notice to vacate for nonpayment guilty of a misdemeanor (a fine of $1 to $25 a day); leave that route to prosecutors and use a civil eviction. No statute prescribes the wording of a notice, lets the lease serve as the notice, or lets the lease waive the three-day notice. Deliver written notices in hand or by registered or certified mail to the place the tenant has designated (or the tenant's last known residence), and keep proof. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. An unpaid late charge counts as rent under the 2007 Act.

title: No Arkansas Rule on Fees for Serving Notices
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that allows, caps or bans a fee for preparing or serving a notice to a tenant (such as a notice to quit or a 14-day notice); a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Charge such a fee only if the lease provides it, and keep it to your actual cost. It is not rent: Arkansas counts late charges as rent but excludes other charges, so you cannot evict on the five-day nonpayment route over an unpaid notice fee. Your recoverable costs of an eviction come instead from the court (court costs) and from the attorney's-fee rules, which require that a lawyer represent you for most fee awards under the 2007 Act.

title: Don't Rely on a Lease Waiver of the Notice to Quit
bodyText: No Arkansas statute lets a lease shorten or waive the three-day written notice to quit required before an unlawful detainer action for nonpayment; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. The 2007 Act also says that, except as it provides, a landlord and tenant may not agree in a lease to waive any of the rights, duties or remedies available under the Act, so do not try to shorten its 7-day, 30-day or 14-day notices either. You rarely need a waiver: under the 2007 Act, rent unpaid five days after the due date is itself legal notice that you may begin eviction. If you use unlawful detainer, give the three-day written notice every time. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Ending a Lease to Move In: Arkansas Has No Owner Move-In Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute giving you, or limiting, a right to end a tenancy so that you or a relative can move in. A week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy can be ended for any lawful reason on 7 or 30 days' written notice. During a fixed term you may end the lease early to move in only if the lease reserves that right; a silent lease gives you none, and the tenant may stay to the end of the term. If you want the option, use the optional owner-occupancy clause and give the notice it sets. If the tenant does not leave by the termination date, recover possession through the court.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute letting you require a tenant to sign a bond, with a confessed judgment, promising to give up possession at the end of the term; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. The bonds Arkansas does have run the other way and are set by the court: a tenant who wants to stay during an unlawful detainer case must post security of at least the delinquent rent plus rent that will accrue; a tenant who appeals an eviction must post a bond to stay it; and you may evict without posting a bond yourself. Do not put a confession-of-judgment or possession-bond clause in the lease; use the security deposit (within the deposit cap) and the court process.

title: Delay in Delivering Possession: No Arkansas Statute
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute on what happens if you cannot deliver possession on the start date (for example because a prior tenant holds over) and no statutory tenant remedy for it. The lease controls: the library's possession-delay clause (rent abates until possession, and the tenant may cancel with a full refund if possession is not delivered within 30 days) is lawful in Arkansas.

Two Arkansas rules start at delivery: the implied quality standards (water, electricity, sewer and plumbing, roof and envelope, and existing heating and air conditioning) must be met when possession is delivered, and you should hand the tenant the move-in defect form when possession becomes available so the safe-harbor works. If a holdover tenant is the cause, you may sue that tenant for possession and damages. The rule is the same for every kind of tenancy.

title: Nuisance Laws That Reach Rental Owners
bodyText: Several Arkansas laws can be used against a rental where drugs, crime or other nuisances occur, and some reach you as owner even if you did nothing wrong yourself. (1) Drug nuisance: a dwelling used to sell, store, make, use or give away controlled substances is a common nuisance; the prosecutor, city attorney, county attorney, Attorney General, any citizen or resident, or a neighborhood organization within 1,000 feet may sue the owner or tenant, and the court may enjoin it, order the building closed or order the responsible person to pay its rental value, and recover costs and damages from the owner. (2) Crime series: premises used to commit three or more crimes can be enjoined, closed or subject to a court-ordered eviction. (3) In a city, conduct that unreasonably interferes with neighbors, or three district-court health-and-safety code convictions on one parcel in a year (or one, if the offense is an imminent threat to health, safety or welfare), is a common nuisance, unless the conduct is permitted by and conforms to city ordinances; and a city of the first or second class may create a criminal nuisance abatement board that can order you to evict the responsible tenants, run background checks on future tenants, close the premises or bring it up to code, with fines up to $250 a day for violations. (4) You can evict quickly: a tenant who lets the home become a common nuisance commits unlawful detainer, and the separate nuisance-eviction procedure is available to you (see the expedited criminal eviction row). Act promptly on reports of criminal activity, document them, and use the lease's criminal-activity terms.

title: The Tenant's Belongings After an Eviction
bodyText: When the court issues a writ of possession, the sheriff serves it on the tenant (or posts it on the front door if no one is found within eight hours). If the tenant is still there 24 hours after service, the sheriff removes the tenant's belongings, with labor and help you must provide, to a public warehouse or another reasonably safe storage place under your control until the court makes a final determination. If the court rules for you and gives you a money judgment, it orders the belongings sold in a commercially reasonable manner, with the proceeds going first to storage costs, then to your judgment, and any excess to the tenant; if it rules for the tenant, the belongings go back at once and you pay the storage. In the separate nuisance-eviction procedure the tenant has seven business days to reclaim stored belongings after paying storage, after which the court orders them sold. Property a tenant leaves behind after the lease ends without a writ (for example, after moving out) is treated as abandoned and you may dispose of it as you see fit; inventory and photograph it first and keep anything of obvious value for a reasonable time, because the abandonment rule does not override the writ procedure when the sheriff removes the property. A former tenant who stays or comes back after the writ may be committing criminal trespass. These statutes do not mention animals; ask the sheriff or local animal control before the writ is executed.

title: No Statutory Redemption Before Eviction
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute letting a tenant redeem the tenancy by paying the judgment or the arrears before the eviction is carried out, no rule on accepting partial rent with set reservation wording, and no rule on payments from charities or agencies; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. You may refuse a late or partial payment; if you accept rent after the court has issued its order to vacate or show cause, the statute says it does not waive the eviction or renew the tenancy. The court may let an unlawful detainer defendant keep possession only on posting security of at least the delinquent and accruing rent. See the forfeiture and pay-and-stay row for the details.

title: False Rental Applications: No Special Arkansas Remedy
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute giving you a special right to end a lease because the tenant's rental application was false. The library's application-accuracy clause makes the truth of the application a lease term, so a material misstatement is a lease violation you enforce like any other: written notice describing it, with termination not less than 14 days after the tenant receives the notice if it is not remedied (a lie usually cannot be remedied, but give the notice anyway).

Arkansas's criminal-record sealing law lets a person whose record has been sealed say that the conduct did not occur and that no sealed record exists; do not treat that answer as false. Fair-housing law limits what you may ask and how you may use the answers.

title: No Right to End the Lease Because a Repair Costs Too Much
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute letting a landlord end a lease because a repair would be uneconomical, and none letting a tenant end it for that reason; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none, and Arkansas has no casualty statute for fire or other damage. For leases entered or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right), you must keep the six implied quality standards (water, electricity, potable water, sewer and plumbing, roof and envelope, existing heating and air conditioning), except when an act of God, a utility failure or another force majeure event temporarily prevents it; if the tenant's rent is current, the defect is not excused (for example, tenant-caused or entry refused) and you do not fix it within 30 calendar days after receiving the tenant's written notice, the tenant's only remedy is to end the lease without penalty and get back the deposit refundable under the deposit statute. If you want a right to end the lease when the property is badly damaged, put a casualty clause in the lease. A week-to-week tenancy can be ended on 7 days' and a month-to-month tenancy on 30 days' written notice before the termination date; a fixed-term lease cannot be ended early for this reason unless it says so.

title: Retaliation: No General Arkansas Ban, but Three Specific Ones
bodyText: Arkansas has no general statute barring a landlord from raising rent, refusing to renew or evicting because a tenant complained about conditions, called an inspector or joined a tenants' group; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none, and there is no presumption of retaliation. Three specific bans do apply. You may not end or refuse to renew a tenancy, refuse to rent, or otherwise retaliate because a tenant, applicant or household member was a victim of domestic abuse shown by a court order within the preceding 60 days (or within 60 days after a tenancy ended because of the abuse). After you are notified that lead hazards are present, you may not take retaliatory action against an occupant, especially eviction or the threat of it, because of the hazards. And you may not retaliate against anyone for opposing housing discrimination or taking part in a fair-housing complaint or investigation. Federal law may add protections in subsidized housing. Even where no statute applies, avoid acting soon after a complaint without a documented, independent reason. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Rent Paid While the Tenant Fights the Eviction
bodyText: In an eviction under the 2007 Act, a tenant who raises defenses or counterclaims must keep paying you the rent as it comes due after the court's order to vacate or show cause, and must also pay the rent you claim was owed before the order (or, if the court allows, submit a receipt or cancelled check showing it was paid). You must give a written receipt for each payment unless the tenant pays by check. If the tenant does not appear within ten days, or fails to make these payments, the court issues a writ of possession; rent is not reduced for conditions the tenant, family or guests caused. If the court finds less rent due than you claimed, judgment is for the amount found; if it finds nothing due, judgment is for the tenant. In an unlawful detainer case the tenant may keep possession only by posting security of at least the delinquent and accruing rent within five days after the writ issues. On appeal, a tenant can stay the eviction by signing a bond to pay the rent as it falls due. Arkansas has no statute making a tenant's counterclaim mandatory. Count the ten days the long way, because the Rules of Civil Procedure (which the Act adopts for computing time) exclude weekends and holidays for short periods.

title: Seasonal and Vacation Rentals in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no special rules for seasonal or vacation rentals of homes; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or other accommodation subject to sales tax on lodging is outside the 2007 landlord-tenant Act, so a short vacation stay taxed as lodging is not a tenancy under it (see the rent-tax row for when lodging tax applies). A seasonal rental that is a tenancy is an ordinary fixed-term lease: it ends when the term expires, and if the tenant stays without your consent you may sue for possession. If you let the tenant stay on and accept rent, it becomes a week-to-week (roomer paying weekly) or month-to-month tenancy that needs 7 or 30 days' written notice to end. City short-term-rental ordinances may also apply.

title: No Self-Help Evictions
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute allowing a residential landlord to evict without a court; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Its forcible entry and detainer law makes it a wrong to enter or keep possession except as the law allows and then only peaceably, and lists as forcible entry breaking open doors or windows, threatening the occupant, putting the occupant's goods out of doors or carrying them away, and turning the occupant out by force or frightening threats. A tenant put out that way can sue you, and in a forcible entry or unlawful detainer case the court awards a dispossessed defendant damages; taking or keeping real estate by force or violence without legal authority is also a misdemeanor, and evicting an Arkansas National Guard member on state active duty, or the member's dependents, outside the statute is a separate misdemeanor. Do not change the locks, remove doors or belongings, or cut off utilities to force a tenant out. Get a court order (an eviction under the 2007 Act or an unlawful detainer action) and let the sheriff execute the writ. The rule is the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Military Tenants: Arkansas and Federal Protections
bodyText: Two layers protect military tenants. The federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act covers federal active duty (not reviewed here; follow it whenever a tenant or spouse is in the armed forces). Arkansas's Soldiers' and Airmen's Civil Relief Act covers Arkansas National Guard soldiers and airmen and their spouses called to state active duty, which federal law does not reach. Under it, the soldier, airman or spouse may terminate the lease of the primary residence if the member is ordered to state active duty for more than 180 continuous days, is assigned to a permanent change of station more than 50 miles away, or is honorably discharged after at least 180 continuous days of active duty. The notice must be written and delivered by mail, courier or personal delivery with a written receipt; must state the service dates, the commanding officer's unit, address and phone, and that the benefits are claimed; and must come with the current month's rent and the next month's rent and regular monthly charges, from which any prepaid rent or deposit you hold may be deducted. That deduction right comes from the military statute and applies even to landlords outside the deposit statute. Also, during the service you may not evict the member or the member's dependents, or take and hold their property, for nonpayment of rent under $1,200 a month unless a court allows it; the court may stay the case up to three months; and taking part in an eviction outside these rules is a misdemeanor. The rights apply to fixed-term and periodic leases alike.

title: No Late-Benefit Eviction Defense
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring a continuance or reinstatement when a tenant's Social Security, other benefit or housing-voucher payment arrives late; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. The ordinary rules apply: rent unpaid five days after it is due lets you end the rental agreement and begin eviction. In an unlawful detainer case the court may let the tenant stay if the tenant posts security for the delinquent and accruing rent, and Arkansas National Guard families on state active duty have their own protection. Federal rules for subsidized housing and vouchers may require more. If a tenant shows you that a benefit payment is simply delayed, a short written payment agreement is often cheaper than an eviction.

title: End of the Lease: Surrender, Belongings and the Deposit
bodyText:
In Arkansas the end of a fixed term ends the tenant's right to possession; there is no good-cause renewal right, so the library's surrender clause works as written. If the tenant stays without your consent you may sue for possession and recover holdover damages; if you consent, the tenancy becomes week-to-week or month-to-month.

Property the tenant leaves after the lease ends, voluntarily or not, is treated as abandoned and you may dispose of it as you see fit; inventory and photograph it first.

Your 60-day deadline for returning the deposit, with an itemized written notice of what you kept, runs from the end of the tenancy and the tenant's delivery of possession, so note the date the keys come back. The deposit statute does not cover an individual who, with a spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units and does not pay a third person to manage them; following the same steps is still the safe course for them.

title: Tenancies Without a Set Term in Arkansas
bodyText: Under Arkansas's 2007 landlord-tenant Act, a rental agreement that does not fix a definite term creates a week-to-week tenancy for a roomer who pays weekly rent and a month-to-month tenancy in every other case. Either side ends it by written notice given at least 7 days (week-to-week) or 30 days (month-to-month) before the termination date stated in the notice. The same rule applies when a tenant stays on with your consent after a lease ends. An older Arkansas statute-of-frauds provision says that leases made by parol (orally) and not put in writing and signed have only the effect of leases or estates at will; the statutes do not say how it fits with the 2007 Act's month-to-month default for home rentals. Treat any unwritten or open-ended home rental as month-to-month (or week-to-week for a weekly roomer), give the full written notice, and put leases longer than a year in writing.

title: Tenant Bankruptcy
bodyText: Arkansas has no landlord-tenant rule of its own for a tenant's bankruptcy; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Federal bankruptcy law governs: once a tenant files, the automatic stay generally stops you from starting or continuing an eviction or collecting past-due rent without the bankruptcy court's permission, with some exceptions. A lease clause making bankruptcy itself a default is generally not enforceable under federal law. Stop collection and eviction steps when you learn of a filing, and get advice before going further. Arkansas law matters only for the exemptions a tenant may claim in the bankruptcy, which the state sets.

title: Damage the Tenant Causes
bodyText:
An Arkansas tenant must not deliberately or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises, or knowingly let a guest do so. Your duty under the implied quality standards does not cover a defect caused by the deliberate or negligent act of the tenant, the tenant's family, another occupant or a visitor, and rent is not reduced in an eviction case for a condition they caused.

If the damage materially affects health and safety and can be repaired, replaced or cleaned, give written notice to fix it within 14 days (or as promptly as an emergency requires); if the tenant does not, you may do the work and the tenant must reimburse you. For other damage, give the 14-day notice and, if not remedied, end the rental agreement; you may recover actual damages, and attorney's fees for a willful violation if a lawyer represents you.

At move-out you may apply the deposit to damages from the tenant's noncompliance, itemized in the written notice due within 60 days. The deposit statute does not cover an individual who, with a spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units and does not pay a third person to manage them; the damage rules above apply to them, but the 60-day deposit rule does not bind them by statute.

Arkansas has no casualty statute, so the lease's damage clause controls who bears rent loss after a fire the tenant causes.

title: When a Tenant Dies: No Arkansas Statute
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute on what happens to a lease, the tenant's belongings or the deposit when a tenant dies. No statute ends the lease at death, and none lets you name a contact person to remove property or receive the deposit. Arkansas's abandoned-property rule applies only after the lease has terminated, so do not treat a deceased tenant's belongings as abandoned while the lease runs.

Deal with the personal representative of the estate (or the person legally entitled to act for it): agree in writing on a move-out date, an inventory of the belongings and the deposit refund.

A month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy can be ended by you or the estate with 30 or 7 days' written notice; whether a fixed-term lease binds the estate for the rest of the term is case law, so negotiate an early end in writing. Keep any surviving co-tenant's rights in mind: a co-tenant on the lease may stay. An optional emergency-contact clause can help you reach someone quickly.

title: Notice to End a Tenancy in Arkansas
bodyText: A week-to-week tenancy ends on written notice given at least 7 days before the termination date stated in the notice, and a month-to-month tenancy on written notice given at least 30 days before it; either you or the tenant may give it, and no reason is needed. A fixed-term lease ends when the term expires without any notice, unless the lease itself requires one. Notices for breaches are different: 14 days for a lease violation the tenant can remedy, and five days after the due date for unpaid rent (see the nonpayment-notice row). Arkansas computes the 2007 Act's time periods under the Rules of Civil Procedure, which exclude intermediate weekends and holidays for periods under 14 days, so give a 7-day notice with extra days to spare, and choose a termination date at least the full period after delivery. Deliver notices to the tenant in hand or by registered or certified mail to the address the tenant designated (or the last known residence), and keep proof. Do not try to shorten these periods in the lease: the Act bars agreeing to waive its rights. A separate rule governs oral leases of farm land (notice by June 30 not to renew for the next year).

title: Squatters and Other Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: Since 2025 Arkansas has a crime of unlawful squatting. A person commits it by knowingly entering and residing on someone else's premises (a dwelling, commercial building or vacant land not open to the public) without lawful authority, when the person cannot produce a deed or mortgage statement, a lease signed by the owner or the owner's representative, a valid written or electronic authorization to enter, or a rent receipt or other reliable proof of a rent payment to the owner within the last 60 days, after the owner has told the person to leave or reported the squatting to police, and with no lawsuit pending between them. It does not reach a current tenant, a person with a valid agreement to occupy, or the owner's immediate family. Only the owner or an authorized representative may make the report; police acting in good faith are immune; a first offense is a Class B misdemeanor, a third a Class D felony, and producing a false document is a Class D felony. You also get a civil claim for damages, restitution and attorney's fees. The statute does not itself set a removal procedure, so ask police to act on the report; if they decline, or the occupant claims a right through a tenant, use the court: an unlawful detainer after a written demand for possession, a forcible entry and detainer action, or ejectment. Criminal trespass also applies to someone who remains unlawfully. A guest or occupant the tenant let in is the tenant's responsibility under the lease; remove the tenant and occupants together by eviction.

title: Accepting Rent During an Eviction
bodyText:
Once an eviction under the 2007 Act has begun with the court's order to vacate or show cause, accepting rent, whether it was owed before the order or comes due after it, does not waive your right to the eviction and does not renew or extend the tenancy; the parties' rights stay as they were when the order issued, and rent keeps accruing at the old rate while the tenant stays.

Arkansas has no statute on accepting rent before that point, for example after a 14-day notice or after a termination date has passed; whether acceptance then waives the breach or creates a new tenancy is case law.

If you want to keep the eviction alive, file before accepting money, or give the tenant a written statement that you accept the payment without waiving the notice or the termination. A lease clause saying acceptance is not a waiver helps but is not a guarantee.

title: A Tenant's Statutory Rights to End a Lease Early in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas gives tenants only two statutory rights to end a fixed-term lease early. (1) Implied quality standards: for leases entered or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than lease-to-purchase), if the unit lacks hot and cold running water, electricity, potable water, code-compliant sewer and plumbing, a functioning roof and envelope, or the heating and air conditioning that served it at signing, the tenant may give written notice by certified mail or the method the lease provides; if rent is current, the defect is not excused (for example by the tenant's own fault, a refusal of entry or a signed move-in form noting no defect) and you do not fix it within 30 calendar days, the tenant may end the lease without penalty and get the deposit back. That is the tenant's only remedy for those defects; the tenant may not withhold rent. (2) Military: an Arkansas National Guard member or spouse may end the lease on state active duty of more than 180 days, a permanent change of station over 50 miles, or honorable discharge, with written notice and payment of the current and next month's rent. Arkansas has no statutory early-termination right for domestic-abuse victims, illness or moves to care, and no rule that leaving a statement out of the lease forfeits rent. Federal military rights also apply. A month-to-month or week-to-week tenant may always leave on 30 or 7 days' written notice.

title: When a Notice Counts as Given or Received in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas's 2007 Act has its own notice rules. A person has notice of a fact if he or she actually knows it, has received a notice of it, or has reason to know it from all the facts. You give notice by taking steps reasonably calculated to inform the tenant in the ordinary course, whether or not the tenant actually learns of it. The tenant receives a notice when it comes to the tenant's attention, or when it is delivered by hand or mailed by registered or certified mail to the place the tenant has designated for notices (or, without a designation, the tenant's last known residence); proof of that mailing counts as notice without proof of receipt. You receive a notice when it comes to your attention or is delivered to your place of business where the lease was made or any place you have held out for notices. The Act has no rule letting you and the tenant add your own delivery method (such as text messages) for notices it requires, so use hand delivery or registered or certified mail and keep proof. Two exceptions: the lease may set the method a tenant uses for a quality-standards defect notice (otherwise certified mail), and if you and the tenant agree to deal electronically, an electronic record the tenant can keep satisfies a writing requirement, though not a requirement to use certified mail. Deposit refunds may be mailed first class. The rules are the same for every kind of tenancy.

title: Addenda and the Lease: No Arkansas Precedence Rule
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute requiring a separate addendum that controls over the lease, or saying which controls when a lease and an addendum conflict. The 2007 Act treats all agreements, written or oral, and valid rules as part of the rental agreement, so an addendum is part of the lease and the library's precedence clause decides conflicts.

One Arkansas form works best as a separate signed paper: the move-in defect form for the implied quality standards, which you supply when possession is available; you are deemed to comply with the standards at move-in if the tenant signs it without noting a defect and takes possession, or does not return it within two business days. Federal disclosures (such as lead-based paint) keep their own rules.

title: Claims Against the Property: No Arkansas Notice Duty
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring you to tell tenants or applicants that the property is in foreclosure or subject to another claim, and none requiring the tenant to tell you about a lawsuit or notice concerning the property; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Federal law protects many tenants after a foreclosure sale (see the foreclosure row). A city criminal nuisance abatement board's order becomes effective seven days after it is posted on the premises and mailed to you, so watch for such postings. Asking tenants in the lease to forward any legal papers about the property is a sensible contract term.

title: Automatic Renewal of a Lease in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute governing automatic renewal of a residential lease of real property; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Arkansas's automatic-renewal law covers a paid subscription or purchasing agreement that renews automatically, with offer terms about recurring charges to the consumer's credit or debit card or third-party account, and its consumer definition speaks of acquiring goods, services, money or credit; a separate section covers automatic renewal of leases of personal property. Neither is written for a home lease, but courts have not been asked. If your lease renews automatically and you also charge renewal rent automatically to the tenant's card or account, the cautious course is to state the renewal term, rent and how to cancel clearly and conspicuously and remind the tenant before it renews. Without a renewal clause, a tenant who stays with your consent after the term becomes a month-to-month (or week-to-week roomer) tenant.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Arkansas Leases
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute specific to arbitration of landlord-tenant disputes: nothing in its landlord-tenant laws permits, requires or bars an arbitration clause in a residential lease, or says which claims must stay in court.

Arkansas's general arbitration statute makes a written agreement to arbitrate valid and enforceable except on ordinary contract grounds, but it does not apply to personal injury or tort matters, so the Arkansas act does not make a lease arbitration clause enforceable for an injury claim; whether the Federal Arbitration Act would enforce one was not reviewed.

The landlord-tenant statutes send possession cases to the courts (eviction in district court under the 2007 Act; unlawful detainer in circuit court), so if you use an arbitration clause, carve out eviction and possession actions and small claims, and make it mutual. A one-sided clause may not be enforced.

The library now offers an optional clause, `arbitration-agreement`, built on these limits: money claims only, with possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury and emergency claims kept in court, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials from both of you.

title: Other Rules Arkansas Does Not Have
bodyText: Several rules found in other states are not in Arkansas's statutes. (1) No special right to end a lease because the rental application was false; enforce accuracy as a lease term with the 14-day notice (see the application-accuracy row). (2) No Arkansas rule on a tenant's bankruptcy; federal law governs. (3) No type-size or bold-print rule for residential leases; the bold-type lien notices in Arkansas law apply to self-storage and marina rental agreements, not homes. (4) No statute on lease guarantors. (5) No duty to give tenants an emergency contact or 24-hour phone number. (6) No tenant-death, seasonal-rental, late-benefit or notice-fee rule. Each item has its own row. One rule Arkansas does have that many states lack: a crime of unlawful squatting (see the unauthorized-occupant row). This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution, not case law or local ordinances.

title: Domestic Abuse Law Citations Check
bodyText: Arkansas's lease protection for domestic-abuse victims has not been affected by any move or renumbering of the protective-order law. The protection turns on a documented incident of domestic abuse, defined as evidence of domestic abuse in an order of any court of competent jurisdiction, so any qualifying court order counts, including an order of protection under Arkansas's Domestic Abuse Act, which is still in the same chapter. The statute defines domestic abuse and stalking itself and lists the sex crimes it covers by criminal-code section; the list was amended in 2025 (Act 662 of 2025). To be protected, the tenant, applicant or household member must be identified in such an order within the preceding 60 days, or within 60 days of a termination of the tenancy because of domestic abuse. Ask for a copy of the court order. If the abuser is under a court order to stay away from a co-tenant, you may refuse the abuser access to the victim's residence unless a court order permits access.

title: No Emergency Contact Law
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour phone number, or regulating an emergency contact a tenant names for you. Giving tenants a way to reach you for urgent repairs is still good practice, especially for the implied quality standards (water, electricity, sewer, roof and heating and air conditioning), whose 30-day repair clock starts when you receive the tenant's written notice. Asking a tenant to name an emergency contact, with the contact's consent, is a lawful lease term; it does not let that person act for the tenant's estate if the tenant dies. The library's optional emergency and death contact clause records such a contact.

title: Checked Across the Whole Arkansas Code
bodyText: The whole Arkansas Code and Constitution, not only the landlord-tenant title, were searched for three things landlords ask about. (1) Squatters: Arkansas does have a rule, in its criminal code: unlawful squatting (2025), with a private claim for damages and attorney's fees; you can also use unlawful detainer, forcible entry and detainer, or ejectment (see the unauthorized-occupant row). (2) Rent receipts: no statute requires a receipt for rent, including cash rent, except that in a possession suit under the 2007 Act in which the tenant raises defenses or counterclaims, you must give a written receipt for each rent payment that comes due after the court's order to vacate or show cause, unless the tenant pays by check (see the rent-receipts row); give receipts anyway. (3) Landlord registration: Arkansas has no statewide rental license or registration as a condition of renting or of winning an eviction, except that an out-of-state limited liability company or corporation doing business here must register with the Secretary of State and may not maintain an eviction or other court action until it does (Ark. Code Ann. §§ 4-38-902, 4-38-913, 4-27-1501, 4-27-1502); the only related statute protects a real-estate licensee who serves as agent for service of process for an out-of-state owner under a city's rental inspection program, so check your city's ordinances. This search did not cover local ordinances or case law.

title: Electronic Signatures and Records in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas has adopted the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act. Between parties who have agreed to do business electronically (which can be shown by the circumstances and conduct), a lease or signature may not be denied effect just because it is electronic, an electronic record satisfies a law requiring a writing, and an electronic signature satisfies a law requiring a signature. Unlike some states, Arkansas's version has no exclusion for eviction, default or cure notices; it excludes only wills and most of the Uniform Commercial Code.

Limits remain: either party may refuse to continue electronically for later transactions, and that right cannot be waived; an electronic record must be one the recipient can print or store, or it is not enforceable against the recipient; and where a law requires a specific delivery method, such as certified mail, that method must still be used. The library's electronic-signature clause records the parties' agreement and works in Arkansas.

title: No Arkansas Rule on Releasing Tenant Energy Data
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on releasing a tenant's energy or utility usage data to the owner, for building benchmarking or any other purpose, and no statute that requires, permits or forbids a lease clause authorizing that release. If you want a tenant's usage data from a utility, get the tenant's written authorization in the lease or a separate signed form, limit it to usage data and the stated purpose, and use the utility's own release process. The same applies to week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Entire-Agreement Clauses in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas lets the lease set its own terms on anything the landlord-tenant act or other law does not forbid, so the library's entire-agreement clause is enforceable as written. Two Arkansas points matter.

First, the act defines the rental agreement to include every agreement, written or oral, plus valid rules, so promises made outside the written lease can become part of the deal; the entire-agreement clause and its rule that changes must be in a signed writing help, but you should still put every side promise into the lease or a signed addendum.

Second, no Arkansas statute lets you change an existing lease by notice to comply with a new law, so the clause's words "as applicable law permits Landlord to change it by written notice" have no Arkansas statute behind them. During a fixed term, change terms only by a signed amendment. In a periodic tenancy, you may end it by written notice (7 days before the termination date for week-to-week, 30 days for month-to-month) and offer new terms.

Whatever the lease says, for a lease entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or with a purchase right), the implied quality standards override a contrary lease term unless the tenant agrees in writing to renovate, remodel or complete construction of the unit, and the lease cannot waive the rights, duties or remedies of the landlord-tenant act. Whether a court will hear evidence of an earlier oral promise despite the clause is case law.

title: Arkansas Law Governs Every Arkansas Rental
bodyText:
The Arkansas Residential Landlord-Tenant Act applies to every rental agreement for a dwelling unit located in Arkansas, wherever the lease was signed, so a lease cannot choose another state's law to avoid it; the library's governing-law clause, which names Arkansas law plus applicable city and county law, matches that. Arkansas courts have jurisdiction over a landlord for conduct governed by the act.

Local law still matters: a city or county housing standard stricter than the state's implied quality standards applies to you, while local control of rent, application fees and security deposits is preempted (see the rent-control row). The act does not reach the arrangements it excludes, such as transient hotel or motel stays subject to lodging sales tax, employee housing conditioned on employment, occupancy under a contract to buy, and agricultural rentals (see the scope row). The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Arkansas Rule on Informal Dispute Resolution
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute that requires, regulates or limits a lease clause asking landlord and tenant to try to resolve a dispute informally (for example by written notice and a meeting, or by mediation) before going to court. The landlord-tenant act says only that a claim or right under the act or the rental agreement that is disputed in good faith may be settled by agreement.

If you add such a clause, make it optional or short, and keep out of it eviction and possession actions, nonpayment of rent, emergencies and health-and-safety breaches, because the statutory timelines (rent unpaid 5 days, the 3-day notice to quit, the 14-day notice to remedy) keep running. Do not let it delay or condition the tenant's statutory rights, such as the tenant's right to end the lease after 30 days when you fail to fix a quality-standard defect, because the lease cannot waive the act's rights or remedies.

Binding arbitration is a separate topic. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Statewide Landlord Registration in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statewide landlord registration or rental licensing requirement, and no statute that makes registration a condition of renting or gives a tenant a right to end the lease if you are unregistered. Three state rules touch the subject. First, state law recognizes city rental inspection programs that require owners who live outside Arkansas to designate an agent for service of process; check your city's ordinances for any registration, inspection or fee rule (see the rental inspection row). Second, an owner may lease and manage his or her own property without a real estate license, but anyone who leases, shows, collects rent or manages rental property for others for compensation generally needs an Arkansas property management or broker license. Third, an out-of-state limited liability company may not do business in Arkansas until it registers with the Secretary of State, naming a registered agent here; until it registers it may not maintain an eviction or other court action, though its leases stay valid, and it faces back fees and a civil penalty of up to $5,000 for each year or part of a year (Ark. Code Ann. §§ 4-38-902, 4-38-903, 4-38-913). Owning property, without more, is not doing business (Ark. Code Ann. § 4-38-905(a)(10)), so whether renting it out is depends on the facts. An out-of-state corporation faces the same rules: it must get a certificate of authority before transacting business, may not maintain an eviction or other court case until it does, and owes back fees plus a civil penalty of up to $5,000 for each year or part of a year (Ark. Code Ann. §§ 4-27-1501, 4-27-1502). An individual who rents under a name other than his or her real name must file an assumed-name certificate with the county clerk; failing to is fined $25 to $100 but does not bar an eviction (Ark. Code Ann. §§ 4-70-202, 4-70-203). The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Arkansas Blank-Space Rule for Leases
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in, and no rule that an incomplete lease is a breach or unenforceable. Fill in every blank anyway, or strike it with "N/A": because the rental agreement includes oral agreements as well as the written lease, a blank on a key term such as the rent, the due date, the term or the deposit invites a dispute over what was agreed orally. If the lease fixes no definite term, the tenancy is month to month (week to week for a roomer who pays weekly), and unless the tenant is told otherwise in writing, rent is payable at the dwelling unit at the start of each month. Whether a court reads an unclear or blank term against you as the drafter is case law. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Arkansas Duty to Deliver a Lease Copy
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring you to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and none making a missing copy a defense to enforcing it. Give the tenant a fully signed copy anyway, and keep your own, including any move-in defect form the tenant signs, because that form is what lets you be deemed in compliance with the implied quality standards. If the lease is signed electronically, the tenant must be able to download, save and print it: under Arkansas's electronic transactions law, an electronic record the sender keeps the recipient from storing or printing is not enforceable against the recipient. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Arkansas Initials Requirement
bodyText: No Arkansas statute requires a tenant to initial any residential lease term, or sets a special format for a term that departs from the statutory default, for the term to bind the tenant; the signatures on the lease are enough as far as the statutes go. One Arkansas rule does turn on a separate written agreement: for leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or with a purchase right), the implied quality standards override a contrary lease term unless the tenant agrees in writing to accept responsibility to renovate, remodel or complete construction of the unit, so put any such agreement in a clearly labeled, signed section or addendum. Initials beside unusual terms (a renovation agreement, a fee, a waiver) are still good evidence the tenant saw them. Arkansas's bold-type notice rules are for self-service storage and marina rental agreements, not homes. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Arkansas Limit on Residential Lease Length
bodyText: Arkansas sets no minimum or maximum length for a private residential lease. If the lease does not fix a definite term, the tenancy is month to month (week to week for a roomer who pays weekly rent), and either side may end it by written notice at least 30 days (or 7 days for week-to-week) before the termination date in the notice. A lease longer than one year should be in a writing signed by the tenant and you (see the statute-of-frauds row). The implied quality standards apply to leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right), so a renewal of an older lease brings it under them. The only statutory caps on lease terms the search found are for public property (such as county leases of public landings and state park leases). This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Arkansas Type-Size Rule for Leases
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute setting a minimum type size or print format for a residential lease, and no evidentiary penalty for small print. The only Arkansas type rules for rental agreements the search found are the bold-type lien notices required in self-service storage and marina rental agreements, which do not apply to a home. Use readable type (10-point or larger) throughout, and set fees, waivers and other unusual terms where the tenant will see them. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Out-of-State Owners: City Agent Rules and LLC Registration
bodyText: No Arkansas statute requires an individual owner who lives outside Arkansas to name an in-state agent in the lease, bars suit until an agent is filed, requires an in-state broker, or requires tenants to withhold state income tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner. An out-of-state limited liability company is different: it may not do business in Arkansas until it files a foreign registration statement with the Secretary of State naming a registered agent here, and until it registers it may not maintain an eviction or other court action, though its leases stay valid (Ark. Code Ann. §§ 4-38-902, 4-38-903, 4-38-913). Owning property, without more, is not doing business (Ark. Code Ann. § 4-38-905(a)(10)), so whether renting it out is depends on the facts; register before you need to file. An out-of-state corporation is under the same rule: it needs a certificate of authority before transacting business, may not maintain a court case until it gets one (its acts stay valid), and owes back fees plus a civil penalty of up to $5,000 for each year or part of a year; owning property without more is not transacting business (Ark. Code Ann. §§ 4-27-1501, 4-27-1502). An individual owner who rents under a name other than his or her real name must file a certificate with the county clerk of each county where the business is done; failing to is punished by a fine of $25 to $100, but the statute does not bar a lawsuit (Ark. Code Ann. §§ 4-70-202, 4-70-203). State law does recognize city rental inspection programs that require out-of-state owners of rental property inside the city to designate an agent for service of process, and it protects a real estate licensee who serves as that agent and forwards papers to the owner's last known address within three business days; check your city's ordinances. If someone in Arkansas will lease, show, collect rent or manage the property for you for compensation, that person generally must hold an Arkansas property management or broker license. Give the tenant a written address for notices and rent, because a notice to you counts as received when delivered at the place of business through which the lease was made or at any place you hold out for receiving notices. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: How Notices Are Delivered in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas's landlord-tenant act says a person gives notice by taking steps reasonably calculated to inform the other person in the ordinary course, whether or not the other person actually learns of it. A notice to the tenant is received when it comes to the tenant's attention, or when it is handed to the tenant or mailed by registered or certified mail to the place the tenant has designated for notices (or, if none, the tenant's last known residence); proof of that mailing is notice without proof of receipt. A notice to you is received when it comes to your attention or is delivered at the place of business through which the lease was made or any place you hold out for notices.

So name a notice address for each side in the lease, and send important notices (termination, notice to remedy, notice to quit) by hand delivery or certified mail and keep proof.

Some notices have their own method: a tenant's notice of a quality-standard defect goes by certified mail or any other method the lease provides; your deposit refund and itemized notice are deemed delivered when sent first-class mail to the tenant's last known address.

Email or a portal works only if both of you agreed to deal electronically, the tenant can save and print the message, and no statute calls for a specific method such as certified mail; a tenant who agreed may refuse further electronic dealings, and the lease cannot take that right away.

Court papers in an eviction are served as the law and court rules provide, not by ordinary notice: in unlawful detainer the sheriff or a process server serves them, and an order to vacate under the 2007 Act is served the way a district court summons is served (see the eviction-service row). Time periods are counted under the Arkansas Rules of Civil Procedure. The same rules apply to every tenancy type.

title: No Arkansas Rule on Move-Out Notice Forms
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on the content of a tenant's notice to vacate or of a move-out form you ask the tenant to sign, and no required warning if the form adds terms the lease does not contain. Keep the form to what the notice needs: the tenant's move-out date and a forwarding address (your deposit refund and itemized notice are deemed delivered when mailed first class to the tenant's last known address, so a current address protects both of you). A tenant ending a periodic tenancy must give written notice at least 7 days (week-to-week) or 30 days (month-to-month) before the termination date in the notice; a fixed-term lease ends on its own terms. Do not use a move-out form to add new obligations: a new charge or waiver binds the tenant only if the tenant actually agrees to it, and no lease or rental agreement can waive the tenant's rights under the landlord-tenant act (a claim genuinely disputed in good faith may still be settled by agreement). Put any new deal, such as an early-release payment, in a separate signed agreement. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: The Notices Clause in Arkansas
bodyText: The library's notices clause works in Arkansas as written: it sends notices to the addresses in the lease and lets any statutory method control. Arkansas law makes the lease's addresses matter, because a notice to the tenant mailed by registered or certified mail to the place the tenant has designated for notices is effective on proof of mailing, and a notice to you is received at the place of business through which the lease was made or any place you hold out for notices. Fill in both notice addresses, update them in writing, and follow the specific methods in the notice-delivery row for defect notices, deposit refunds and electronic notices. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Where Arkansas Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Arkansas's landlord-tenant act lets the lease include any term not prohibited by the act or other law, and many of its rules are defaults the lease can change.
