The lease decides: when and where rent is paid (otherwise at the dwelling unit, at the start of each month or shorter term); the length of the tenancy (otherwise month to month, or week to week for a roomer paying weekly); whether the tenant may use the unit for something other than a dwelling (the act says "unless otherwise agreed"); the method for the tenant's notice of a quality-standard defect (certified mail or any other method the lease provides); whether the tenant takes on renovation or remodeling responsibility in place of the implied quality standards (only by the tenant's written agreement); attorney's fees in a contract suit (the general fee statute yields to the contract); late charges and other fees (no statute caps them, and late charges count as rent); the deposit amount, up to two months' periodic rent (the cap does not bind an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their entities, owns five or fewer units, unless a third person manages them for a fee); and, for a landlord with fewer than 12 rental units, limits on flag display. Some things the lease cannot do: waive the act's rights, duties or remedies, waive a domestic-abuse victim's right to call police or emergency help, or bar an Arkansas qualifying medical-marijuana patient's non-smoked medical use. A lease is also not needed for the default tenant duties (keeping the unit clean and safe, not disturbing neighbors, allowing reasonable entry), which apply anyway. See each topic's row for details. The defaults are the same for every tenancy type except where the row says otherwise.

title: No Arkansas Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Arkansas has no plain-language statute for residential leases: no readability test, no required statement listing the tenant's waivers, and no Attorney General preapproval process. Arkansas's Deceptive Trade Practices Act bars unconscionable, false or deceptive acts in business, commerce or trade, but its definitions do not clearly say whether it reaches a lease of a home, and case law on the point was not checked, so treat it as possibly applying. Write the lease in plain words anyway, and set fees, waivers and other unusual terms where the tenant will see them; terms that the landlord-tenant act forbids (such as a waiver of its rights or remedies) are unenforceable however plainly written. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Arkansas Rules That Depend on How Many Units You Own
bodyText: Arkansas's landlord-tenant act has no small-landlord exemption: its rules, including the implied quality standards, apply whatever the size of your portfolio. A few other Arkansas rules turn on size, and each exemption needs every condition it lists. (1) Security deposits: the deposit cap, return and penalty rules do not apply to dwelling units owned by an individual if that individual, his or her spouse and minor children, and any entities formed to rent dwelling units of which they are officers, owners or majority shareholders, together own five or fewer dwelling units; the exemption is lost for any unit whose management, including rent collection, is done by a third person for a fee. (2) Flags: the ban on rules or agreements that stop a person from properly displaying the U.S. flag does not apply to landlords of private rental property who operate fewer than 12 rental units. (3) Fair housing: Arkansas has two fair housing statutes with different exemptions. One does not apply to a two-family building where the owner or the owner's family lives in one unit, to renting rooms in a single-family home where the lessor or family lives, or to a home the owner occupied for at least three months and rents for up to 12 months while temporarily away. The other exempts some rentals by owners of no more than three single-family houses who rent without a broker or discriminatory advertising, and some owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units, and anyone who owns a dwelling for five or more families counts as in the rental business; federal fair housing exemptions are narrower, so treat every rental as covered unless your lawyer confirms an exemption. (4) Disability access: the state right of people with visual, hearing or other physical disabilities to equal access to rental housing does not reach a single-family residence of which a portion is rented; that limit applies only to the equal-access right, not to the separate right of a person with a disability to be accompanied by a service animal in housing accommodations, which has no size or building-type exemption. (5) Licensing: an owner may lease and manage his or her own property without a real estate license. The thresholds are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Arkansas Renter's Insurance Rules
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on requiring renter's insurance: none lets the tenant choose the carrier by law, limits a force-placed policy or its fee, requires an advisory that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings, or requires a flood or insurance notice before signing. You may require renter's insurance by lease, as the library's clause does. To keep it fair and defensible, let the tenant choose any licensed insurer, state the minimum liability coverage, and ask for proof at move-in and on request. Requiring insurance does not shift your own duties: your implied quality-standard duties stay with you unless the tenant agrees in writing to take on renovation, and Arkansas limits your injury liability for defects to repairs you agreed or undertook to make. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers in Arkansas
bodyText: When you sell or transfer a rental, whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends is bound by Arkansas's deposit rules, so move each tenant's deposit to the buyer at closing (see the deposit-on-sale row). The deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee. No Arkansas statute requires a written notice to tenants of a sale or a new manager, releases the seller on notice, or protects tenants when a lender forecloses; the act does count as a landlord a manager who fails to disclose as the act requires, yet contains no disclosure section, so the safe course is to tell tenants in writing the owner's and manager's names and addresses for notices and rent. That notice also matters because rent is payable at the dwelling unit unless the tenant is told otherwise in writing, and a notice to the landlord counts as received at the place of business through which the lease was made or any place held out for notices. A lender that takes possession counts as an owner. You may show the unit to prospective buyers and lenders, and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to that entry. A sale does not end an existing lease under any Arkansas statute found; if you want the right to end a lease on a sale, the lease must say so. Federal law gives tenants of foreclosed properties notice and lease rights. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: What Arkansas Landlord-Tenant Law Covers
bodyText: The Arkansas Residential Landlord-Tenant Act of 2007 applies to rental agreements for dwelling units in Arkansas, including landlord-owned mobile homes. It does not govern: residence in an institution incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services; occupancy under a contract to buy the unit; fraternity or social organization housing; transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or other lodging subject to sales tax on lodging; employee housing conditioned on employment; condominium owners and cooperative proprietary-lease holders; agricultural rentals; and charitable or emergency shelters. Property leased solely so the tenant can renovate it is not a dwelling unit under the act. Within the act, the implied quality standards apply only to leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021, and not to a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right. The security deposit subchapter has its own exemption for an individual owning five or fewer units (with spouse, minor children and their rental entities) unless a third person manages them for a fee. Older Arkansas statutes still apply alongside the act: unlawful detainer (with its 3-day notice to quit), the criminal failure-to-vacate statute (10-day notice), the abandoned-property and landlord-lien statute, the landlord tort-immunity statute, and special rules for mobile homes on leased lots and oral farmland leases. Commercial leases have their own eviction rent rules. The act's rules are the same in every county and city, though local housing codes stricter than the quality standards also apply.

title: Written Leases and Long Terms in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas's landlord-tenant act treats oral as well as written agreements as part of the rental agreement, so a month-to-month or other short tenancy can be created orally. Arkansas's statute of frauds, however, lists a lease of land for a longer term than one year among the agreements that cannot be enforced unless they are in a writing signed by the party to be charged. Put every lease of more than a year, and every renewal or extension that runs past a year, in a writing signed by you and every tenant; an electronic signature works if both sides agreed to deal electronically (see the electronic signatures row). A second old statute says a lease made orally and not put in a signed writing has only the effect of a lease at will, and a lease for more than a year may be assigned or surrendered only by a signed writing. Under the landlord-tenant act an open-ended home rental is month-to-month (week-to-week for a roomer paying weekly), which either side can end on 30 (or 7) days' written notice. Arkansas has no separate rule requiring a residential lease to be recorded to be valid. Exactly how the statute treats an unwritten long lease, and whether part performance takes a lease outside it, are questions of case law.

title: State-Prescribed Forms in Arkansas Rentals
bodyText: Arkansas prescribes no lease form and no verbatim wording for a residential lease or for your ordinary notices (termination, notice to remedy, notice to quit, deposit itemization); you write those yourself, meeting each statute's content and timing rules. The only statutory forms in Arkansas landlord-tenant law the search found are court forms: the notice the court clerk issues for the sheriff or process server to serve in an unlawful detainer case, the notice served with a summons in a nuisance eviction, and the tenant's appeal bond and order staying execution. The move-in defect form that lets you be deemed in compliance with the implied quality standards has statutory content (it must let the tenant list any defects in the six listed items) but no prescribed wording; the library's Arkansas move-in defect form clause supplies it. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Arkansas Tenant Portal Law
bodyText: Arkansas has no law on tenant portals. Rent is payable at the time and place the lease sets, so the lease may make an online portal the agreed way to pay (no statute requires you to accept cash or checks), and leases, renewals and notices may be handled electronically if both you and the tenant agreed to do business electronically. Three limits come from Arkansas's electronic transactions law. A tenant who agreed to electronic dealings may refuse to handle later transactions (such as a renewal or amendment) electronically, and the lease cannot take that right away, so keep a paper option. A document the tenant cannot save or print is not enforceable against the tenant, so let tenants download everything. And where a statute calls for a particular delivery method, such as certified mail, the portal does not replace it. The lease may name the portal as a method for the tenant's notice of a quality-standard defect, since the statute allows certified mail or any other method the lease provides. No statute addresses portal fees; state any convenience fee in the lease. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Rent Records and Tenant Data in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring you to keep a rent ledger, give the tenant a payment history on request, or attach a ledger to a nonpayment notice. The only receipt rule is in eviction cases: when a tenant raises defenses and pays rent while the case is pending, you must give a written receipt for each payment unless the tenant pays by check (see the rent receipts row). Keep a complete ledger anyway; you will need it to prove the rent claim in court and to itemize deposit deductions. For applicant and tenant data, Arkansas's Personal Information Protection Act covers a person's name combined with a Social Security number, driver's license or state ID number, a financial account or card number with the code that opens the account, medical information or biometric data. If you hold that information about an Arkansas resident, keep reasonable security procedures for it; destroy (shred, erase or make unreadable) records containing it once you no longer keep them; and if computerized data containing it is breached, notify the affected Arkansas residents without unreasonable delay, and the Attorney General if more than 1,000 people are affected, unless a reasonable investigation finds no reasonable likelihood of harm. Limit who can see application data and store it securely. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Tenant's Property Insurance in Arkansas
bodyText:
The library's tenant's-property clause, which says your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings, that you are not liable for their loss, and that the tenant must carry renter's insurance, works in Arkansas as written: no Arkansas statute voids that kind of lease term or regulates a renter's-insurance requirement.

Arkansas also shields you from injury and property-damage claims caused by a defect or disrepair unless you agreed (for consideration) or undertook by your conduct to maintain or repair the premises and failed to do it reasonably, so a lease promise to repair can create that liability.

Requiring renter's insurance does not move your own duties onto the tenant's policy: your implied quality-standard duties (water, electricity, sewer and plumbing, roof and building envelope, heating and air conditioning) stay with you unless the tenant agrees in writing to take on renovation, and no lease term can waive the landlord-tenant act's rights or remedies. The tenant remains liable for damage the tenant, family or guests cause. Whether a court would enforce the "not liable" sentence against your own negligence is case law. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Changing Lease Terms Mid-Tenancy in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute setting a notice period for changing a term of an existing tenancy (other than rent, which has no notice rule either; see the rent-increase row). During a fixed term, terms change only by a signed amendment the tenant agrees to, or as the lease itself provides. In a week-to-week or month-to-month tenancy, the way to change a term (a fee, a rule, a utility arrangement) is to end the tenancy by written notice at least 7 days (week-to-week) or 30 days (month-to-month) before the termination date and offer a new tenancy on the new terms; to be safe, give the notice so the change takes effect at the start of a rental period and say plainly that the tenant may stay on the new terms. Raising a fee the lease already provides follows the same rule. Arkansas has no section governing rules adopted during a tenancy, so do not assume a new rule binds a current tenant without the tenant's agreement or a new tenancy. No agreement may waive the landlord-tenant act's rights or remedies. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Sunset on Arkansas Tenant Laws
bodyText: None of Arkansas's core landlord-tenant statutes is on a repeal or expiration date: the Arkansas Residential Landlord-Tenant Act of 2007 (including the implied quality standards added in 2021), the security deposit statute and the unlawful detainer statute have no sunset clause. The act's only timing rules look backward: transactions entered into before July 31, 2007 and not extended or renewed on or after that date stay under the earlier law, and the implied quality standards reach leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Arkansas Lease Translation Duty
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring a residential lease, or any landlord notice, to be translated or provided in a language other than English, including when you advertise or negotiate in another language. If you negotiate with a tenant in another language, consider giving a translated copy for reference while stating which version controls, and make sure the tenant understands the key terms (rent, term, fees, deposit, notices); federal fair housing rules on national origin may bear on language practices. Arkansas's Deceptive Trade Practices Act also lists as a deceptive practice knowingly taking advantage of a consumer who is reasonably unable to protect his or her interest because of inability to understand the language of the agreement; whether that Act reaches a home lease is not settled by its text, so do not press a tenant to sign terms you know the tenant cannot read. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing in Arkansas
bodyText: Several Arkansas notices must be in writing, and your lease should not suggest that a spoken notice will do. In writing: your notice of a lease violation giving 14 days to remedy before termination; your 14-day notice to remedy a health-and-safety breach (or as promptly as an emergency requires) before you repair at the tenant's cost or terminate; a notice ending a week-to-week (7 days) or month-to-month (30 days) tenancy, from either side; the unlawful detainer demand for possession and the 3-day notice to quit for unpaid rent; the 10-day notice to vacate under the criminal failure-to-vacate statute; your itemized notice of deposit deductions; any notice changing where rent is paid; the tenant's notice of a defect under the implied quality standards; a tenant's agreement to take on renovation; a service member's lease-termination notice; and, for a mobile home left unoccupied on a leased lot with rent 60 days past due, your certified-mail notice to the lessee and lienholder. Nonpayment itself needs no written notice for a landlord-tenant act eviction: rent unpaid 5 days after the due date is legal notice that you may begin eviction. These rules apply to every tenancy type except where a period is tied to the tenancy type.

title: Animals Left in an Arkansas Rental
bodyText: Arkansas gives you no special statutory right to enter a rental to check on, feed or remove a tenant's animal, and no procedure for taking custody of an animal a tenant leaves behind. Your entry comes from the tenant's duty not to unreasonably withhold consent to entry for listed purposes (such as inspecting the premises or supplying agreed services) and from the lease; the library's pet clause lets you remove a pet in stated emergencies only to the extent applicable law permits. If you find an animal left without care, try to reach the tenant and any emergency contact, and call local animal control or law enforcement rather than keeping, rehoming or disposing of the animal yourself. Although Arkansas treats property left after a lease ends as abandoned, do not treat a living animal as ordinary abandoned property; let animal control take it. To plan ahead, ask the tenant to name in writing someone you may let in to care for or remove the animal if the tenant cannot. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution. The library does not offer a separate animal-care designee clause for Arkansas; the pet policy's emergency provisions apply, and a landlord who wants a named caregiver can add their own clause and should take advice first.

title: Service and Assistance Animals in Arkansas Rentals
bodyText:
Two sets of rules apply.

First, Arkansas's own statute gives a person with a visual, hearing or other disability the right to be accompanied in housing by a service animal especially trained to do work or perform tasks for the person, with no extra fee or charge, though the person is liable for damage the animal causes; people with visual, hearing or other physical disabilities are entitled to full and equal access to rental housing, subject only to limits established by law that apply to everyone. The equal-access section does not require you to modify the unit or provide a higher degree of care, and that section does not cover a facility designed and used primarily as a single-family residence of which a portion is rented; the separate service-animal right has no such exception, so allow a service animal there too. Denying or interfering with these rights is a misdemeanor.

Second, federal and Arkansas fair housing law require reasonable accommodations, including for emotional support animals; Arkansas lets a private property owner ban emotional support animals only where the federal Fair Housing Act does not prohibit it, so in covered housing evaluate each request under fair housing rules.

Arkansas also sets standards a healthcare provider must meet before giving documentation for an emotional support dog (license details in the documentation, a client relationship of at least 30 days unless the person is verified homeless, a yearly evaluation and a warning about misrepresentation); the statute disciplines the provider but does not say you may reject a letter that falls short, and it does not change fair housing accommodation rights, so treat a shortfall as a reason to ask for more reliable information, not as an automatic denial.

Do not charge pet fees for any accommodated animal. The library's Arkansas clause keeps the direct-threat and damage limits for other assistance animals but not for a trained service animal. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Arkansas Pet and Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Arkansas has no requirement to give a tenant a state fact sheet or other notice about pets and eviction, at signing or when you learn the tenant has a dog or cat. If an eviction or move-out may leave animals behind, tell the tenant in writing to take every animal, and call animal control rather than disposing of an animal yourself (see the animal-care row). The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Pet Deposits, Pet Rent and Pet Fees in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas has no pet-fee statute, so the deposit rules decide. A refundable pet deposit is a security deposit however it is labeled: it counts with the regular deposit and any other security money toward the cap of two months' periodic rent, and it must be returned within 60 days after the tenancy ends, less only accrued unpaid rent and damages from the tenant's noncompliance, itemized in a written notice. These deposit rules do not apply to units owned by an individual who, together with a spouse, minor children and any rental entities they own or control, owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third person manages the units (including collecting rent) for a fee.

Monthly pet rent is a charge you set by the lease; state it as a fixed amount (see the fees-as-rent row on when a charge counts as rent). If you want a one-time fee you keep, call it a fee for a stated purpose, not a deposit, and say it is not refundable; whether a court would treat it as a disguised deposit is unsettled.

Never charge a pet deposit, pet rent or any other extra fee or charge for a trained service animal (the tenant remains liable for damage the animal causes), and do not charge pet fees for any assistance animal you accommodate under fair housing law. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: No Arkansas Rule on Pet Liability Insurance
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on requiring a tenant with a pet to carry liability insurance, naming you as an interested party, or limiting breed or insurance rules. The library's pet-insurance clause works as written, and it rightly does not apply to an assistance animal: Arkansas bars any extra fee or charge for a trained service animal, and an insurance requirement for an assistance animal is risky under fair housing law. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Pet Rules Are Set by Your Lease in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute on pets in rentals: you may ban pets, limit their number, kind or size, require approval, and charge pet fees within the deposit rules (see the pet-fees row). No Arkansas statute gives seniors or anyone else a right to keep a pet.

Three limits apply: a trained service animal is not a pet and must be allowed without extra charge; other assistance animals, including emotional support animals, must be considered as reasonable accommodations under fair housing law; and the tenant must not damage the premises or disturb other tenants' peaceful enjoyment, so a nuisance animal can be grounds for a 14-day notice to remedy.

No Arkansas statute addresses removing a pet during the tenancy; the library's pet clause allows removal in emergencies only to the extent applicable law permits, so in practice call animal control. Property left after the tenancy ends is treated as abandoned, but do not dispose of a living animal yourself. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Penalty for Refusing a Service Animal in Arkansas Housing
bodyText: Refusing a tenant or applicant with a disability the right to be accompanied by a trained service animal in housing can be a crime in Arkansas. Any person, firm or corporation, or its agent, who denies or interferes with the admittance to or enjoyment of housing accommodations by an individual with a visual, hearing or other physical disability, or otherwise interferes with that individual's rights, is guilty of a misdemeanor. Those rights include being accompanied by a service animal especially trained to do work or perform tasks for the person, with no extra fee or charge (the person is liable for damage the animal causes), and full and equal access to rental housing subject only to limits that apply to everyone. The equal-access right does not reach a facility designed and used primarily as a single-family residence of which a portion is rented, but the service-animal right has no such exception. Fair housing law separately covers emotional support and other assistance animals, with its own civil remedies. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Service and Support Animal Misrepresentation in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas penalizes two kinds of misrepresentation. An individual who misrepresents an animal as a service animal or service animal in training to a person or entity that operates a public accommodation may face a civil penalty of up to $250 per violation; the statute speaks of public accommodations, so treat it as not reaching a tenant's request to you for a housing accommodation. Separately, knowingly and fraudulently representing an emotional support dog as entitled to a service animal's rights, or a seller's failure to give the required written notices, carries civil penalties of $500, $1,000 and then $2,500, which only the Attorney General or a prosecuting, county or city attorney may enforce, and that section expressly does not change federal or state rights to reasonable accommodation and equal access to housing. Neither statute lets you deny an accommodation on your own finding of misrepresentation: evaluate every request under fair housing rules, ask for reliable documentation when the need is not apparent, and refer suspected fraud to the authorities. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Assigned Parking Spaces in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute on assigned parking spaces in rentals. A space you promise the tenant is part of the leased premises under the landlord-tenant act, so take it away or move it only as the lease allows; the library's assigned-space clause lets you reassign a comparable space on reasonable notice, which is lawful in Arkansas.

Arkansas's parking-lot towing statute lets the lessee of a space in a parking lot, as well as the lot owner, have a vehicle parked in that space without consent removed and stored at the vehicle owner's expense, following the state's private-property towing procedures (a licensed towing firm and the owner's or agent's signed written statement), but only if a readable sign at each lot entrance says who may park there and forbids parking by others; decide in the lease or rules whether tenants may call a tow themselves or must ask you. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Tenant EV Charging Right in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute giving a tenant the right to install or use an electric vehicle charger, and none requiring you to approve a request, provide charging, or follow any procedure. Whether to allow charging is your choice under the lease; if you allow a tenant-installed charger, treat it as an alteration needing your written consent, and put in writing who installs it (a licensed electrician), who pays for installation and electricity, insurance, and whether it stays or is removed at move-out. If you sell charging to tenants, Arkansas's public-utility definition excludes a person who buys electricity from a utility and furnishes it exclusively to charge electric vehicles for compensation, so a landlord-run charger does not by itself make you a public utility. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution. An addendum letting a tenant install a charger (your consent, a licensed electrician, who pays, removal at move-out) is lawful, but the library does not offer one for Arkansas, because the terms depend on the property's wiring and parking; a landlord who wants one should add their own and take advice first.

title: EV Chargers When an Arkansas Lease Ends
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on what happens to a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when the tenancy ends: no rule on removal, restoration or reimbursement. Settle it in the written approval: whether the charger stays (and whether you pay anything for it) or the tenant removes it by a licensed electrician and restores the wall and circuit, and that the cost of any restoration may be deducted from the deposit as damages, itemized in the written notice. Property the tenant leaves after the lease ends is treated as abandoned and may be disposed of as you see fit, but a charger wired into the building is better handled by agreement than by that rule. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Arkansas EV Charger Installation Rules for Rentals
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute setting installation, insurance, metering or approval requirements for electric vehicle chargers in rental housing, and no deadline for answering a tenant's request. Set your own conditions in a written approval: a licensed electrician, any permits the local building code requires, a separate meter or a stated way to bill electricity, insurance, and responsibility for damage. Selling charging to tenants does not by itself make you a public utility. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Arkansas Rules on EV Charging in Shared Areas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on electric vehicle charging in shared parking areas of rental property: no tenant right to a shared charger, no rule on assigning or reserving charging spaces, and no cost-sharing formula. If you provide shared chargers, adopt written rules on use, time limits, fees and towing or removal of vehicles that block them (towing must follow Arkansas's private-property towing rules; see the towing row). The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Parking Areas and Vehicle Damage in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute on residential parking areas. The library's parking clause, which limits tenants to designated areas, says you do not provide security, and says you are not liable for damage to or theft of a vehicle, works as written: no Arkansas statute voids that kind of term.

Arkansas also shields you from injury and property-damage claims caused by a defect or disrepair of the premises unless you agreed, for consideration, or undertook by your conduct to maintain or repair them and failed to do so reasonably, so do not promise security or lot maintenance you will not deliver. A parking area you hold out for tenants or promise to a tenant is part of the leased premises.

Whether the "not liable" sentence would protect you against your own negligence, or against a crime you could have prevented, is case law. Towing rules are in the towing row. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Arkansas Parking Rules Notice Law
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring parking or towing rules to be delivered before the lease is signed, given a prescribed heading, limited in mid-term changes, or limited in the vehicle information you may ask for. Give tenants your parking rules in writing with the lease anyway, and change them during a fixed term only as the lease allows (see the term-change row). The only Arkansas notice rule here is the towing sign: to have unauthorized vehicles removed from a parking lot, post a readable sign at each entrance saying who may park there and forbidding parking by others (and, to be free of liability for the removal, use an insured wrecker service and an insured storage company), and check whether your city requires the sign to name the towing firm, its charges and accepted payment methods. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Vehicle Rules and Towing a Tenant's Car in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas lets the lease set vehicle rules (operable, registered passenger vehicles only; no trailers or RVs without consent; no repairs on site), and no statute limits what vehicle information you may ask for.

Towing is narrower than the rules: Arkansas's private-property towing statute lets you, as owner or agent, have a vehicle removed only if it is abandoned or parked without the authorization of the property owner or person controlling the property, by a licensed towing firm and after signing the firm's written removal statement. A tenant's car parked where your rules forbid (another tenant's space, a fire lane, a no-parking area) is parked without authorization; a tenant's car parked in the tenant's own space is not clearly unauthorized just because its registration has expired or it does not run.

The library's vehicle-rules clause allows towing "in accordance with applicable law", so for an expired-registration or inoperable car in an authorized spot, give written notice to fix or move it first, and tow only if the lease makes such a vehicle unauthorized and local ordinances allow it. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Storage Space Leased With an Arkansas Home
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute aimed at storage space leased with a home. The library's storage clause (exclusive use, no hazardous, flammable or perishable items, and no landlord liability for stored items) works as written; no Arkansas statute voids it.

Do not rely on Arkansas's self-service storage law to enforce unpaid charges against a tenant's locker: that law gives a storage operator a lien and sale procedure, but only under a storage rental agreement that contains the bold-type lien notice the statute requires, and it is built for storage facilities rather than homes.

For a residential tenant, things left in the storage space after the lease ends are treated, like the rest of the premises, as abandoned, and Arkansas gives you a lien on property the tenant places on the premises for sums the tenant agreed to pay; how that lien is enforced is not set out in the statute, so get legal advice before selling anything. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Towing From Your Arkansas Rental Property
bodyText:
Arkansas regulates towing from private property. As owner or agent you may have a vehicle (or trailer, implement or machinery) that is abandoned on your property, or parked there without the authorization of the owner or person controlling the property, removed by a towing and storage firm licensed by the Arkansas Towing and Recovery Board.

Before the tow, the firm must get your signed written statement giving your name, address and phone number, stating that you own or control the property and that the vehicle is abandoned or unauthorized, identifying the vehicle by make, model and VIN, and giving where it will be taken; keep the copy the firm leaves and show it on request to anyone claiming the vehicle. The firm must notify local police or the sheriff within two hours. The firm may not pay you or your agent a referral fee or any other compensation for the tow. Directing an unlawful removal is a Class B misdemeanor, each vehicle a separate offense.

For a parking lot, you (or a tenant who leases a space) avoid liability for removing an unauthorized vehicle only if a readable sign at each entrance says who may park there and forbids others, and the vehicle is towed and stored by insured companies.

Cities and counties may limit towing distances and charges (any excess over a local cap is billed to the property owner who requested the tow), require signs naming the tow firm, its charges and accepted payments, and regulate wheel clamps (boots). See the vehicle-rules row before towing a tenant's own car. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Arkansas Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no unbundled-parking law: you may include parking in the rent or charge for it separately, as you and the tenant agree. If parking is separate, put the space, the charge (as a fixed amount) and what happens to the parking if the lease ends in writing. Under the deposit statute, every payment due under the rental agreement counts as rent, so a separate parking charge is part of the rent base for deposit purposes; whether it is rent for eviction purposes depends on how the lease treats it (see the fees-as-rent row). Whether a separate parking charge is subject to sales tax was not reviewed; ask a tax adviser. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: Medical Marijuana in Arkansas Rentals
bodyText: Arkansas allows only medical marijuana, under an amendment to the state Constitution; it has no adult-use (recreational) law, so marijuana use by anyone who is not a registered qualifying patient remains illegal and may be banned like any other illegal activity on the premises. For registered qualifying patients and designated caregivers: you may not refuse to lease to, or otherwise penalize, a person solely for being a qualifying patient or designated caregiver, unless doing so would put you in violation of federal law or regulations (this matters for federally assisted housing). You may ban smoking marijuana on the property, but you may not prohibit a qualifying patient's medical use by means other than smoking (such as edibles, oils, tinctures or patches); because the amendment treats vaporizing as different from smoking, the cautious course is not to ban a patient's vaporized medical marijuana either (see the smoking row and the library's Arkansas smoking clause). You may ban growing marijuana: the amendment allows growing only at licensed dispensaries and cultivation facilities and does not authorize patients, caregivers or anyone else to grow it. Possession beyond the amendment's limits, sale, and use by non-patients are not protected. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Use of the Property and Common Areas in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas lets the lease restrict how tenants use the unit and common areas (no holes or fixtures without consent, balcony limits, no candles, no exterior signs), and no Arkansas statute protects waterbeds, clotheslines, drying racks or solar devices for renters.

One statute limits you: no private entity may adopt a rule, policy or agreement that prevents a person who otherwise has the legal right to properly display the U.S. flag on private property from doing so, though display may be restricted when the flag is used in or as advertising. That flag rule does not apply to landlords of private rental property who operate fewer than 12 rental units. The library's common-area clause already exempts displays the law protects. Tenants must in any case use the facilities and appliances reasonably and keep the parts of the premises they use reasonably safe and clean. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: No Arkansas Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no law letting a tenant take in people displaced by a tornado, flood, fire or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none limiting such stays or deciding when a displaced guest becomes a tenant. Your lease's guest and occupancy terms apply, subject to fair housing law (two persons per bedroom is presumed a reasonable occupancy limit) and local codes. After a disaster, consider giving written, time-limited consent to displaced guests rather than treating the stay as a default, and remember that Arkansas's price-gouging law limits rent increases on rental housing after an emergency declaration (see the disaster row). If a guest will not leave after you or the tenant have withdrawn permission, do not use self-help: a person who lawfully came into possession and holds it after a written demand to surrender possession commits unlawful detainer, which you pursue in court. The same applies to every tenancy type. This finding covers the Arkansas Code and Constitution.

title: No Arkansas Statute on Grills or Open Flames at Rentals
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute that limits, or requires, lease rules on grills, barbecues, charcoal or other open-flame devices at a rental, or that sets a distance from the building. The library's grilling clause is a lease rule you may use as written.

Fire codes adopted by the state fire marshal or by your city, which this search did not cover, may set their own limits on open-flame cooking on balconies and near multifamily buildings, so check them and make your lease rule at least as strict. The tenant must already keep the unit reasonably safe and not damage the premises, and you may give the 14-day written notice for a breach of the grilling rule. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: Firearms: No Arkansas Rule for Residential Leases
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that bars, or protects tenants against, a lease rule on firearms in a rental home, and none about firearms kept in vehicles in a residential landlord's parking area. The firearm-in-vehicle law Arkansas does have protects an employee's lawfully owned firearm in the employee's locked vehicle in a private employer's parking lot, with a related liability shield for the property owner; it concerns employers and their employees, not landlords and tenants (that law lets an employer bar such a vehicle where the lot is on the grounds of a tenant-occupied single-family detached home being used as a residence; check it if you employ staff on site). The Arkansas Constitution gives citizens the right to keep and bear arms for their common defense; it limits the government, and whether it limits a private lease term was not reviewed (no case law was searched). The cautious course is to limit a firearm rule to unlawful possession, discharge except in lawful self-defense, and safe storage, rather than a total ban, and to apply it evenly. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law. The library does not offer an Arkansas firearm-conduct clause, because no statute invokes one; a landlord who wants one can add their own, limited as above, and should take advice first.

title: Guest Rules in Arkansas: A Lease Matter
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute on how long a tenant's guests may stay, on guest fees, or on when a guest becomes an occupant. Guest rules are lease terms, and the library's guest clause is lawful as written.

Arkansas law already makes the tenant answer for guests: the tenant must not knowingly let anyone on the premises with the tenant's permission damage the premises, and must require those persons not to disturb other tenants' peaceful enjoyment. A breach of a guest rule is a non-rent breach, so give the 14-day written notice before ending the tenancy for it.

Apply guest limits evenly: fair housing law bars different terms because of familial status and the other protected traits, and a disabled tenant's live-in aide may need to be allowed as a reasonable accommodation. One statute lets you keep a person out: you may refuse access by a domestic abuse offender to a victim's residence unless a court order permits access. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Statutory Guest-Day Limit in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas sets no number of days after which a guest becomes an occupant or tenant, and no rule on how a lease may count guest days. The 14-consecutive-day and 14-days-in-six-months limits in the library's guest clause are your choice and are lawful in Arkansas.

Under the 2007 Act a tenant is the person entitled under the rental agreement to occupy the unit, so a guest who stays past the limit does not become your tenant unless you accept the person as one, for example by taking rent from him or her; enforce the limit promptly with the 14-day written notice for a non-rent breach, and see the guest policy row for the rest. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Statutory Rights for Tenants' Guests or Visitors
bodyText: Arkansas gives a tenant's guests, visitors, caregivers or delivery people no statutory right of access to a rental, and bars no guest fee. Guest access is governed by the lease. Three statutes touch guests: the tenant answers for damage and disturbance by people the tenant lets onto the premises; you are not liable to a tenant's licensee or invitee for injury from a defect or disrepair unless you agreed or undertook to maintain or repair and failed to do so reasonably; and you may refuse access by a domestic abuse offender to a victim's residence unless a court order permits it. Apply any guest rule evenly under fair housing law. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: Periodic Inspections: The Tenant May Not Unreasonably Refuse
bodyText: Arkansas lets you inspect the unit during the tenancy: the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to your entry to inspect the premises, and also to make repairs, supply services, investigate possible rule or lease violations or criminal activity, or show the unit. Arkansas sets no notice period for entry, so the notice in your lease (the library's access clause gives at least 24 hours) is what you must give; see the landlord entry row. If the tenant refuses lawful access, you may ask the district court for an order compelling access, without posting a bond, or end the rental agreement, and in either case recover actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. Do not use inspections to harass; keep them reasonable in number and timing. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: Keys and Locks in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute on how many keys you must give, key deposits or fees for lost keys, or rekeying between tenants. The library's keys clause, including charging the tenant the cost of rekeying when keys are not returned, is a lawful lease term.

Two statutes apply. A tenant may not change the locks without your permission. But if a tenant or household member is a victim of domestic abuse shown by a court order, the locks may be changed at the tenant's expense with your prior consent, by you or by a tenant who is not the abuser, and whoever changes them must give the other a copy of the new key right away; you are immune from civil liability for changing locks in good faith under that rule (see the domestic-abuse lock change row). Rekeying between tenants is not required but is the cautious course. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: Calls for Police Help Cannot Be Waived; No Crime-Free Lease Law
bodyText: Arkansas has no crime-free lease statute, no law requiring you to join a crime-free housing program, and no statute requiring you to give police information about tenants or access to a unit without legal process. One rule protects tenants who call for help: a residential tenant may not waive in the tenancy the right to request law enforcement or other emergency assistance, so do not use a lease term that limits or penalizes calls for police, fire or medical help. You may still enforce criminal-activity and nuisance terms against conduct itself, and Arkansas gives you strong tools for that (see the criminal activity and nuisance rows); the tenant may not unreasonably refuse your entry to investigate possible criminal activity. Two reporting duties apply to everyone, landlords included. Anyone present at or with knowledge of a death must promptly notify the county coroner, the prosecuting attorney and the sheriff or police chief if, among other things, the death occurs in the home, appears violent, accidental, a suicide or drug-related, or is sudden and unexplained; failing to do so is a Class A misdemeanor (Ark. Code Ann. § 12-12-315). And any person 18 or older who observes abuse, sexual abuse or sexual exploitation of a child is a mandated reporter who must immediately notify the Child Abuse Hotline; knowingly failing to is a Class A misdemeanor (Ark. Code Ann. §§ 12-18-402(a), (b)(43), 12-18-201). The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Candidate or Canvasser Access Rule in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring you to let political candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or voter-registration volunteers into an apartment building, gated community or other multi-unit property, and no statute on political signs at rentals. Whether outsiders may enter common areas is up to you and your lease rules; apply them evenly. A tenant's right to display the United States flag is covered in the display-rights row. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Tenant Right to Install a Window or Portable Air Conditioner
bodyText: Arkansas gives tenants no statutory right to install a window, portable or other cooling unit, and no statute requires a lease to say whether such units are allowed. Your lease decides, and the library's consent-before-alterations and fastening terms cover window units. What the law does say: for leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021, you must keep a functioning heating and air conditioning system only to the extent one served the premises when the lease was signed, so a unit you supplied is covered by that standard and a unit the tenant adds is not; and the tenant must use heating, ventilating and air conditioning facilities in a reasonable manner. A tenant with a disability may ask for a cooling unit as a reasonable accommodation. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy; treat a periodic tenancy that began before November 1, 2021 as covered by the standard, since each new period may count as a renewal. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Tenant Right to Plug-In or Balcony Solar in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas gives tenants no right to install a plug-in, portable or balcony solar device, or other solar equipment, at a rental, and has no statute voiding lease, covenant or association restrictions on solar equipment. Your lease decides: the library's consent-before-alterations and fastening terms cover solar devices, and you may allow them on conditions (placement, safe wiring, no fastening to exterior surfaces, removal and repair at move-out). Utility interconnection and net-metering rules, set by the Public Service Commission, were not reviewed. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Recycling Notice Duty; Watch County Trash Fees
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to tell tenants where or how to recycle, to provide recycling containers or service, or to put recycling information in the lease, whatever the building's size. Counties may regulate solid waste locally, including requiring wastes to be separated by type before collection, so check your county and city ordinances. One state rule affects your costs: where a county ordinance makes the occupant responsible for county solid-waste fees, you as owner are treated as the occupant unless, before the fifth day of the month of service, you register with the county the tenant's name and address and either the lease end date or that the lease is month-to-month; otherwise the fees can be collected from you with your property taxes. Say in the lease who pays trash and recycling service. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays: No Arkansas Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute giving tenants a right to display religious or cultural items, such as a mezuzah on a door frame, a cross or holiday decorations, against your lease rules, and none barring you from limiting them. Fair housing law still applies: you may not discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, or in services or facilities, because of religion, so apply any display rule evenly, without singling out one faith, and consider allowing small door-frame items. The state fair housing subchapter does not reach certain small owners (for example an owner-occupied building of up to four units, or a private owner of no more than three single-family houses renting without a broker or discriminatory advertising), but the Arkansas Civil Rights Act separately protects the right to engage in property transactions without discrimination because of religion, with no small-landlord exemption, and federal fair housing law applies separately too. The library's shared fastening and signs clause already leaves room for any display the law protects. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: House Rules in Arkansas: Enforceable as Lease Terms
bodyText:
Arkansas's 2007 Act tells tenants to comply with the lease and with rules "enforceable pursuant to" the Act, and counts valid rules as part of the rental agreement, but the Act has no section saying when a rule is enforceable or how you may adopt or change one. So treat rules as lease terms: give the tenant your written rules before signing and attach them, or have the lease refer to rules the tenant has received.

A rule you adopt during a fixed term is a change to the lease, and the cautious course is to make it bind the tenant only if the tenant agrees in writing or it is part of a renewal. For a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy, the library's Arkansas rules clause also lets you change rules by written notice at least as long as the notice to end the tenancy (30 or 7 days).

Keep rules reasonable and apply them to all tenants alike; fair housing law bars different terms for protected groups. A rule breach is a non-rent breach: give written notice that the tenancy will end in not less than 14 days if it is not remedied. You may enter, with the tenant's consent, which the tenant may not unreasonably withhold, to investigate possible rule violations.

title: No Smoke-Drift Waiver Rule in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on tobacco or marijuana smoke drifting between units, and none authorizing a lease clause in which the tenant gives up claims over drifting smoke, so the library does not offer a smoke-drift waiver for Arkansas. Arkansas has no statute voiding exculpatory lease terms either, so whether such a waiver would hold up is a question of case law. Two statutes frame the risk: you are not liable to a tenant for injury from a defect or disrepair on the premises unless you agreed or undertook to maintain or repair and failed to do so reasonably, and each tenant must make people on the premises with the tenant's permission behave so as not to disturb other tenants' peaceful enjoyment. The better tools are a smoke-free policy (see the smoking row, including the medical-marijuana limits) and, if smoking is allowed in nearby units, telling applicants so in writing before they sign. The state Clean Indoor Air Act does not reach a private residence, but it bans smoking in the enclosed areas of a place of employment, which includes hallways, stairs and elevators under an employer's control that employees use while working, unless the employer has fewer than three employees and exempts itself. If your own staff work in a building's enclosed common areas, the cautious reading treats those areas as smoke-free. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: Snow and Ice Removal: No Arkansas Statute
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute saying whether the landlord or the tenant must clear snow and ice at a rental, and no rule that a tenant's snow duty must be in a separate writing. The library's snow-removal clause, which puts the duty on the tenant for the areas the tenant uses unless you provide the service, is a lawful lease term (see the yard-work and chores row).

Keep two points in mind. If you promise in the lease, or start by your conduct, to clear snow, a court may treat that as an undertaking to maintain the premises, and Arkansas's shield against injury claims for defects and disrepair does not protect a landlord who agreed or undertook to maintain or repair and failed to do so reasonably.

And city ordinances may require owners or occupants to clear public sidewalks; check yours. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: U.S. Flag Display: Landlords With 12 or More Units May Not Prevent It
bodyText:
If you operate twelve or more rental units, you may not adopt a rule or policy, or make a lease term, that prevents a tenant who otherwise has the right from properly displaying a flag of the United States on the property.

The protected flag is one of fabric, cloth or paper, suitable for display from a pole or staff or in a window, no larger than 10 feet long or 8 feet wide; it does not include flag designs made of lights, paint, siding, plants, balloons or similar materials. You may restrict a flag used as, or with, an advertising display. The rule also binds homeowners' and property owners' associations, but it does not apply to landlords who operate fewer than twelve rental units or to property owned by churches or religious organizations.

The winner of a lawsuit to enforce the right recovers court costs and reasonable attorney's fees. The statute does not mention size or placement rules; reasonable rules on where and how a flag is mounted, which do not prevent display, are the cautious limit.

Arkansas has no statute protecting other flags, banners or political signs against your lease rules, so a term requiring your consent for signs visible from outside is lawful; the library's shared signs clause already exempts displays the law protects. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: Tenant Security Cameras and Video Doorbells: No Arkansas Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute giving a tenant a right to install security cameras or a video doorbell, and none limiting your lease rules on them. Your lease controls: the library's terms requiring your written consent before the tenant fastens anything to the property or makes alterations cover cameras and doorbells, and you may allow them on conditions (placement, no recording into other units or private areas, removal and repair at move-out). Arkansas criminal law makes video voyeurism a felony, which reaches anyone, tenant or landlord, who uses a camera to secretly view or record a person in a private area out of public view where the person has a reasonable expectation of privacy and has not consented (security monitoring run by an occupant of a residence, or by the owner of a building, is excepted, but that exception is no license to aim a camera into private spaces); tell tenants that cameras may not point into neighbors' homes or shared private spaces. If you install cameras in common areas yourself, keep them out of private spaces. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: Waterbeds: No Arkansas Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in rentals: nothing requires you to allow them, bars you from banning them, or sets insurance or installation rules. Your lease decides. The library's shared fastenings and heavy-items rule requires your written consent before a tenant keeps a waterbed or other water-filled furniture, and you may condition consent on proof of insurance, a liner and frame, or a ground-floor location. The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises, and you may apply the deposit to damage beyond normal wear and tear under the deposit statute (see the deposit-use row). The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Duty to Disclose Association Obligations to a Tenant
bodyText: Arkansas does not require a lease of a condominium unit (a horizontal property regime) or of a home in a homeowners' or property owners' association to disclose the association's obligations, or require you to give the tenant the master deed, bylaws or rules. Still give your tenant the association's rules before signing and make compliance a lease term: the association's documents bind the property, and the association may charge you, as the owner of a rented condominium unit, additional assessments for the extra costs a rented unit causes (see the condominium and HOA row). The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to disclose a unit's bed bug history to an applicant or tenant, to give a bed bug information sheet, or to follow a treatment timeline. See the bed bug and pest row for the tenant's cleanliness and access duties and for how to word any treatment promise. Arkansas's implied quality standards cover only running hot and cold water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, the roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning, and you are shielded from injury claims for defects or disrepair unless you agreed or undertook to maintain or repair. Whether keeping quiet about a hazard you know of is fraud or concealment is case law; the cautious course is to tell applicants in writing, before they sign, about any such hazard you know of. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Certificate-of-Occupancy Disclosure in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to tell a tenant whether the rental has a certificate of occupancy, to give the tenant a copy, or to state it in the lease, and no statute makes a lease of a unit without one unenforceable or bars collecting rent for it. Certificates of occupancy come from building-code enforcement, mainly by cities and counties; some require one, or a rental inspection, before a unit is occupied, so check local ordinances. The implied quality standards still apply to leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or with a purchase right), and stricter local housing standards are preserved. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Defective Drywall Rule in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on defective, corrosive or sulfur-emitting drywall in rentals: no disclosure duty, no remediation standard and no tenant remedy specific to drywall. Arkansas's implied quality standards cover only running hot and cold water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, the roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning, and you are shielded from injury claims for defects or disrepair unless you agreed or undertook to maintain or repair. Whether keeping quiet about a hazard you know of is fraud or concealment is case law; the cautious course is to tell applicants in writing, before they sign, about any such hazard you know of. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Electric Submetering Disclosure in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not require a lease disclosure when you submeter or bill tenants for electricity, and sets no submeter billing rules in its statutes; the Arkansas Code and Constitution were searched, but Public Service Commission rules were not. Disclose the arrangement in the lease anyway: see the submetering and utility-billing row for what to state and for billing only your actual cost. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Flood Disclosure Rule in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to tell a tenant whether a rental is in a flood zone or floodplain, whether it has flooded before, or whether you carry flood insurance, and has no flood disclosure form or flood-based termination right for tenants. Arkansas also has no statute on ending a lease when a flood or other casualty damages the home, so put a casualty clause in the lease (see the casualty row). Arkansas's implied quality standards cover only running hot and cold water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, the roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning, and you are shielded from injury claims for defects or disrepair unless you agreed or undertook to maintain or repair. Whether keeping quiet about a hazard you know of is fraud or concealment is case law; the cautious course is to tell applicants in writing, before they sign, about any such hazard you know of. Remind tenants that your insurance does not cover their belongings. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Foreclosure Disclosure Duty in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to tell an applicant or tenant that the rental is in foreclosure, before signing or during the tenancy, and has no state statute protecting tenants when the property is foreclosed. Federal law may let a bona fide tenant stay for the lease term or a notice period after a foreclosure sale; see the foreclosure row, which also covers who must return the deposit. Telling tenants early is good practice. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Good-Cause Eviction Notice in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law, so there is no notice telling tenants whether such a law covers the unit, and nothing to put in the lease about one. A fixed-term lease ends when its term expires; a month-to-month tenancy ends on 30 days' written notice and a week-to-week tenancy on 7 days' written notice. See the for-cause eviction row for the limits that do apply (such as the domestic-abuse protections). Public and federally assisted housing may have federal good-cause rules, which this library does not cover. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No General Contamination Disclosure in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to tell a tenant that a rental is or was contaminated with hazardous substances, and no statute requires recorded environmental use restrictions to be written into residential leases. The one contamination rule aimed at rentals concerns former methamphetamine labs: a contaminated property may not be entered by unauthorized persons until it is properly remediated, and once it is remediated and the state notifies you, no one must disclose the past contamination (see the meth row). If your property is subject to recorded environmental restrictions, your tenant's use must respect them, so say so in the lease. Arkansas's implied quality standards cover only running hot and cold water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, the roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning, and you are shielded from injury claims for defects or disrepair unless you agreed or undertook to maintain or repair. Whether keeping quiet about a hazard you know of is fraud or concealment is case law; the cautious course is to tell applicants in writing, before they sign, about any such hazard you know of. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: Renting in a Condominium or HOA Community in Arkansas
bodyText:
If your rental is a condominium unit, Arkansas calls the condominium a horizontal property regime. Its administration is governed by bylaws recorded with the master deed, so read the master deed and bylaws for any leasing limits, approval or registration rules before you lease. The regime's board may charge you, as the owner who makes a unit available for rent or lease, additional assessments, limited to the amount reasonably calculated to cover the extra security, wear and tear, trash pickup and other costs a rented unit causes; the charge is yours, and your lease may pass it to the tenant only if it says so. The 2007 landlord-tenant act does not govern an owner living in his or her own condominium unit, but it does govern your tenant.

For homes in a homeowners' or property owners' association, no Arkansas statute sets how the association treats tenants; the recorded covenants and association rules govern, so check them the same way. Two statutes reach associations directly: an association may not adopt a rule that prevents proper display of the United States flag, and the state home-business law does not override an agreement between an association and a homeowner.

Give your tenant the association's rules before signing and make compliance a lease term (the library's association clauses). The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: Making the Tenant Follow Association Rules in Arkansas
bodyText: The library's association-compliance clause, which makes the tenant follow the association's rules and pay fines the tenant's violations cause, is a lawful lease term in Arkansas; no statute caps or lists the fines or charges you may pass to a tenant, and none requires a separate notice. A fine the lease passes to the tenant is not rent under the 2007 Act, so nonpayment is a non-rent breach, curable on 14 days' written notice. A condominium's extra assessment for rented units is charged to you as owner, not the tenant, unless your lease shifts it. Satellite dishes and antennas: Arkansas has no statute, but a federal rule limits restrictions on small dishes in areas a tenant exclusively uses (see the telecom row). The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Duty to Disclose Code or Condemnation Orders
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to give applicants or tenants copies of outstanding code-violation notices, inspection orders or condemnation orders, or to disclose them before signing. Cities and towns may order the removal or razing of buildings that the council finds dilapidated, unsightly, unsafe, unsanitary or detrimental to the public welfare, and set the procedure by ordinance, so notice to occupants depends on your city's ordinance. A known code violation affecting water, electricity, plumbing, the roof or envelope, or heating and air conditioning also bears on the implied quality standards. Arkansas's implied quality standards cover only running hot and cold water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, the roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning, and you are shielded from injury claims for defects or disrepair unless you agreed or undertook to maintain or repair. Whether keeping quiet about a hazard you know of is fraud or concealment is case law; the cautious course is to tell applicants in writing, before they sign, about any such hazard you know of. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Landlord Liability Insurance Mandate in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to carry liability insurance on a rental, to file proof of insurance with a city or county, or to tell tenants whether you are insured. Insurance is still wise: Arkansas shields you from injury claims for defects or disrepair only if you did not agree or undertake to maintain or repair, and a lease promise to repair can remove that shield. Some local rental programs may require insurance; check local ordinances. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: Lead-Based Paint Disclosure in Arkansas: Federal Rule Only
bodyText: For housing built before 1978, the federal lead-based paint disclosure applies: before the lease is signed, give the tenant the Lead Warning Statement, disclose any known lead-based paint or hazards and any records or reports, give the federal pamphlet, and keep the signed acknowledgment (the library's lead disclosure clause does this). Arkansas adds no state lead disclosure, notice or certificate at lease signing. Arkansas's own lead law works after a hazard is found: the Department of Health notifies you and the tenant of its findings, you must abate within 30 days, and you may not retaliate against the occupant, especially by eviction or threat of eviction, because of the lead hazard (see the state lead law row).

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate for Arkansas Rentals
bodyText: Arkansas has no lead-safe or lead-free certification for rental housing and no certificate that must be obtained or attached to a lease. For housing built before 1978, the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet apply. Arkansas's lead law instead lets the Department of Health investigate and order abatement of lead hazards, and the state licenses lead-based paint abatement work; see the state lead law row. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: Arkansas Lead Law: Health Department Orders and No Retaliation
bodyText: Arkansas adds no state lead notice, certificate or information packet that must be given with a lease; for housing built before 1978, the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet still apply. Arkansas's lead poisoning law puts duties on you as owner once a hazard is found. The Department of Health may investigate lead hazards where children with elevated blood lead levels live, may get a court warrant to enter a dwelling (or enter without one in an exigent health threat), and after inspecting notifies you and the tenant in writing of its findings, with abatement instructions. If the hazard is not properly abated within 30 days after you receive the notice, you are in violation. After you receive notice of lead hazards, you may not retaliate against the occupant, especially by eviction or threat of eviction, because of the hazard; you may, by agreement with the occupant, find other suitable housing during abatement if that is in the occupant's best interest. Cities and counties may adopt the same or stricter lead ordinances. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge Rule in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on a meter conservation or energy-efficiency charge attached to a rental's utility meter, and no landlord notice or rent deduction for one. Utility rates and any on-bill programs are set by the Public Service Commission and local utilities, whose rules this search did not cover. If a utility bill the tenant will pay carries a special charge, say so in the lease. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: Former Meth Labs: Cleanup Before Anyone Moves In
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring you to tell a tenant that a rental was once used to make methamphetamine or other controlled substances, but its cleanup law controls when the property may be lived in. If you find or learn of evidence of a drug lab on your property, you must have it inspected, under the Division of Environmental Quality's guidelines, by a contractor the Division certifies; if the contractor verifies a lab, the Division puts the property on its public list of contaminated properties. If you find an abandoned lab with no police involvement, notify local law enforcement.
