When police find a lab, they order everyone out of the residually contaminated part and post a warning notice; it is a crime for anyone other than the Division, police, the owner or an owner's representative who has signed a liability waiver to enter that part until the Division establishes it has been properly remediated, and you as owner are responsible for the remediation. So do not lease or let a tenant back into a contaminated unit before then. After the property is remediated and you receive official notice from the Division, no one, including you and your real estate agent, must report or disclose the past contamination. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No Military Base or Air Zone Disclosure in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not require a lease disclosure for a rental near a military base or airfield, or in an aircraft noise or accident potential zone, and gives tenants no right to end a lease because of such a location. Arkansas's military rules for tenants concern service members' rights to end a lease, covered in the servicemember row. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Mold Disclosure Rule in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to disclose mold to an applicant or tenant, to give a mold information sheet, or to follow a mold remediation standard. Mold often follows a failed roof, envelope or plumbing, which are among the implied quality standards. Arkansas's implied quality standards cover only running hot and cold water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, the roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning, and you are shielded from injury claims for defects or disrepair unless you agreed or undertook to maintain or repair. Whether keeping quiet about a hazard you know of is fraud or concealment is case law; the cautious course is to tell applicants in writing, before they sign, about any such hazard you know of. The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Arkansas requires none of the three pre-signing disclosures some states group together. Ordnance: no duty to disclose a former military ordnance or munitions site near the rental. Demolition: no duty to tell applicants or tenants that you plan to demolish the unit or have applied for a demolition permit; historic-district and local permit rules govern demolition itself. Shared meters: no statute requires you to disclose that a tenant's meter serves other areas or to sign an allocation agreement; if you split a shared bill, state the method in the lease (see the utility apportionment row). If you plan to demolish, a fixed-term lease still binds you for its term, and a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy needs the ordinary 30- or 7-day written termination notice. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Owner or Manager Identity Disclosure Rule in Arkansas
bodyText:
Arkansas does not require you to give a tenant, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the owner, a property manager or an agent for notices and legal papers, and no statute bars or delays an eviction because you did not.

One loose end: the 2007 Act defines "landlord" to include a manager who fails to disclose as the Act requires, but the Act contains no such disclosure requirement, so a manager who does not want to be treated as the landlord should name the owner in the lease to be safe.

Put the owner's and any manager's names and notice addresses in the lease anyway: a notice to you counts as received when delivered to your place of business through which the lease was made or to any place you hold out for receiving notices, and the library's notices clause sends notices to the addresses the lease states. The library's optional Arkansas management-and-notices clause does this. A person who manages other owners' rentals for pay generally needs an Arkansas real estate license (see the landlord registration row). The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Pest Control or Pesticide Notice Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to tell tenants about a pest control contract, to give notice before pesticide is applied in a unit or common area, or to post pesticide notices in a rental building. Pest control companies are regulated by the state. Entry for treatment rests on the tenant's duty not to unreasonably withhold consent to entry for repairs and agreed services, so give reasonable notice and use the lease to set preparation duties (see the bed bug and pest row). The rules are the same for every type of tenancy. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: Private Wells: No Testing or Disclosure Duty, but Water Must Be Drinkable
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to test a private well serving a rental or to give tenants well test results. But for leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or with a purchase right), the implied quality standards require a source of potable drinking water and an available source of hot and cold running water, both when possession is delivered and during the tenancy, so a well serving the unit must produce safe drinking water. Testing the well before each tenancy, sharing the results, and saying in the lease who maintains the well and pump are the cautious course (see the tenant maintenance row on wells and septic systems). Treat a periodic tenancy that began before November 1, 2021 as covered too, since each new period may count as a renewal. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no law like California's Proposition 65: no duty to warn tenants about exposure to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm on rental property, and no warning-sign requirement for rentals. Specific hazards have their own rules, covered elsewhere in the library: lead paint (federal disclosure and Arkansas's lead law), former meth labs, and smoke and carbon monoxide detectors. Arkansas's implied quality standards cover only running hot and cold water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, the roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning, and you are shielded from injury claims for defects or disrepair unless you agreed or undertook to maintain or repair. Whether keeping quiet about a hazard you know of is fraud or concealment is case law; the cautious course is to tell applicants in writing, before they sign, about any such hazard you know of. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Property-Tax Share-of-Rent Statement in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to tell tenants what part of their rent goes to property taxes, whether annually, when the rent changes or otherwise, and gives renters no property-tax credit that depends on such a statement. The only property-tax rule touching tenants found is about county solid-waste fees: a county may collect those fees from a tenant you have registered as the occupant, with the tenant's personal property taxes, and otherwise from you (see the recycling row). If your lease passes tax increases through to the tenant, see the tax escalation row. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Radon Law for Arkansas Rentals
bodyText: Arkansas has no radon law for rentals: no duty to test for radon, to disclose radon test results or a radon hazard to tenants, or to give a radon information sheet, whatever the floor level of the unit, and no radon-resistant construction mandate in its statutes; the word appears in the Arkansas Code only once, in legislative findings about lung cancer. Arkansas's implied quality standards cover only running hot and cold water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, the roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning, and you are shielded from injury claims for defects or disrepair unless you agreed or undertook to maintain or repair. Whether keeping quiet about a hazard you know of is fraud or concealment is case law; the cautious course is to tell applicants in writing, before they sign, about any such hazard you know of. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: Disclosures for an Arkansas Lease: The Short List
bodyText: Arkansas has no single list of required lease disclosures, no state form that must be the first page of a lease, and no notice telling tenants whether a just-cause or rent-increase law covers the unit (Arkansas has neither). What applies, each in its own library entry: (1) for housing built before 1978, the federal lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet; (2) for a property covered by the federal CARES Act, its 30-day notice to vacate rule; (3) a former meth lab may not be occupied until it is properly remediated, and after remediation and the state's notice no disclosure is required; (4) the fact or suspicion that a property was the site of a homicide, suicide or felony is not a material fact that must be disclosed. Two Arkansas forms are optional but protect you: the move-in defect form for the implied quality standards (if the tenant signs it noting no listed defect and takes possession, or does not return it within two business days, you are deemed to comply at move-in), and a lease method for the tenant's defect notices. A management-and-notices clause naming the owner, any manager and the notice address is also good practice. Arkansas requires no deposit, fee, mold, radon, flood, bed bug, sex-offender or owner-identity disclosure. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Required Tenant Rights Guide in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not publish a state guide to landlord and tenant rights that you must give tenants before signing or at renewal, and requires no signed acknowledgment of one. The only required consumer brochures found in the Code concern rental-car and self-storage insurance, not homes. Because Arkansas's residential rules are spread across the 2007 Act, the general landlord-tenant chapter, the deposit subchapter and the unlawful detainer statutes, a plain-language summary in your welcome materials is good practice, but it is not required. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Code Variance Notice in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to give tenants a copy of a variance from a housing, health, building or sanitary code, or to attach one to the lease. No Arkansas statute was found that sets a statewide housing or sanitary code for rentals; local housing standards stricter than the implied quality standards still bind you, and any variance under them is governed by the local ordinance or agency rule that grants it, which this search did not cover. Follow any conditions a variance imposes. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: Sex Offender Information: No Disclosure Duty in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to tell applicants or tenants that a registered sex offender lives nearby, or to put a sex offender registry notice in the lease. Real estate licensees and appraisers cannot be sued for failing to ask about, disclose or release information that a property is in the vicinity of a registered offender; that shield names licensees and appraisers, not owners, but no statute puts a disclosure duty on owners either. Separately, the fact or suspicion that a property was the site of a homicide, suicide or felony is not a material fact that must be disclosed in a real property transaction, which includes a lease. Information about registered offenders reaches the public through local law enforcement, which discloses it under state guidelines when needed for public protection; you may point tenants to it. Do not misstate what you know if asked (no case law was searched on misrepresentation). The rules are the same for every type of tenancy.

title: No First-Page Occupancy Notice or Font Rule in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no rule requiring a notice at the top of the first page of a lease, or in a larger type size, about a tenant's lawful occupancy, and no presumption that a tenant lacks lawful occupancy unless the lease is notarized or states particular facts. Arkansas sets no general type-size rule for residential leases (see the lease type-size row). Removing people with no right to be there works through Arkansas's unlawful squatting crime and the court eviction routes (see the unauthorized occupant row). A written lease signed by both parties and kept on file is your best proof that a tenant is lawfully in possession. This search covered the Arkansas Code and Constitution; it did not cover agency rules, city or county ordinances, or case law.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring a lease to disclose public access to a shoreline, beach or waterfront, or the tenant's rights to use one; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none, and Arkansas has no ocean coastline. If the property is on a lake or river, describe in the lease only the access you actually control (a private dock, boat ramp or shared waterfront, and any rules for it), and do not promise rights to land or water you do not own. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Source-of-Income Protection
bodyText: Arkansas law does not protect a tenant's source of income: no statute requires you to accept a housing choice voucher (Section 8) or other rental assistance, or bars refusing an applicant because the rent would be paid by a program, and a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Arkansas's fair housing laws protect race, color, religion, national origin, sex, disability and familial status, not income source. You may therefore decide whether to take part in a voucher program, but apply the decision the same way to every applicant: a no-vouchers policy used selectively, or as a cover for turning away families with children, people with disabilities or a racial group, can still be discrimination. If you already accept a voucher tenant, or your property has federal or tax-credit financing, the program contract and its rules bind you. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring a lease or a notice to tell tenants whether the building has a fire sprinkler system, or to describe it; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. If the building has sprinklers, it is still sensible to say so in the lease and tell tenants not to hang items from sprinkler heads, cover them or tamper with them, and to report leaks or damage at once; if it has none, do not suggest that it does. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Offenders Nearby
bodyText: Arkansas law says that the fact, or even a suspicion, that a property is psychologically impacted, meaning it was or was ever suspected to be the site of a homicide, suicide or felony, is not a material fact that must be disclosed in a real property transaction, and the statute counts a lessee or tenant as a party to such a transaction. So you do not have to volunteer to an applicant or tenant that such an event happened at the home. Real estate licensees (including a licensed property manager acting as your agent) and appraisers also cannot be sued for not asking about, disclosing or releasing that information, or the fact that a registered offender lives nearby; that second protection names only licensees and appraisers, not owners. Do not lie if a tenant asks a direct question: the statute removes a duty to disclose, not protection for a false answer. Other conditions, such as defects or meth contamination, have their own rules. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Tenant Rights Statement
bodyText: Arkansas does not require you to give tenants a state-prepared statement or summary of their rights, attach one to the lease, or get a signed acknowledgment of one, and no lawsuit or eviction depends on having done so; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. The closest statutory document is optional: the written move-in defect form for the implied quality standards, which, if you supply it at the start of the tenancy and the tenant signs it without listing a covered defect and takes possession (or does not return it within two business days), lets you be deemed in compliance (see the move-in defect form row). The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Law
bodyText: Arkansas has no truth-in-renting statute: no law requires a lease to carry a state notice that some terms may be unenforceable, and no law bars offering a lease that contains a term violating the tenant's legal rights or sets a penalty for doing so; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Terms the law forbids are still unenforceable, most importantly any lease term waiving or giving up the rights, duties or remedies of the landlord-tenant act (see the prohibited lease terms row), so leave such terms out rather than relying on them. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Tenant Protection Act Notice
bodyText: Some states require a lease notice telling tenants about a statewide rent cap, just-cause eviction protections or a tenant right to buy the building. Arkansas has none of these laws, so no such notice is required and none should go in your lease; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Arkansas instead bars cities, counties and other local governments from enacting, keeping or enforcing any ordinance that controls the amount charged for rent, rental application fees or rental deposits on private residential property (the state's own two-month deposit cap still applies, except to an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units and does not pay a third person to manage them). Rent is set by the lease, and a periodic tenancy ends on the written notice the landlord-tenant act requires (7 days for week-to-week, 30 days for month-to-month) without any stated cause, subject to the fair housing, domestic-abuse and other specific protections described in their own rows. A fixed-term lease runs to its end date.

title: No Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some states require a lease statement telling tenants that a property is exempt from a statewide rent cap or just-cause eviction law. Arkansas has neither law, and local governments may not control rent, so there is nothing for a property to be exempt from and no exemption notice belongs in your lease (see the tenant protection notice row). The Arkansas rules that do turn on the size of your portfolio, such as the security deposit exemption for individuals who (with their spouse, minor children and their rental entities) own five or fewer units and do not use a paid third-party manager, the fair housing exemptions and the flag-display exception for landlords with fewer than 12 units, are explained in their own rows. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: Arkansas does not require a separate utility disclosure attachment to the lease (for example, a statement of how shared or submetered utilities are divided, past bills or a billing formula) before you may charge a tenant for utilities; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Your right to bill a tenant for a utility comes only from the lease, so write the terms into it: which utilities the tenant pays to the provider, which you bill, the method (submeter or formula), the rate, the billing cycle and due date, and any fee. The details are in the rows on shared-utility billing and submetered-utility disclosures. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit
bodyText: Since 2025 Arkansas has required cities to allow at least one accessory dwelling unit (a self-contained unit with its own cooking, sleeping and sanitation facilities) by right on a lot that contains a single-family home. An attached or detached unit may be no larger than 75% of the home's floor area or 1,000 square feet, whichever is less. A city may not require that the owner live in the home or the unit, may not require a family, marriage or employment relationship between the occupants of the two, and may not require extra parking, matching design, separate water and sewer, or development impact or application fees above $250; any city rule in effect on or after January 1, 2026 that conflicts is invalid to that extent. So you may rent an accessory unit to an unrelated long-term tenant. Limits remain: the unit must meet building, fire and other code requirements, the city may regulate short-term rentals (30 days or less), and private restrictive covenants (such as subdivision or HOA rules) are not overridden. The statute addresses cities. Once rented, the unit is a dwelling unit like any other: the landlord-tenant act applies, and it counts toward the five-unit threshold for the security deposit rules, which do not apply to an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units, unless a third person manages them for a fee. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Alarm Tampering Fee Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that allows, sets or caps a fee for a tenant who removes, disconnects or disables a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. You may make it a lease breach to tamper with an alarm you provided and require the tenant to pay the actual cost of repair or replacement. A flat fee beyond that cost is untested, so keep any charge to your real cost. That charge is not rent, so you cannot use the five-day nonpayment route for it; enforce it with a written notice giving at least 14 days to remedy, or, if the security deposit rules apply to you (they do not apply to an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units, unless a third person manages them for a fee), deduct it as damage on the itemized deposit notice. Separately, a tenant may always install a battery or plug-in detector at the tenant's own expense, and is then solely responsible for checking it, keeping it working and any damage from installing or removing it (see the smoke and carbon monoxide detector row). The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Asbestos: No Rental Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring a landlord to disclose asbestos to tenants, to inspect a rental for it, or to put an asbestos notice in the lease; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. The asbestos statutes Arkansas does have regulate asbestos abatement: a consultant or contractor must hold a Division of Environmental Quality license before any asbestos demolition, renovation or response action, and the Division sets the training and performance standards; they do not deal with tenancies. Before renovating or demolishing an older building, assume federal and state environmental rules on asbestos inspection, notification and licensed abatement apply, keep tenants away from the work, and tell them in writing about work that may disturb asbestos. Do not describe a unit as asbestos-free unless it has been tested. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Balcony Inspection Mandate
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks, stairs, railings or other elevated exterior elements of rental buildings, or a report to tenants; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Balconies are also not among the six items in Arkansas's implied quality standards (water, electricity, drinking water, sewer and plumbing, roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning). Liability works differently in Arkansas: a landlord is not liable to a tenant or the tenant's guests for injury or property damage caused by a defect or disrepair on the premises unless the landlord agreed, for consideration, or took on by conduct, a duty to maintain or repair the premises and then failed to perform it reasonably. A lease promise to repair can therefore create that duty. Whatever the lease says, inspect balconies and railings yourself, repair hazards promptly, and close off any balcony you know is unsafe; local building and property maintenance codes may impose their own duties. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Waiving Casualty and Mitigation Rules
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on what happens to a lease after fire or other casualty and none requiring you to re-rent (mitigate) after a tenant leaves early, so there is no statutory casualty or mitigation rule for a lease to waive, and no statute saying whether such a waiver is allowed. Two statutory limits still matter. First, the implied quality standards (including a functioning roof and building envelope) are excused only while you are temporarily prevented by an act of God, a utility failure or another force majeure event; otherwise, for leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or a lease with a purchase right), a tenant whose rent is current may give written notice and, if the problem is not excused (for example, tenant-caused or entry refused) and you do not fix it within 30 calendar days after receiving the notice, end the lease without penalty, and the lease cannot waive that remedy because neither side may agree in a lease to give up the rights, duties or remedies of the landlord-tenant act. Second, whether you must try to re-rent before collecting rent for the rest of a fixed term is case law, so a clause excusing you from mitigating may not be enforced; make and document reasonable efforts to re-rent instead. You may still give yourself a termination right after a casualty in the lease. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Children in the Household
bodyText: Arkansas fair housing law protects familial status: households with a child under 18 living with a parent, legal custodian or the custodian's written designee, someone in the process of getting custody of a child, and pregnant persons. You may not refuse to rent, set different terms, steer, or advertise a preference because a household has or will have children (for example, "adults only", higher deposits for children, or limiting families to certain floors). You may set a neutral occupancy limit that applies to people of all ages: an occupancy limit of two persons per bedroom is presumed reasonable in Arkansas, and an owner's own reasonable occupancy standards are protected only if they apply to persons of all ages and were adopted and published before the event in question, so put your standard in writing in your rental criteria and lease before you apply it. Any lower limit set by a state or local occupancy code also applies. The familial status rules do not apply to qualifying housing for older persons (housing for persons 62 or older, or 55-and-older housing meeting the 80% occupancy and published-policy tests). Small owner-occupied buildings and some owners of three or fewer single-family houses are exempt from parts of the law, but the advertising ban still applies to them and federal law may still apply. The Arkansas lease does not have to list children by name, but list every occupant in the lease. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Don't Use a Confession of Judgment
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that specifically bans a confession-of-judgment (cognovit) clause in a residential lease; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. But do not use one. Arkansas's general procedure for judgment by confession, in its civil procedure title, is framed around a debtor who appears in court with the creditor's assent and confesses judgment for a debt that is briefly stated, not around a pre-signed lease clause that lets the landlord take judgment without notice or a hearing; Arkansas bans such clauses outright in rental-purchase agreements for goods; and a lease term giving up the tenant's rights or remedies under the landlord-tenant act, including the notice and hearing the eviction procedure gives, is unenforceable. Collect unpaid rent and recover possession through the ordinary eviction or unlawful detainer process instead. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Deceptive Trade Practices Act and Leases
bodyText: Arkansas's Deceptive Trade Practices Act bars deceptive and unconscionable trade practices, including knowingly taking advantage of a consumer who cannot reasonably protect his or her interest because of physical infirmity, ignorance, illiteracy or inability to understand the language of the agreement, and any other unconscionable, false or deceptive act or practice in business, commerce or trade. Whether it reaches a residential lease of real property is not settled by its text: the Act defines goods as tangible property "bought or leased" and services as things purchased without physical characteristics, and Arkansas's appellate decisions on the point were not searched. Its list of specific practices does not include leaving blanks in a lease or failing to hand over a copy at signing. If it applies, the Attorney General can seek injunctions, restitution and penalties up to $10,000 per violation, and a tenant can sue only for an actual financial loss caused by relying on the practice (no private class actions), with possible attorney's fees and a jury trial. Treat it as applying: advertise accurately, disclose all fees, do not misstate the condition of the home or the tenant's rights, and do not press a lease on someone who plainly cannot understand it. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Victim Information: No Confidentiality Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that requires a landlord to keep confidential the information a tenant or applicant gives about domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking (such as a protection order, police report or new address), or that limits whom you may share it with; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. The Arkansas rule that does apply is the domestic-abuse protection for tenants: when a court order documents the abuse within the preceding 60 days (or within 60 days after a tenancy ended because of the abuse), you may not end, refuse to renew or refuse a tenancy because of it, and you may refuse the abuser access where a court order keeps the abuser away (see the domestic-abuse eviction protection row). Arkansas's only address confidentiality program the search found is in its driver's license law, and it governs only what the state discloses, not landlords. Protect the information anyway: keep orders and reports in a locked or restricted file, share them only with staff who need them to apply the law or change locks, never give a victim's new address or unit number to anyone without the victim's written consent, and never disclose it to the abuser. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Right to Call Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: An Arkansas residential tenant may not waive, in a residential tenancy, the right to request law enforcement or other emergency assistance. The sentence sits in the domestic-abuse protection statute but is not limited to abuse victims, so treat it as covering every residential tenant. Do not put anything in a lease, rules or addendum that limits, penalizes or counts as a violation a tenant's calls to police, fire or medical help (for example, a fee per police call, a limit on the number of calls, or a crime-free clause that treats a call as a breach). The statute bars only the waiver, but ending or refusing to renew a tenancy because the tenant called for help would undercut the right (and, for a documented abuse victim, is separately barred), so do not do it. You may still act on the underlying conduct of a tenant who commits crimes or disturbs neighbors, using the ordinary notice and eviction routes. No Arkansas statute limits city nuisance ordinances that count police calls. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Eviction Penalty Statute
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute aimed at lease clauses that charge the tenant a fee or penalty because you served a notice or filed an eviction, and none that expressly allows or bans passing your filing costs to the tenant; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. What you can recover comes from the statutes and the court: actual damages for the tenant's breach; after termination, possession, rent, actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees; attorney's fees for willful non-rent breaches or for nonpayment that is not in good faith, but only if a lawyer represents you; costs and fees in a nuisance eviction; and court costs as the court awards them. A flat "eviction fee" or "notice fee" in the lease is not rent (Arkansas rent excludes charges other than late charges), so it cannot support a nonpayment eviction, and a large flat charge risks being treated as an unenforceable penalty. Leave such fees out and claim your actual costs and any fees the statutes allow. The rules are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies.

title: Liability Waivers in Arkansas Leases
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that voids a lease clause releasing the landlord from liability or requiring the tenant to indemnify the landlord; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Arkansas instead limits landlord liability by statute: you are not liable to a tenant or the tenant's guests for death, injury or property damage caused by a defect or disrepair on the premises unless you agreed, for consideration, or took on by conduct, a duty to maintain or repair the premises and then failed to perform it reasonably; the implied quality standards do not expand that tort liability. Two limits apply to waivers: a lease may not waive or give up any right, duty or remedy of the landlord-tenant act (for example, the tenant's right to end the lease after an uncorrected quality-standard failure), and a tenant may not waive the right to call police or emergency help. A clause that tries to excuse your own negligence or intentional acts is also likely to be read narrowly or refused by a court. Keep any "not liable" clause limited to losses you do not cause, such as the tenant's own property not covered by insurance, and pair it with a renters insurance requirement. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant (No Usufruct in Arkansas)
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that Arkansas property law does not use, so the rule about leases granted by a usufructuary does not arise in Arkansas. The closest Arkansas interest is a life estate (for example, a surviving spouse who holds a home for life while the children own the remainder). Arkansas's statutes on leases by a life tenant deal only with oil, gas and other mineral leases, which need a court proceeding; no statute says what happens to a residential lease signed by a life tenant when the life estate ends, and that is case law. The cautious course if you lease as a life tenant: say so in the lease, keep the term short or month-to-month, and have the remainder owners sign the lease or agree in writing that it will continue if your life estate ends first. The same applies to every tenancy type.

title: Arkansas Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Three Arkansas laws bar housing discrimination, and their exemptions differ, so check each. (1) The Fair Housing Commission law bars refusing to rent, setting different terms, misstating availability and discriminatory advertising because of race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin, and requires reasonable accommodations and modifications for disability. It exempts a single-family house rented by a private owner who owns no more than three such houses, and rooms or units in an owner-occupied building of up to four units, but only if you use no broker and publish no discriminatory advertisement; the advertising ban itself has no exemption. Qualifying housing for older persons is exempt from the familial status rules, religious organizations and private clubs may prefer members in non-commercial housing, and you may refuse someone convicted of illegally making or distributing a controlled substance. (2) The Arkansas Fair Housing Act (enacted in 1995) bars the same practices in any real estate transaction, with a narrower exemption: a two-family building where the owner or immediate family lives in one unit, a room in a single-family home where the owner or family lives, and the owner's own home rented for up to 12 months while temporarily away; that exemption covers its advertising rule too. (3) The Arkansas Civil Rights Act declares a right to engage in property transactions free of discrimination because of race, religion, national origin, gender or disability, with a lawsuit for compensatory and punitive damages for intentional discrimination and no small-landlord exemption. Remedies: a complaint to the Fair Housing Commission within one year (civil penalties of up to $11,000 for a first violation, more for repeat violations, plus damages and fees), or a lawsuit within two years for compensatory and punitive damages and attorney's fees; after the Commission issues a charge, any party, including you as respondent, may elect to have the case decided in court within 20 days of service. It is also unlawful to retaliate against anyone who opposes discrimination or takes part in a complaint, or to intimidate someone because of a protected trait or because they rent a home. Arkansas fair housing law adds no classes beyond federal law except that the Civil Rights Act treats discrimination because of a natural, protective or cultural hairstyle as race or national origin discrimination; separately, Arkansas bars refusing to lease to or penalizing a registered medical marijuana patient or caregiver solely for that status, unless doing so would put you in violation of federal law or regulations, and bars ending, refusing or not renewing a tenancy because of documented domestic abuse (see those rows); source of income, age, marital status, sexual orientation and gender identity are not state-protected (federal law may differ). No Arkansas statute makes a landlord's sexual harassment of a tenant a separate crime (it is sex discrimination). The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Which Fire Code Applies
bodyText: Arkansas's statewide fire code is the Arkansas Fire Prevention Code, adopted by the State Fire Marshal. One Arkansas statute, in the security and alarm licensing chapter, defines it for that chapter as the International Fire Code, the International Building Code and the International Residential Code, as amended and adopted by the State Fire Marshal. It applies to rental buildings as it does to other buildings, and cities may add their own codes; Arkansas's implied quality standards expressly keep any stricter local housing standard in force. A few statutes speak to rentals directly: hotels, motels, apartment buildings and similar multiple-occupancy buildings with more than three floors above ground must have fire escape stairways or ladders and a fire alarm system meeting the Fire Prevention Code, and emergency lighting (failure is punishable by a fine of $250 to $1,000 for each day); a residential development outside cities and towns whose lots are each at least one acre does not have to maintain two separate fire apparatus access roads; and an owner's right to repair rental property does not limit state building codes and fire prevention standards that apply equally to owner-occupied and rental single-family homes. Which edition of the code applies, and how it treats existing buildings, is set by the Fire Marshal's adoption and by your city, so ask your local fire official before renovating or changing the use of a building. The rules apply whatever the tenancy type.

title: Fire Sprinklers: No Retrofit Statute
bodyText: No Arkansas statute requires a landlord to install fire sprinklers in an existing rental home or apartment building, or sets a sprinkler duty specific to rentals; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Sprinkler requirements, where they exist, come from the Arkansas Fire Prevention Code and local codes for new construction, additions and changes of use, so ask your local fire or building official before a renovation. If a building has a sprinkler system, keep it inspected and maintained as the fire code requires, and tell tenants not to hang things from, paint or cover sprinkler heads. The statutory rules for older multiple-occupancy buildings of more than three floors call for fire escapes, a fire alarm system and emergency lighting rather than sprinklers (see the fire code row). The rules apply whatever the tenancy type.

title: Foreign-Party Limits on Leasing Land
bodyText: Arkansas restricts certain foreign parties, and the restrictions can reach leases. (1) A business entity in which a "prohibited foreign party" owns a controlling interest (50% or more) may not acquire any interest in public or private land in Arkansas by purchase, lease or otherwise, and may not lease any interest in land. Prohibited foreign parties include citizens or residents (other than U.S. citizens) of countries subject to the federal International Traffic in Arms Regulations country list, those countries' governments and entities, entities they substantially control, and entities of particular concern designated by the U.S. State Department. (2) A prohibited foreign party, including an individual, may not acquire or hold any interest, including a lease, in agricultural or forest land, with an exception for resident aliens while they reside in Arkansas; separately, a prohibited foreign party may not hold any interest in agricultural land within ten miles of critical infrastructure (such as a military installation, utility, dam or railway), a rule the statute does not tie to the resident-alien exception. Violations are felonies for the foreign party and can lead to a court-ordered sale; your title is not invalidated by a former owner's violation. For an ordinary home lease to an individual, the business-entity rule does not apply and the agricultural-land rule applies only if the home is on agricultural land. The statutes say that a person not subject to them is not required to determine or inquire whether another person is subject to them, so you do not need to, and should not, ask applicants about citizenship or national origin; doing so risks a national-origin fair housing claim, and Arkansas's Constitution forbids legal distinctions between resident aliens and citizens in the possession and enjoyment of property. If the proposed tenant is a company, a corporate lease is where to confirm ownership. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Which Code Edition Applies
bodyText: A few Arkansas statutes that affect rentals tie a standard to a fixed date rather than to whatever edition is current. (1) Plumbing and sewer: the implied quality standard requires a sanitary sewer system and plumbing that conform to the building and housing codes in existence when they were installed, not today's code, so older plumbing that met the code of its day satisfies that standard. (2) Accessible design: for new multifamily buildings first occupied after February 1, 2004 (buildings of four or more units with an elevator, and ground-floor units in other four-plus-unit buildings), meeting the ANSI A117.1 accessibility standard as in effect on January 1, 2001 satisfies Arkansas's fair housing design rules. (3) Drug definitions in the fair housing law refer to the federal Controlled Substances Act as in effect on January 1, 2001. (4) Service dogs: the Arkansas right to be accompanied by a service dog in housing uses the federal Americans with Disabilities Act definition as it existed on January 1, 2017. Most other codes are not frozen in statute: the Arkansas Fire Prevention Code is adopted by the State Fire Marshal, and the electrical and other trade codes are set by their boards, which adopt newer editions over time. Local housing codes stricter than the state standards still apply. Ask your building official which edition governs a renovation. The rules apply whatever the tenancy type.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText:
Arkansas has no statute that bars, or expressly allows, passing to a tenant a fine or penalty a city, county or agency imposes on you as owner, and none limiting pass-through to fines the tenant caused. So it is a lease term like any other: you may require the tenant to reimburse a fine that results from the tenant's own conduct or that of the tenant's household or guests (for example a trash, noise, parking, animal or nuisance citation), but only if the lease says so (the library's optional clause does this).

Fines for conditions that are your responsibility, such as code violations from repairs you must make, stay with you; shifting them by lease would run into the rule that a lease cannot waive the landlord-tenant act's duties. Never charge a tenant for a penalty arising from a call to police or emergency help.

A fine reimbursement is not rent, so enforce it with a written notice giving at least 14 days to pay, or, if the deposit rules apply to you (they do not apply to an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units, unless a third person manages them for a fee), as an itemized deduction for damages from the tenant's noncompliance. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Waiving Arkansas's Quality Standards
bodyText: For leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or with a purchase right), a lease cannot waive Arkansas's implied quality standards, with one narrow exception. The six standards (available hot and cold running water and electricity, drinking water, code-conforming sewer and plumbing, a functioning roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning to the extent a system served the premises at signing) override any contrary lease term, and neither side may agree in a lease to give up the rights, duties or remedies of the landlord-tenant act. The exception: the standards do not override the lease if the tenant agrees in writing to take responsibility to renovate, remodel or complete the renovation, remodeling or construction of the unit; use it only for a genuine renovation arrangement, described in a separate signed writing. Arkansas has no rule letting a tenant accept a listed defect in exchange for lower rent, so do not offer one. The full explanation, including the force majeure excuse and the move-in defect form, is in the row on whether the lease can change the quality standards. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Immigration Status: No State Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that requires, forbids or limits asking rental applicants about immigration or citizenship status, and none that bars renting to a person unlawfully present or makes renting to one a crime; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. National origin is a protected class under Arkansas fair housing law, and Arkansas's Constitution forbids legal distinctions between resident aliens and citizens in the possession and enjoyment of property. The safe practice: do not ask about immigration status or citizenship; verify identity and ability to pay with documents any applicant can supply (for example, a passport, a foreign or consular ID or an individual taxpayer identification number as well as a Social Security number), and apply the same criteria to everyone. Arkansas's foreign-party land rules reach controlled business entities and agricultural land and say you need not inquire (see the foreign ownership row). The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Jury Waivers in Arkansas Leases
bodyText: Arkansas's Constitution guarantees the right to a jury trial in all cases at law and allows it to be waived by the parties only "in the manner prescribed by law". No Arkansas statute prescribes a lease clause as a way to waive it, and none addresses jury waivers in residential leases; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none (the only statutory ban on pre-signed jury waivers the search found is in motor-vehicle franchise law). Whether a court would enforce a jury waiver signed in a lease before any dispute is a case-law question, and the constitutional wording makes it doubtful. Arkansas's statute of frauds also makes an agreement that results in a waiver of a right protected by the Arkansas or United States Constitution unenforceable unless it is in writing and signed by the party giving up the right, so any waiver must at least be a signed writing. The library does not offer a jury-waiver clause for Arkansas; if a jury matters to you, waive it in the case itself, in the way the court rules provide. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Penalty for Including a Void Term
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that penalizes you simply for putting a prohibited term in a lease or for knowingly using a lease that contains one; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. The term itself is unenforceable: the implied quality standards override any contrary lease term, a lease may not waive the rights, duties or remedies of the landlord-tenant act, a tenant cannot waive the right to call police or emergency help, and a condition in a written instrument that limits use or occupancy because of a protected trait is void and may not be inserted. Money exposure comes when you act on a void term or break the underlying rule: for example, if the deposit rules apply to you (they do not apply to an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units, unless a third person manages them for a fee), wrongfully keeping a deposit costs the amount due plus twice the amount wrongfully withheld, costs and attorney's fees, unless you show a bona fide error despite reasonable procedures or a good-faith dispute; and fair housing violations carry damages and civil penalties. A tenant might also invoke the Deceptive Trade Practices Act; its text does not clearly say whether it reaches a home lease. The full list is in the prohibited lease terms row. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: What an Arkansas Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute listing what a residential lease must contain, no required lease form and no rule that a lease missing a term is invalid; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. A rental agreement may be written or oral and may include any terms not prohibited by the landlord-tenant act or other law. Where the lease is silent the statute fills in: rent is payable without demand or notice at the dwelling unit unless the tenant is told otherwise in writing, at the start of each month (or of each shorter term), and a tenancy with no definite term is week-to-week for a roomer who pays weekly and otherwise month-to-month. Some terms matter only if you include them, such as a lease method for the tenant's notices of defects (otherwise certified mail) and the optional move-in defect form. The disclosures that do apply (the federal lead paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing, among others) are listed in the required disclosures row. Write the lease so it states at least the parties, the property, the term, the rent and due date, the deposit, utilities, and notice addresses. The rules are the same for every tenancy type, except the default term rules above.

title: Landlord-Tenant Act Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Arkansas has one general non-waiver rule for residential leases. Except where the landlord-tenant act itself provides otherwise, neither the landlord nor the tenant may agree in a lease or rental agreement to waive or give up any of the rights, duties or remedies available under the act. Although the sentence sits in the implied quality standards section, it covers the whole act (notice and cure periods, termination notices, eviction procedure, access rules and remedies), not only the quality standards. The act's own exceptions are where it says a term applies "unless otherwise agreed" or lets the lease choose (for example, the use-only-as-a-dwelling rule, and the tenant's written agreement to take on renovation work). Separately, a tenant may not waive the right to call police or emergency help, and the deposit rules (which do not apply to an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units, unless a third person manages them for a fee) should be treated as non-waivable too (see the deposit non-waiver row). A waiver clause is unenforceable even if signed, so leave such clauses out. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: Arkansas has no plain-language law for residential leases: no readability standard, no requirement that a lease be divided into captioned sections or printed in a minimum type size, and no consumer-contract statute that reaches leases by a dollar ceiling; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Arkansas's Deceptive Trade Practices Act does make it unlawful to knowingly take advantage of a consumer who cannot reasonably protect his or her interest because of illiteracy or inability to understand the language of the agreement, but its text does not clearly say whether it reaches a home lease, and case law was not checked, so treat it as possibly applying. Write the lease in plain words with headings anyway, and explain unusual terms, fees and waivers to the tenant. The details are in the plain-language and consumer statement row. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Pools at Arkansas Rentals
bodyText: Arkansas regulates swimming pools through its health laws, and the definition of a public swimming pool there includes pools at apartment buildings, subdivisions, mobile home parks, motels and similar places that people may use with or without a charge. If your rental property has a shared pool, assume it is subject to the Department of Health's swimming pool rules, permits and fees, which deal with matters such as water quality, safety equipment and posted rules, and check them before opening the pool each season. Operating a public swimming pool requires an annual Department of Health permit, posted at the pool, and each day of operating in violation after notice is a separate offense with a fine of $50 to $500. A private pool at a single rented house is generally outside that definition, but local codes may still require a fence or barrier. No Arkansas statute requires a pool safety notice in the lease or a landlord-specific pool barrier duty; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Put pool rules (hours, no lifeguard, children supervised, no glass) in the lease or posted rules, and keep gates and covers in good repair. Remember that a lease promise to maintain a pool can create the repair duty that makes a landlord liable for injuries caused by disrepair. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Lease Terms Arkansas Law Voids or Limits
bodyText: Arkansas has no single list of prohibited lease provisions (it did not adopt the uniform act's prohibited-provisions section), so the limits are scattered. A residential lease may not: (1) waive or give up any right, duty or remedy of the landlord-tenant act, except where the act allows; (2) contradict the six implied quality standards in a lease entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021 (other than a lease to purchase or with a purchase right), unless the tenant agrees in writing to take on renovation work; (3) forbid the tenant from correctly installing a battery or plug-in smoke or carbon monoxide detector at the tenant's expense; (4) waive the tenant's right to call police or emergency help; (5) limit use or occupancy because of religion, race, color, national origin, sex, disability or familial status (such a term is void and may not be inserted); (6) charge a person with a disability an extra fee for a service animal (the handler remains liable for damage the animal causes); (7) prohibit a medical marijuana patient's use of medical marijuana by means other than smoking, or refuse to lease to someone solely for being a qualifying patient or caregiver, unless federal law requires it (you may ban smoking it); (8) prohibit proper display of the U.S. flag, unless you operate fewer than 12 rental units (you may still restrict a flag used as or with an advertising display); or (9) require a security deposit, however labeled, of more than two months' periodic rent, if the deposit rules apply to you (they do not apply to an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units, unless a third person manages them for a fee). Other terms are limited rather than void: a returned-check charge above Arkansas's $30 collection fee (plus bank fees) is not recoverable under the bad-check statute; an arbitration clause cannot reach injury or other tort claims under Arkansas's arbitration act; confession-of-judgment and pre-signed jury-waiver clauses are unlikely to be enforced; and large flat penalties may be unenforceable. Arkansas does not void exculpatory clauses by statute, late fees are not capped, and no penalty applies just for including a void term. Each item has its own row. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Questions About Protected Traits
bodyText: Arkansas fair housing law has no separate rule barring a landlord from asking rental applicants about, or keeping records of, race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status or national origin; its only inquiry-and-record rule applies to lenders' financing application forms. But the law does bar making, printing or publishing any notice or statement about renting a dwelling that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on those traits, and asking about them invites the inference that the answer was used. So keep protected traits off your application and out of interviews: do not ask about religion, national origin or citizenship, pregnancy or plans for children, marital status as a proxy for familial status, or whether an applicant has a disability or what it is. You may ask questions every applicant must answer about rental history, income, the number of occupants, and (where relevant) a requested accommodation or the disability-related need for an assistance animal when the disability is not obvious. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Severability and Void Terms
bodyText: Arkansas's landlord-tenant statutes knock out offending lease terms one at a time rather than voiding the whole lease: the implied quality standards supersede any contrary lease provision, a term waiving the act's rights, duties or remedies is unenforceable, and a discriminatory occupancy condition is void, while the rest of the lease stands. No Arkansas statute makes an entire residential lease void because it contains a prohibited term. A severability clause (the library's shared clause) is therefore consistent with Arkansas law, but it cannot save a term the law forbids, so leave such terms out rather than relying on severability. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Registered Sex Offenders as Tenants
bodyText: Arkansas puts residency limits on certain registered sex offenders, not on landlords. A registered sex offender assessed as Level 3 or Level 4 may not knowingly reside within 2,000 feet of the property of a public or private elementary or secondary school, public park, youth center or daycare facility, and a Level 4 offender also may not knowingly reside within 2,000 feet of a church or other place of worship; violation is a felony committed by the offender. No Arkansas statute requires a landlord to check the registry, refuse an offender, evict one, or include an offender statement in the lease, and none makes it a crime for a landlord to rent to two offenders who live together; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. You may screen for registered status as part of a written criminal-history policy applied the same way to every applicant (see the tenant screening row), and you are not required to tell other tenants that an offender lives nearby (see the sex offender information row). If you learn that a tenant's residence is unlawful under the 2,000-foot rule, the tenant's illegal occupancy can be a lease breach, but get legal advice before acting. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No State Limit on Renting in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that limits renting a home in a single-family zone, requires the owner to live on the lot, or caps the number of rentals in a neighborhood; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Two state laws limit what cities can do: a city may not require that the owner occupy either the main home or an accessory dwelling unit on the lot (and must allow one accessory unit by right), and an owner's statutory right to repair and maintain the owner's own premises yields only to building codes, fire standards, permit rules and nuisance abatement that do not distinguish between a primary residence and a single-family rental. Cities may still regulate short-term rentals (30 days or less), and zoning, subdivision covenants and HOA rules may restrict leasing; check them before you buy or rent out a home. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Steam Radiators: No Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring a landlord to install radiator covers or guards on steam or hot-water radiators, to offer them on request, or to add a radiator rider to the lease; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. If a unit has exposed steam radiators, especially where young children live, consider covers as a safety measure, and remember that the implied quality standards require a functioning heating system only to the extent one served the premises when the lease was signed. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute setting a minimum or maximum water heater temperature for rentals or requiring you to reset a unit's water heater before each new tenant; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. The implied quality standard requires only an available source of hot and cold running water. To reduce scald risk, set tank water heaters to about 120 degrees Fahrenheit at turnover, make sure the temperature and pressure relief valve is working, and tell tenants not to raise the setting. Plumbing code and local housing codes may set requirements. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Window Guard Requirement
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute requiring window guards, window stops or other fall-prevention devices in rentals, or a window-guard notice in the lease; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Where young children live above the ground floor, consider window stops that limit openings to about four inches, keep furniture away from windows, and remember that any guard must still let windows serve as emergency exits where the fire code requires. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Veterans Rental Incentive
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute giving landlords a tax credit, deposit guarantee or other incentive for renting to veterans, and no state rule requiring or forbidding a preference for veterans; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Veteran and military status are not protected classes under Arkansas fair housing law, but a preference for veterans must not be used to screen out people for a protected trait such as disability or familial status. Servicemembers on active duty have lease-termination and eviction-stay rights under Arkansas's soldiers' and airmen's law and the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (see the servicemember rights row). The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Voucher Program Inspections
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute on housing choice voucher (Section 8) inspections: nothing lets a landlord refuse or delay a program inspection, sets inspection deadlines for a housing authority, or lets a landlord treat a failed or late inspection as a reason to reject a voucher holder; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. Because Arkansas does not require you to accept vouchers (see the source of income row), participation is your choice; if you do take part, the housing assistance payments contract and federal program rules control inspections, rent abatement for failed inspections and repairs. Give the tenant the notice of entry your lease requires before an inspection; Arkansas sets no statutory entry-notice period, and a tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry for inspections. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Sharing Tenant Information
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute that bars a residential landlord from disclosing information about a tenant or applicant (such as rental history, payment records or contact details) or that requires the tenant's consent before you share it; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. The only landlord-type rule found is for self-storage operators disposing of an occupant's personal information. Arkansas's Personal Information Protection Act does require a business that holds Arkansas residents' personal information to use reasonable security procedures (see the rent records and tenant data row). Good practice: share tenant information only to run the tenancy (with your manager, vendors who need it, a court, or a prospective landlord or lender when the tenant authorizes it in writing), answer reference requests with facts you can document, keep Social Security, bank and ID numbers secure, and dispose of records securely. Federal consumer-report rules apply if you use or furnish screening reports. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Housing for Your Employees
bodyText:
Arkansas's Residential Landlord-Tenant Act of 2007 does not govern occupancy by an employee of the landlord whose right to occupy is conditional on employment in and about the premises, such as a resident manager or maintenance worker living on site as part of the job. For that arrangement the act's rules (its notice and cure periods, termination notices, implied quality standards and district-court eviction procedure) do not apply; the occupancy ends as the employment agreement provides, and if the former employee will not leave, you recover possession through unlawful detainer after a written demand for possession or at the end of the agreed period.

No Arkansas statute requires a separate disclosure of the occupancy terms, a grace period to move out, or an offer of a regular lease when the job ends. The exclusion turns on the occupancy being conditional on the job, so say so in writing (the optional employee housing clause does this). If the employee pays market rent and the home is not tied to the job, treat it as an ordinary tenancy under the act.

The security deposit rules have no employee exclusion, so if they apply to you (they do not apply to an individual who, with spouse, minor children and their rental entities, owns five or fewer units, unless a third person manages them for a fee), any deposit you take follows them. The rules are the same whether the arrangement is periodic or for a fixed term.

title: Tenant Organizing: No State Right
bodyText: Arkansas has no statute giving tenants a right to form or join a tenants' association or union, to meet in common areas, or to distribute materials, and no statute barring retaliation against tenants for organizing; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. The specific retaliation bans Arkansas does have protect domestic-abuse victims, occupants after a lead-hazard notice, and anyone who opposes housing discrimination or takes part in a fair housing complaint (see the retaliation row), so action against tenants who organize to oppose discrimination is covered. Even where no rule applies, acting against organizers invites claims; apply your rules on common-area use, signs and solicitation neutrally to every resident. Federal rules for subsidized housing may protect tenant organizing. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Screening Applicants in Arkansas
bodyText: Arkansas has no tenant-screening statute: no limit on look-back periods for criminal history, no rule that criminal history be checked only after a conditional offer, no cap on income multiples, no duty to give written reasons for a denial under state law, and no statutory shield from negligence claims for renting to someone with a record; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. What does apply: (1) fair housing law, so use written criteria applied the same way to every applicant, and avoid blanket policies that screen out a protected group without a real justification; Arkansas expressly allows refusing someone convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance. (2) Sealed records: once an Arkansas record is sealed, the conduct is treated by law as never having occurred and the applicant may lawfully say it did not occur, so do not treat that answer as a lie or deny an applicant for a sealed record you learn of (the library's application accuracy clause carries this). (3) Medical marijuana: you may not refuse to lease to someone solely because the person is a qualifying patient or designated caregiver, unless that would violate federal law (for example, in some federally assisted housing). (4) Application fees: cities and counties may not cap them; the amount is up to you, but disclose it and what it covers. Federal law also applies: the Fair Credit Reporting Act's permissible-purpose, adverse-action notice and disposal rules for consumer reports. Arkansas's credit freeze law does not apply to consumer reporting agency files used for tenant background screening. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: No Unconscionability Statute for Home Leases
bodyText: Arkansas did not adopt the uniform landlord-tenant act's unconscionability section, and no Arkansas statute lets a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable term in a lease of a home; a search of the Arkansas Code and Constitution found none. The statutory unconscionability rule Arkansas does have is in the Uniform Commercial Code article on leases of goods (cars, equipment, furniture rentals), not real property. Two other routes remain: the Deceptive Trade Practices Act lists "unconscionable" acts in business or trade among its prohibited practices, though its text does not clearly say whether it reaches home leases, and courts may refuse to enforce an unconscionable contract term under general contract law. Keep terms balanced, especially fees, penalties, waivers and one-sided remedies, and leave out terms the landlord-tenant act forbids. The rule is the same for every tenancy type.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Farmland
bodyText: If you rent a home together with farmland, Arkansas law keeps the right to hunt or fish on the farmland, and to let others hunt or fish there, with you as owner: the tenant has no hunting or fishing right on leased or rented farmland unless you grant it expressly in writing. You keep the right to cross the farmland, use its water and put up blinds, docks and similar structures for hunting and fishing, and to grant those rights to others, even while it is leased. If you want the tenant to be able to hunt or fish, say so in the lease or a signed writing and describe any limits; if you will keep using the land for hunting or let others do so, tell the tenant in the lease where and when, since you will be crossing land the tenant occupies. The rule is the same for every type of tenancy. It does not apply to a home rented without farmland.

title: Time Limit to Sue for Rent or Damages
bodyText: Arkansas sets general time limits for lawsuits that also reach a landlord's claims for unpaid rent or damage. A suit to enforce a written obligation, such as a written lease, must be filed within five years after the claim arises, and a partial payment or a written acknowledgment of default tolls that five-year period. A suit for rent not reserved by a written instrument under seal, and suits on unwritten contracts, must be filed within three years. Which period a court applies to rent under a written lease that is not under seal is a case-law question, so the cautious course is to treat three years as your deadline for every rent or damage claim, written lease or not. The limits are the same for week-to-week, month-to-month and fixed-term tenancies; for a periodic tenancy each unpaid installment starts its own clock.

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property
bodyText: Arkansas's criminal trespass law makes it a crime to purposely enter or remain unlawfully on premises owned or leased by another person, but it is a defense that the person was a guest or invitee, was there for a business or health and safety reason, was authorized by law, or that the privately owned premises were open to the public. So to keep a non-tenant (a former tenant, a troublemaker, a tenant's ex) out of parking lots, hallways and other common areas, give that person a written notice that he or she may not enter the property, keep a copy, and tell police you have done so. A person a tenant invites into the tenant's own unit is the tenant's guest, so a ban there is enforced against the tenant through the lease (the guest and occupant rules and the 14-day notice for a lease violation), not by trespass. A person harmed by a criminal trespass may also sue for actual damages, attorney's fees and punitive damages. The rules are the same for every tenancy type.

title: Empty Mobile Home on a Rented Lot
bodyText: If you rent a lot or site where someone else's manufactured or mobile home sits, and the home is unoccupied (no one is living in it) while the lot rent is 60 days or more past due, you must notify the lessee and, if someone other than the lessee or occupant holds a lien on the home, the lienholder. Send the notice in writing by certified mail and include, if known or readily available: your name and mailing address; the lessee's name and last known mailing address; the lienholder's name and mailing address; the home's street address or location; the monthly lot rent; the home's serial number; and its make, model, year, dimensions and identification marks. Tell the lienholder that unless the home is removed within 30 days after the lienholder receives the notice, the home will be subject to a lien in your favor for lot rent from the date the lienholder received it. If the lienholder does not remove it in 30 days (and is not prevented by law), the home is subject to that lien at the monthly rent stated in your notice. The lienholder never owes rent from before the notice, and the lessee stays liable for all unpaid rent. Whether the 2007 landlord-tenant act covers a lot lease under a tenant-owned home is unsettled (its dwelling-unit definition names landlord-owned mobile homes), so use the unlawful detainer route to recover the lot.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Arkansas follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Ark. Code Ann. § 4-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Ark. Code Ann. § 4-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Arkansas's landlord-tenant act imposes a duty of good faith: every duty under the chapter, and every act that must be done before using a right or remedy under it, carries an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement (Ark. Code Ann. § 18-17-302). That binds you and the tenant alike. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: No Communal or Tribal Land Lease Approval
bodyText: Arkansas has no communal, tribal or native land system, and no Arkansas statute requires a government officer to approve a residential lease, or voids it, because of how the land is held. A search of the whole Arkansas Code for tribal, tribe, Indian nation and Indian land near lease, lessee or rent found no such rule. If land is held in trust by the United States for a tribe or a tribal member, federal law, not searched here, governs its leasing.

title: Recording a Lease Is Optional
bodyText: No Arkansas statute requires you to record a residential lease or register it with a state or local office; a whole-Code search for leases near recording found only an oil and gas rule. Recording matters for priority. An instrument by which the title to real estate may be affected is not good against a later buyer for value without actual notice, or against a creditor of the person who signed it who gets a judgment lien, unless it is filed for record with the clerk and ex officio recorder of the county where the property is (Ark. Code Ann. § 14-15-404(b)). An instrument affecting title that the law requires to be acknowledged and recorded is constructive notice to everyone from the time it is filed for record (Ark. Code Ann. § 14-15-404(a)(1)). Whether a residential lease is such an instrument, and whether a tenant's possession gives a buyer notice, are questions of case law. For a long lease, the cautious course is to have it acknowledged and record it, and to tell any buyer or lender about it in writing.

title: No Special District Statement Required
bodyText: Arkansas has many improvement districts, but no Arkansas statute requires a residential lease to say that the property is in one, requires you to tell a tenant about district assessments, or gives a tenant a vote or seat because the tenant rents there. A whole-Code search for districts near tenant or lessee and assessment, tax or notice, and for improvement districts near tenant, lessee or lease, found only statutes letting districts lease or sell their own property and similar powers. If your lease passes any district assessment to the tenant, state the amount or the method in the lease.

title: Renting to Students
bodyText: No Arkansas statute sets special rules for renting a house or apartment to students: no student-housing license, no rule on academic-year leases or parent guarantors, and no dormitory exemption, since Arkansas has no rent-cap or just-cause eviction law to be exempt from. A whole-Code search for student, student housing, dormitory and residence hall near landlord, lessor, tenant, lessee, lease or rent found only a military-base canteen statute. A student renting from you is an ordinary tenant under Arkansas's general landlord-tenant law, and the same lease applies.
